blocks.text: “Qubic is doomed to succeed. Aigarth? Depends on miners.”
The story of Qubic begins long before Bitcoin and contains many vivid stages. To study the path that the visionary Come-from-Beyond lays beneath his own feet is genuinely interesting.

My father spent a significant amount of time studying this subject and, being a master of religious studies, looked at Qubic on a somewhat larger scale than is customary. The main challenge for the ordinary person who today takes an interest in Qubic is to grasp the scale, the structure, the functions, and the meaning of every detail of a large mechanism. Believe me, this is a whole universe with a rich history and many secrets we’ll be uncovering over time. Come-from-Beyond, like an ancient artist, is painting a large picture. Elements that seem unconnected gradually begin to fuse and take shape.
This book does one simple thing: it gathers what’s been scattered into a single fresco, structures it, and presents it in plain language.

Who should read this? Anyone who’s even a little connected to Qubic will find something here for themselves. A newcomer will learn the basic principles of how it works and see connections where they didn’t see them before. An experienced holder can enjoy the history and the beautiful allegories my father’s speech is so full of. The professional and the master can take a look at the overall picture from the outside and, perhaps, see something they used to miss.

All Cfb quotes used in this book are taken verbatim from open primary sources — the official Qubic Discord, his publications on X, the team’s scientific papers. All of them appear in our book. If you spot an inaccuracy — write in. The book is alive; the next edition will incorporate corrections. A caveat is in order: Come-from-Beyond’s style is a wild ride on a motorcycle off-road. In the Qubic universe, you rarely find information laid out in a structured way. That’s why we believe this book will be a pleasant addition to every Qubic holder’s library. The book is distributed absolutely freely. The best thanks for us would be your appraisal, your criticism, your remarks. P A r T i The Problem
Useful waste.
There’s a kind of thing you learn to see one day — and then you wonder how you didn’t notice it before. One of those things is the difference between work and its waste.

Take any furnace. Something burns inside it, something gets heated, and the desired product comes out. But besides the product, there’s always something else left over. Smoke. Steam. Smell. Noise. Heat going off into the walls. For centuries people treated those leftovers as garbage — the inevitable companion of useful work, something that had to be disposed of somehow or simply released into the air.
Sometimes a person comes along who looks at this garbage more attentively than the rest. And asks a strange question: what if we don’t release it?

This whole book is about a question of that kind, asked with respect to one particular kind of garbage. But to understand why this question matters, we first have to tell two old stories — about coal, and about the man who figured out how to light cities with it.
Both happened in England.
1709. Coalbrookdale

In the west of England, in the county of Shropshire, there is a valley with the river Severn flowing along its floor. The place is green, hilly, not particularly remarkable. In the early eighteenth century, a man named Abraham Darby moved there — he was in his thirty-second year, he was a Quaker, and he already had a notable record in industry behind him.

Quaker — that’s an important detail, even if at first glance not the flashiest. The Society of “Friends” (as the Quakers called themselves) in the England of that time was a community whose members did not wear military uniforms, did not swear oaths in court, avoided ostentatious luxury, and took honesty in their dealings very seriously. Quaker dynasties of craftsmen were famous for the fact that their products weren’t counterfeited and their prices weren’t inflated. Darby was part of such a dynasty — and grew up inside an ethic in which reputation was worth more than momentary profit. This detail is worth remembering: we’ll come back to it when we talk about Bitcoin. Darby had a problem, and it was common to all of English metallurgy at the time. Cast iron was smelted using charcoal — specially charred wood that burns hotter than ordinary firewood. But by 1700 England had cut down most of its forests. Charcoal was getting more expensive, there was less and less of it, and foundries were closing one after another. A country that depended on iron for everything — from plows to cannons — found itself facing what today would be called a resource crisis.

Coal in England did exist. There was plenty of it. But cast iron couldn’t be smelted with it — sulfur and other impurities ruined the metal. Iron made on coal came out brittle, unfit for serious work.

Here it’s worth saying how Darby arrived at his solution, because this wasn’t the feat of a lone genius. Darby had spent several years before that working in the copper industry in Bristol, and before that he had apprenticed with a Quaker who made malt kilns for brewing. In both copper smelting and malt production, the technique of heating coal without access to air had already been used — out came coke, a fuel without sulfur, which burned cleanly and steadily. In copper smelting it worked well. In iron smelting, no one had tried it systematically before Darby.

Darby did two things. The first — he transferred a known technological technique from one industry to another. The second — he came to Coalbrookdale, where at hand he had at the same time low-sulfur coal, deposits of iron ore not far below the surface, and a fast river to power the bellows. By January 1709 he produced his first commercial cast iron, smelted on coke.

No one wrote down Darby’s exact words when he first saw the finished casting from the coke furnace. But the consequences of that moment rewrote the next two hundred years of world history. Bridges. Railways. Steamships. The frames of skyscrapers. Tanks. Engines. All the iron of industrial civilization — from the first cast-iron beam to the last rail of the Trans-Siberian — traces back to the fact that an experienced Quaker copperindustrialist guessed that a technique that works in one production can be transferred to another, where no one had yet tried it.
That’s the first story.
1792. Cornwall

More than eighty years after Darby, on the other side of England, an engineer by the name of William Murdoch was at work — a Scotsman, the son of a small farmer, by then thirty-seven years old. He served at the company Boulton & Watt — the very one that built James Watt’s steam engines. Murdoch had been sent to Cornwall to look after the engines installed at the tin mines.
He lived in the small town of Redruth, in a small house. And here’s what Murdoch noticed one day.

When you make coke — that same coke that Darby learned to produce eighty years earlier — a great deal comes out of the coal during heating. The coke stays in the furnace. And outside, into the air, a thick combustible gas escapes. It smells of sulfur and burning, looks like a dirty cloud, and everyone who worked with coke furnaces fought with this gas: it’s poisonous, sometimes it explodes, and it stinks up the whole neighborhood. People tried to dissipate it, lead it away, so it wouldn’t get in the way. Murdoch collected this gas into a pipe.

In 1792 he began his experiments. By 1794 he had a working system: in an iron retort in his back yard he heated coal, the gas went through a pipe into the house, and at the end of the pipe stood a simple burner. The first pipe for the gas line was an old gun barrel. He lit it — and got a clean bright flame, without smoke, without soot, much brighter than candles or oil lamps. On an evening in 1794, Murdoch sat in his living room in Redruth by the light of what everyone else considered garbage.
What happens next is a curious thing that comes up in the history of technology more often than people tend to think.

Murdoch invented the system. But he was not the one who commercialized it. In 1802, when the Peace of Amiens was being celebrated, Murdoch managed to convince the management of Boulton & Watt to put on a public demonstration — and that evening the facade of the Soho Foundry in Birmingham was lit by gas. The town came running to look. It was a triumph. But Murdoch, as his contemporaries wrote, “by character kept to the shadows,” and his employers were in no hurry to patent the discovery. Meanwhile another man, Frederick Albert Winsor — a German by origin who had moved to London — had read a paper by the Frenchman Lebon on combustible gas, saw the potential, and began giving lectures at the Lyceum Theatre in London. Winsor was a brilliant promoter and a poor engineer. Contemporaries wrote that “he knew almost nothing of chemistry and was so incompetent in mechanics that he could not give instructions for the building of apparatus.” But he knew how to convince investors and how to gather a crowd.

In January 1807 it was Winsor, not Murdoch, who lit the world’s first gas streetlamps — on Pall Mall in London. By the fourth of June that same year, on the birthday of King George III, he put on a whole show: along the wall between Mall street and the gardens of Carlton House, thirty-two gas burners lit up, connected by a thin tin tube. The crowd stood there until midnight.

The first industrial factory lit entirely by gas — the Phillips & Lee mill in Manchester — was put into service by Murdoch’s hand only in 1805–1806. By that time Winsor was already drafting an act to create the world’s first gas company. By the 1820s, forty thousand gas streetlamps were burning in London. By the middle of the century, gas lighting stood across the entire Western world.

Murdoch did not patent his discovery and died in 1839 a respected engineer, known in narrow circles. The name “father of gas lighting” stayed with him in the history of technology, but the commercial empire was built by a man who didn’t invent the technology — he sold it. This split between the inventor and the one who carries the invention to a mass market is a pattern we’ll meet in this book more than once. That’s the second story.
What they have in common
Pay attention to the structure.

Darby didn’t invent coal. Coal had been mined in England for centuries before him. Darby didn’t invent the technique of coking either — it was already in use in copper smelting and in brewing. Darby transferred a known technology from one industry to another, where no one had tried it systematically before. Before him, coal in metallurgy was useless. After him, coal became the foundation of industry.

Murdoch didn’t invent combustible gas. Gas had been coming out of coke furnaces from the very moment Darby first lit a furnace in 1709. For eighty-three years the gas went up into the sky over England, and nobody paid any attention. Murdoch didn’t create a new resource — he saw value in what everyone else was throwing away. And one more detail, which may seem unimportant for now but later turns out to be key. Neither Darby nor Murdoch destroyed what came before them. Charcoal kept being produced and used long after Darby. Oil lamps and candles kept burning long after gas lighting became available. The new technology didn’t replace the old by decree from above. It simply began to work in parallel — and people gradually crossed over when they saw it was more advantageous for them.
In parallel, not instead.
Remember that phrase.
How this relates to Bitcoin
Now let’s look at our own time.

In 2008 a person (or group of people) under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto published a nine-page document describing a way to create digital money without a bank in the middle. A few months later, in January 2009, he launched a system called Bitcoin. The fundamental difficulty Satoshi solved was known in computer science as “the double-spending problem”: how to make sure that a digital file — money — can’t be copied and spent twice, without a central arbitrator watching the accounts. The solution was elegant. All participants in the network jointly maintain a ledger in which transactions are recorded. Each page of this ledger is protected by a mathematical problem that’s very expensive to solve — you have to spend a colossal amount of electricity and computation. Whoever solves the problem first is rewarded with new bitcoins. And since the solution takes enormous resources, rewriting pages that have already been recorded becomes practically impossible: you’d have to outspend the entire network. This mechanism is called Proof-of-Work.

This was a discovery of the Darby class. Before Satoshi, it was thought that digital money without an intermediary was in principle impossible. After Satoshi, it exists, has been working for its sixteenth year, is more strongly protected than any bank vault in the world, and has a market capitalization larger than the GDP of most countries. But this solution has one feature that few people pay attention to. The mathematical problems that Bitcoin’s miners solve are, in themselves, meaningless. A miner takes a list of transactions, adds a random number to it, runs it through a cryptographic function, and looks at whether the result has enough zeros at the beginning. If not — he adds another random number, runs it through again, checks again. And so on, billions of times per second, until he gets lucky. All the energy that gets spent in that moment — and as of 2026 that’s about 170 terawatt-hours a year, roughly as much as Poland or Ukraine consumes — goes into one thing: picking a random number that meets the condition.
There’s no by-product benefit from this picking. No one uses the results of these computations. No one needs them, except the network itself.
Bitcoin is Darby. The first great discovery of its class.
And what comes out into the air around Bitcoin — billions of computational cycles that nobody needs — is Murdoch’s gas of 2009, which no one has yet collected into a pipe.
What exactly comes out into the air

It’s worth saying more concretely what kind of “gas” is being talked about. The modern Bitcoin network consists of hundreds of thousands of specialized devices — ASIC miners. These are computers sharpened for one single operation: hashing using the SHA-256 algorithm. They can do nothing else, and nothing else is required of them. Each such device makes trillions of attempts per second to pick the necessary number.

If you add up all the work of all the miners in the world, you get computing power comparable to the combined power of all the supercomputers in the planet’s research centers, multiplied by thousands. This is one of the largest computational resources humanity has ever assembled into a single structure.
And this entire resource is spent on one action: picking random numbers to fit a hash condition.

Imagine you have a million highly educated specialists — scientists, engineers, doctors, architects — and you make them spend the whole day flipping a coin and writing down whether it came up heads or tails. They handle the task excellently, the coin really is being flipped, the results really are being written down. But all their education, their experience, their abilities — go unused. Each of them could, in the same time, write a scientific paper, design a bridge, treat ten patients, solve a hard engineering problem. Instead — the coin.

Roughly that’s what’s happening in Bitcoin. Computing power that could be solving real problems — training AI models, modeling the climate, searching for new medicines — is directed at picking random numbers.

Does it protect the network? Yes. Does it work? Yes. Is there a structural flaw in this? Absolutely. And this flaw is not Satoshi’s mistake, just as the abundant gas from the coke furnaces wasn’t Darby’s mistake. It’s simply a consequence of the fact that the first great discovery rarely notices its own by-products.
Under the hood. GHash.IO, summer 2014
There’s one episode from the early history of Bitcoin that’s useful to break down — because it foreshadows much of what will happen later in this book.

In 2013–2014, the largest mining pool in Bitcoin became GHash.IO. A pool is an association of miners who put their computations together and split the reward in proportion to contribution. GHash.IO grew quickly. In January 2014 its share approached 50 percent, the community panicked, some of the miners voluntarily left, and the share temporarily decreased. But in summer everything repeated in a far more serious form. From eleven o’clock in the morning of June twelfth to ten o’clock in the morning of June thirteenth, 2014 — for nearly twenty-four hours straight — GHash.IO held approximately 55 percent of Bitcoin’s total hashrate. Not 51. Fifty-five.

For Bitcoin, this is a catastrophic figure. If a single participant controls more than half of the network’s computing power, he can theoretically rewrite the history of transactions in his own interests, double-spend the same coins, block someone’s transfers. The network ceases to be decentralized at the moment majority control appears. People expected an attack. They expected exploitation. They expected the end of the decentralized era.
Nothing happened.

Here’s what happened. The pool’s owner, the exchange CEX.IO, published a statement saying it had no intention of attacking the network. The key Bitcoin developers, academic researchers, and large holders simultaneously began a pressure campaign: miners were urged to leave GHash.IO for other pools, CEX.IO’s reputation was publicly dissected in the press, the price of bitcoin sank by about five percent over the course of a few hours. On July ninth, 2014, a roundtable was held in London with representatives of all the major mining pools and equipment manufacturers. At that roundtable it was proposed that GHash.IO voluntarily limit its share with a ceiling of 39.99 percent. On July sixteenth the pool publicly agreed to this restriction and called on the other pools to do the same. GHash.IO’s share began to decline. By the end of summer it had fallen to thirty-five percent. By 2016 the pool had closed.
Why didn’t a pool that held the technical ability to destroy Bitcoin in its hands use that ability?
The official answer: reputation, trust, long-term interests. Breaking the network you yourself earn from is irrational.

That’s the right answer. But it’s not the full one. Because “breaking the network you yourself earn from is irrational” is not a self-evident truth. It’s the consequence of very specific structural conditions. What exactly has to be set up so that such behavior becomes irrational? Why does it work in some systems and not in others? Why did community pressure in July 2014 work — while in other cases, with other networks, pressure doesn’t work and attacks happen?

These questions were answered in 1980 by a political scientist from Michigan. His name was Robert Axelrod, and what he discovered explains not only the behavior of GHash.IO but almost everything this book is about.
But that’s for the next chapter.
The promise we begin with

Before we close the chapter, allow me to formulate what awaits us further. The story of coal, which I began to tell, is in fact longer than two scenes — Darby and Murdoch. It consists of five phases, each of which was opened by its own person, and each of which made what had previously been considered waste into the main product of the next industry.
At first, coal was simply burned for heat — and was considered a poor fuel, because it stinks.

Then Darby transferred the coking technique from copper smelting to iron — and everything that came out during the production of coke was considered garbage. Then Murdoch collected the gas — and everything that was left over from the production of gas was considered garbage.

Then in 1856 an eighteen-year-old chemist named William Perkin, trying to synthesize a malaria drug, accidentally discovered that synthetic dyes could be made out of this “garbage” — and on those grew the entire chemical industry of the twentieth century. Aspirin, the first plastics, the first antibiotics, the first polymers — all out of what had been considered the waste of gas production.

And in the end, by the middle of the twentieth century, coal stopped being called fuel. People began to call it feedstock — raw material. From one and the same coal they learned to extract simultaneously coke, gas, tar, sulfur, ammonia, and dozens of chemical compounds. Each output went into its own industry. The heat from burning the leftovers became the cheapest and least valuable result.

What happened to coal is what’s now beginning to happen, with us, to computation. Bitcoin in this story plays the role of Darby’s coke — the first structural breakthrough that showed that compute can be turned into something valuable (the protection of digital money). It was a discovery of historic scale, and we’ll be unpacking its consequences in this book more than once. But just like coke in 1709, Bitcoin uses its resource one-dimensionally: compute turns into hashes, hashes turn into security, all the rest goes off into the air. For three hundred years humanity has been learning to see that around the main operation — coke, iron, hashes — there are streams that are considered garbage only until the person comes along who looks at them. The Murdoch step — when people start collecting what until now they’ve been throwing away — falls, in digital history, on 2022. That is Qubic. And it’s one of those engineering ideas about which people later write “how did no one do this earlier” — it’s that logical in hindsight and that radical at the moment of appearance. Because Qubic doesn’t try to compete with Bitcoin on Bitcoin’s own field. It makes a move that didn’t exist on this field at all. What exactly Qubic “collects into a pipe,” how it’s set up technically, and why it works — is the main subject of this book. We’ll get to it gradually, chapter by chapter, because explaining it fast is impossible: the idea looks simple only after all the layers under it have been broken down.

And then — if everything goes as planned by the people who are building Qubic — what awaits us is the third step. The same one that happened to coal in the twentieth century, when it ceased to be “fuel” and came to be called feedstock, raw material for dozens of industries at once. If Qubic delivers what it promises, computation will pass into the same kind of state: out of one and the same compute cycle, security, artificial intelligence, economic value, and several more things we don’t yet know how to formulate today will be extracted simultaneously. This is an ambition of roughly the same scale as Darby’s in 1709 — and how exactly it’s implemented, we’ll see in this book down to the last screw.
The main thing — this step has not yet been made. It’s planned for April 2027. And we’ll honestly see whether it works.

This book is a map between the phases. It will not move linearly, because the story of Qubic itself didn’t move linearly: it was made by different people, in different places, solving different tasks, and only afterwards did it become visible how those tasks add up into one big task.

But before we move on to the Coalbrookdale of the digital age, we have to deal with one simple truth. This truth Murdoch knew intuitively in 1792, and Abraham Darby — did not. Without it, gas lighting would never have become an industry. Without it, Bitcoin would have stopped at hashes. Without it, Qubic wouldn’t work for a single day. This truth is formulated in four lines of code.
It was proven in 1980, in a tournament that fourteen programs took part in.

In June 2014, one person (more precisely, one exchange) had in its hands, for twentyfour hours, the technical capacity to destroy Bitcoin. He didn’t destroy it. The standard explanation — “it’s irrational to break the network you earn from” — is correct, but it doesn’t explain why it’s irrational. Because there are networks where breaking is profitable. There are situations where people destroy what they earn from. There are countries where elites kill the country they rule. There are relationships where partners methodically annihilate each other. Irrational? Yes. Happens all the time. So the question isn’t why GHash.IO didn’t attack. The question is: under what conditions does honest behavior become rational and cheating — not.

This turned out to be a concrete, technical, verifiable question. And the answer to it was first found not by a philosopher and not by an economist. It was found by a thirtyeight-year-old political scientist who in 1977 was sitting in his office at the University of Michigan, watching computer programs play chess.

This chapter is about what he eventually figured out. But to understand why his discovery matters for Qubic, Bitcoin, and everything we’ll be talking about later, we have to first break down one very simple game.
The Prisoner’s Dilemma

Imagine that you and your accomplice have been caught. There isn’t much evidence on either of you — they can solidly prove only a minor crime, for which each of you will get a year. But the investigators suspect you pulled off something big together, and they want to prove it.
You’ve been split up into separate cells. An investigator comes to each of you and offers a deal.

“Listen. If your accomplice keeps quiet, and you give testimony against him — he goes down for five years, and you walk free. If you both give testimony — you both go down, but you get not five but three years each. If you both keep quiet — we won’t be able to prove the major crime, and each of you only gets a year for the minor one.” You sit in your cell and think.
If my accomplice keeps quiet — it pays for me to give him up. I walk, he goes down. If my accomplice gives me up — it also pays for me to give him up. I’ll get three years instead of five.

Any variant of his behavior leads to one conclusion: it pays me to give him up. The accomplice in the next cell over is thinking the same thing. And he too arrives at the conclusion: it pays for him to give me up.
In the end, you both give each other up and you each get three years. If you’d both kept quiet, you’d each have gotten a year.

That’s the Prisoner’s Dilemma. In its pure form, it looks like this: there are two participants, each can choose to “cooperate” (keep quiet) or “defect” (give up). The payoffs are arranged so that the individually rational choice is always to defect, but when both do it, both lose.

The game isn’t complicated. They came up with it in 1950 at the RAND Corporation — two mathematicians, Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher, were trying to come up with an example that would stump the rational-behavior theories of the day. Their colleague Albert Tucker formalized it and gave it the story about the two prisoners, in which we know it.

Since then — for seventy years — this game has become one of the most studied objects in the humanities and social sciences. Because it turned out to be everywhere. Arms race — Prisoner’s Dilemma. It pays each country to build more weapons than the neighbor. But when everyone builds — everyone is worse off.
Tax evasion — Prisoner’s Dilemma. It pays each person not to pay. But when nobody pays — the state stops working.

Pollution of the environment — Prisoner’s Dilemma. It pays each factory to dump its waste in the river. But when everyone dumps — there’s no river left for anyone. Corruption, cartel collusion, overfishing, traffic jams, harvesting on common fields — everywhere the same structure. And everywhere — the same result: each person’s rational choice leads to a bad result for all.

John Nash, a mathematician from Princeton, in 1950 proved one unpleasant thing about this game and got a Nobel Prize for it. He showed that “both defect” is an equilibrium. Meaning: if you’re both in this state, neither of you benefits from a unilateral change of strategy. If my accomplice gives me up, and I decide to keep quiet — I lose. If I give him up, and my accomplice keeps quiet — he loses. Both giving up — stable. Not good. But stable.
The Nash equilibrium. The system stuck in a bad but durable state.
That was the diagnosis. The trap was described. Whether you could get out of it — for a long time there was no answer to that question.
Michigan, March 1980

Robert Axelrod was the name of the man I mentioned at the beginning of the chapter. By 1977 he had been teaching at the University of Michigan for six years, had defended his PhD at Yale in political science in 1969, specialized in conflicts between states. Forty years old, son of Lithuanian Jews, he had spent his whole life on the question of how people manage to come to agreement at all.

Axelrod had a whole closet’s worth of papers on the Prisoner’s Dilemma. He’d read them all and was unhappy with them. The papers were mostly trying to prove one of two things: either that people in real life are “irrational” and cooperate contrary to theory, or that you have to change the payoff matrix — add a tax on defection, an outside arbitrator, something like that. Neither explanation satisfied him. He was interested in a concrete question. The game was run once — the rational move is to defect. Fine. But what if you run it many times? If two participants know they’ll be playing each other not for one round but for two hundred? Will that change anything?

Intuition suggested it should. If I defect now, and we’re going to play another one hundred and ninety-nine rounds, my accomplice will have many opportunities to take revenge on me. He’ll stop cooperating too. We’ll both get little. Most likely it’ll be more profitable to cooperate from the very start.

But how exactly? Which strategy in the iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma is the most profitable? The intuition wouldn’t formalize. Different theorists proposed different strategies — some complex, others simple — and no one could convincingly show whose was best.

Axelrod was at the time following computer chess tournaments. By the late seventies, chess programs had begun outplaying each other — and you could see that victory belonged to whoever had written the most complex, deep, multi-tiered algorithms. The programs were getting longer, smarter, more cunning.
And then a thought occurred to him.

What if you set up a tournament like that for the Prisoner’s Dilemma? Send out invitations to all the well-known specialists who had published on this game. Ask each of them to send in a program. A program in Fortran — a simple one, that takes as input what the opponent has done in past rounds, and returns a decision: cooperate or defect. Bring all the programs together in a single tournament, each with each, two hundred rounds. Tally the points. See who wins.

In 1977–78 Axelrod sent out the invitations. His assistant Jeff Pynnonen wrote, in Fortran, the environment in which the programs would play. By the start of 1980, fourteen programs had been received.

The senders were world-class specialists. Economists. Mathematicians. Political scientists. Psychologists. One sociologist. They had all been publishing papers on the Prisoner’s Dilemma for years. Each was convinced that his strategy was the best. Axelrod opened the envelopes. He read the code. And launched the tournament. What was in the envelopes I won’t retell all fourteen strategies. But it’s worth breaking down a few — to understand against what background the main thing happened.

One program always defected. The author reasoned this way: if the theory says the only equilibrium is “defect,” let’s just do that. The program got a guaranteed bad result against other defectors and an excellent one — if it ran into someone who always cooperates.

Another program always cooperated. The author reasoned: if everyone does that, everyone will be well off. The program played excellently with itself and against other cooperators, but constantly lost when running into defectors.

Some programs were cunning. One — a program by the name of JOSS — cooperated in ninety percent of cases after the opponent’s cooperation, but in ten percent of cases it randomly defected “as a test.” The author thought this would let it pick up a bonus from naive partners.

Another program — DOWNING — tried to model the opponent’s behavior. It assessed what was the probability that the opponent would cooperate after its defection, and what — after cooperation. If the opponent was predictable, DOWNING tried to exploit him. If not — it adapted.
Some programs were openly complex. One used regression analysis. Another — Markov chains. One program was seventy-seven lines long in Fortran — the author was proud of its multi-level logic.
And somewhere in the middle of an envelope from Toronto lay a program four lines long.
The four-line winner
The program from Toronto worked like this:
First move — cooperate. Every following move — do what the opponent did in the previous move.
If the opponent cooperated — cooperate. If the opponent defected — defect. Next time, look again at what he did in response, and mirror.
That’s all of it. No modeling. No regression. No “when to exploit, when to forgive” logic. A mirror. Literally a mirror.

The author called it TIT FOR TAT — an everyday English expression. Though a more accurate name for what the program actually does would be: “mirror.”Axelrod saw this program, read the code — and decided someone had sent it as a joke. Then he looked at the sender’s name. This person didn’t like jokes.
His name was Anatol Rapoport.

Axelrod launched the tournament. Fourteen programs played each other, every one with every one, two hundred rounds each. Plus each played against itself. Plus one neutral program was added as a benchmark. All the points were counted. When the last round ended, the results were such that Axelrod rewrote his entire research program.
Tit-for-Tat won. By a wide margin.

Everything complicated lost. The long seventy-seven-line program took a middling place. JOSS with its random defections — below average. DOWNING with its modeling of the opponent — mediocre. Programs that always defected — at the bottom. Programs that always cooperated — also at the bottom, because they got exploited. Four lines of code from Toronto beat fourteen years of work by experts. The man from Lozovaya It’s worth pausing for a minute and telling who the man was who wrote the winning program. Because this isn’t just some random mathematician.

Anatol Borisovich Rapoport was born on May 22, 1911, in Lozovaya, in the Kharkov Governorate of the Russian Empire. Today Lozovaya is in eastern Ukraine, in the Kharkiv region. In December 1921, when Anatoly was ten years old, his family fled from Soviet Ukraine to Poland. Across the frozen border river Zbruch. On skates. To be precise, he was the one fleeing on skates — a ten-year-old boy who, dressing warmly and buying himself new skates, walked up to the river, crouched by a fence, watched the carefree Polish children skating on the Polish side of the dam, waited for the moment when the border guards got distracted, and rolled out. Suddenly, from somewhere above, a Red Army soldier spotted him and started shouting. Anatol picked up speed, raced over to the Polish children, wedged himself into their circle — and calmly skated off with them, away from the Soviet border. Many years later he would describe this moment in his memoirs.

A year later the family made it to the United States and settled in Chicago. Anatol was sent to study music. At sixteen he was already a promising pianist. At eighteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory. Until 1934 he studied there as a composer, pianist, and conductor. He gave concerts in Austria, Poland, Hungary, Italy. He spoke four languages.

Then the Nazis came to power in Germany. The career of a Jewish concert pianist in central Europe ended before it had begun. Rapoport returned to the States and discovered that in America too, no one needed yet another pianist from Chicago. At the age of twenty-three he enrolled at the University of Chicago. Seven years later he defended his dissertation in mathematics.

Then for fifteen years he worked on mathematical biology — modeling the spread of epidemics, the behavior of parasites and symbionts. In 1955 he came to the University of Michigan as one of the founders of the Mental Health Research Institute. There he began studying the behavior of people in conflict situations — through laboratory games, including the Prisoner’s Dilemma. It was Rapoport who introduced this experiment into broad scientific use, in his 1965 book Prisoner’s Dilemma: A Study in Conflict and Cooperation.

In 1970, when the Vietnam War entered its dirtiest phase, Rapoport left the United States for Canada. He wrote later that he wanted to live “in a country not committed to a messianic role.” He took a position in Toronto, where by 1980 he was already a professor emeritus on a pension — a seventy-year-old elder, the author of twenty books and three hundred articles, who had spent his whole life on one question: how to get people to stop killing each other.

By this moment Rapoport was one of the world’s most well-known researchers in game theory and conflict. And one of the most consistent pacifists. He founded Science for Peace. He wrote that war is “a contagious disease with a fatal outcome.” When the invitation came from Axelrod, Rapoport sat down and wrote four lines. Sent it.

Many years later he confessed to Axelrod that he himself didn’t much like Tit-forTat. Too harsh, he said. Too ready to take revenge. Not really suitable as a moral position for a peace researcher. But he wanted to see how it would play. It won.
Why the mirror won
Axelrod spent the next two years trying to understand why.
After analyzing all the played matches, he singled out four properties of the winning strategy.

First: niceness. Tit-for-Tat never defects first. On the first move it always cooperates. On any move after the opponent’s cooperation — it cooperates. This property divides all fourteen programs into “nice” (never defect first) and “mean” (defect at some point without provocation). Eight of the fourteen programs were “nice.” In the final results table, all eight of the nice programs took the top places. All six mean ones — the bottom.

Second: retaliation. Tit-for-Tat answers a defection immediately. Not after a delay, not in reserve, not with some probability — exactly on the next move, exactly once. This protects it from exploitation. The “nice” programs that didn’t know how to retaliate (always-cooperate) got mercilessly exploited and in the end lost.

Third: forgiveness. Tit-for-Tat doesn’t hold grudges. If the opponent cooperated on the last move — it forgets everything that came before and cooperates in response. Programs that piled up grudges and started taking revenge forever after a single defection got stuck in eternal war and lost points. Forgiveness restores cooperation. Fourth: clarity. Tit-for-Tat is predictable. It’s easy for the opponent to understand what it’s doing and why. That means cooperation can quickly be established with it — all it takes is one try at cooperating, and it’ll cooperate too. Programs that tried to be cunning and unpredictable (like JOSS with its random defections) confused their partners and destroyed cooperation that could otherwise have been established. Niceness, retaliation, forgiveness, clarity. All in four lines of code. Axelrod published the results in March 1980 in the Journal of Conflict Resolution. The article was called “Effective Choice in the Prisoner’s Dilemma.” It made an impression, but the scientific community received it with the usual healthy skepticism: well, one program won one tournament. Maybe it was a fluke. Maybe the others didn’t try. Maybe if you ran the tournament differently, somebody else would win. Axelrod read the criticism and decided to run a second tournament.
The second round
For the second tournament, Axelrod did three things.

First: he published a full report on the first tournament. All the programs, all the matches, all the results, a full analysis of why TfT won. All future participants got this report. That is, now no one could say they hadn’t known the weaknesses of their own strategy or the strengths of their opponent.

Second: he ran an announcement in computer magazines — like Creative Computing and Personal Computing. He invited everyone, not just academic experts. In the end he received sixty-two programs from all over the world — from professors to teenage hobbyists. In the first tournament there were fourteen programs. In the second — almost five times as many.

Third: he changed the rule for ending the game. In the first tournament there were exactly two hundred rounds. This created the “last move” problem — on the last round there’s no point in cooperating, so you should defect; but then there’s no point on the second-to-last either; and so on all the way back to the start. This is called “backward induction” and theoretically destroys the whole construction. In real life backward induction doesn’t work, because nobody knows the exact moment of the end. Axelrod modeled this: in the second tournament, after each move, with probability 0.00346 the game ended. On average this gave about 200 moves, but no one knew in advance which move would be the last.

The participants knew everything. They knew TfT had won. They knew which properties make a program successful. They knew that Axelrod had even specifically suggested a strategy that might beat TfT — Tit-for-Two-Tats, a softer version that forgives two defections in a row before retaliating.

Out of sixty-two programs, many tried to beat TfT directly. Some were more aggressive. Others — more cunning. Still others used complex models of the opponent. One person looked at all this commotion, sat down, and once again wrote four lines. Anatol Rapoport submitted Tit-for-Tat again.
The second tournament TfT won too.

Axelrod published the results in September 1980. And he added something else I haven’t mentioned. He ran six variants of the second tournament — with different ecological conditions, where certain types of programs were represented more or less. In five out of six variants TfT won again. In the sixth it took second place. And one more thing: Axelrod ran an evolutionary simulation. He imagined that each program produces offspring in proportion to its success. The less successful die out, the more successful reproduce. After a thousand generations TfT dominated. After several thousand — it occupied most of the population. Cooperation, which had seemed like a naive alternative to rational selfishness, turned out to be a stable evolutionary attractor.

The picture was clear. Cooperation is stable. Cooperation is profitable. Cooperation wins in repeated interactions — provided that the strategy that implements it has four properties: niceness, retaliation, forgiveness, clarity.
Three conditions

Axelrod went further. Over the next several years, he and his colleagues worked on understanding under which conditions exactly the picture described above works. Because it’s one thing to show that TfT wins in a specific tournament. It’s another thing to understand why.

In the 1984 book The Evolution of Cooperation, and even more sharply — in articles from 1985–1987 with the biologist William Hamilton, Axelrod formulated the answer. It turned out that for cooperation to be able to arise and be sustained through something like TfT, three conditions are needed. All three. Remove any one of them — cooperation collapses.

Condition one: iteration. The game has to repeat. If I know I’ll meet you only once in life, the optimal strategy is to defect. Take and run. You won’t find me anyway. In the tournament each pair of programs had two hundred rounds. In real life iteration arises when people live in the same village, work at the same company, trade in the same market for many years. When I know I’ll see you tomorrow, I behave differently than if I know I’ll never see you again.
Destroy iteration — and you get the behavior of a tourist in an unfamiliar city. You can leave no tip. You can be rude. No consequences.

Condition two: memory. Participants have to remember what the opponent did in past rounds. Without memory TfT doesn’t work — you can’t “answer in the mirror” to something you don’t remember. In the tournament memory was built into the mechanics: each program got, as input, the full history of interaction. In real life memory arises when I recognize you by face, remember our past conversations, have an idea of how you’ve behaved with others.

Destroy memory — and you get the behavior of a big anonymous crowd. Nobody remembers anybody. Every interaction is the first and the last. To deceive is safe. Condition three: clarity. Or reputation, or observability — it’s formulated in different ways. The essence is one: behavior has to be visible. Not only to the one I’m interacting with, but also to other participants. Because if I cheated you and no one besides the two of us knows about it, I can go and cheat the next person. But if news of my cheating spreads through the community — they’ll stop letting me through to the next ones. Destroy clarity — and you get the behavior of a world where you can buy a new name and move to another town. Whatever I do, the trail doesn’t follow. Three conditions. Iteration, memory, clarity. Remove any one — and the optimal strategy shifts from TfT toward pure selfishness.
How this connects to the Nash equilibrium
Remember the Nash equilibrium from the start of the chapter? In the Prisoner’s Dilemma it was “both defect.” Stable but bad.

Axelrod found another equilibrium. When the three conditions are satisfied — when the game is repeated, the participants remember, and behavior is visible — a new equilibrium appears: both cooperate by TfT. If one deviates and starts to defect, the other mirrors — and both become worse off. If one returns to cooperation — the other does too. Stable. And good.

This is fundamental. Nash described the trap: the system gets stuck in a bad state because unilateral movement out of it isn’t profitable. Axelrod showed the way out: if there’s the right structure around the game (three conditions), a second equilibrium appears in which everyone cooperates. And this equilibrium is also stable — unilateral deviation from cooperation is automatically punished.
The task, then, isn’t to convince people to “be better.” The task is to create a structure where selfishness leads to cooperation. Not to change people. To change the rules of the game.
Five paths to one idea

For millennia before Axelrod, a similar idea had independently been found five times. Confucius, around 500 BCE, taught: do not do unto others what you do not wish for yourself. This is formulated in the Analects, in a conversation between the disciple Zigong and Confucius. Zigong asked: is there one word by which one might live one’s whole life? Confucius answered: perhaps, “reciprocity.”

Rabbi Hillel the Elder in Jerusalem around 30 BCE, when a gentile asked him to lay out the whole essence of the Torah while standing on one foot, answered: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor — that is the whole Torah, the rest is commentary.
Jesus of Nazareth, around the year 30 CE, said something similar but in a positive formulation: as you would have people treat you, so treat them. Later this would be called the Golden Rule.

Immanuel Kant in 1785 proved this logically, as the categorical imperative: act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law. If you can’t will that everyone lie — don’t lie.
Anatol Rapoport in 1980 proved it mathematically. Four lines of code in Fortran. Five independent paths. Two and a half thousand years. Different cultures, religions, eras, instruments. One formula.

You can say this confirms a deep moral truth — that the Golden Rule has always existed and is found everywhere. You can also say it differently: this confirms a structural truth. In repeated interactions with memory and clarity, Tit-for-Tat is the optimal strategy. That is exactly why any culture, any philosophy that has seriously thought about the question “how to live among others” finds it. That is exactly why a mathematical proof gives the same answer as moral intuition.
The problem, as Rapoport himself formulated it, is not in the rule. The problem is in the architecture of its application.

The three conditions have to be satisfied. In a family, between friends, in a small business — they’re often satisfied of themselves. We interact iteratively, we remember each other, we see behavior. TfT works intuitively, without mathematics. In big anonymous systems — the state, the global economy, the crowd — the conditions break. And the Golden Rule stops working not because people have gotten worse. But because the architecture is broken.
Axelrod and Rapoport showed what makes the architecture right. And, by the same token, showed what makes it wrong.
Return to Bitcoin
Now we can return to the question we started the chapter with.
Why didn’t GHash.IO attack Bitcoin in July 2014?
Because in Bitcoin all three of Axelrod’s conditions are satisfied.

Iteration. Each block is a new round of the game. A block comes out every ten minutes. Twenty-four hours is one hundred and forty-four rounds. A year is fifty-two thousand rounds. A mining pool that wants to earn over five years will play this game a quarter of a million times. This isn’t a one-off situation. The shadow of the future is longer than any possible one-time gain.

Memory. The blockchain is literally the network’s shared memory. Every transaction, every block, every miner — all of it is on the record. If GHash.IO had tried to rewrite transaction history in July 2014, that attempt would have stayed in the blockchain forever. Forever — in the cryptographic sense of the word. To erase is impossible. Clarity. The hashrate of every mining pool is publicly visible. This isn’t secret information. Any researcher, any journalist, any community member can look in real time at what share which pool occupies. When GHash.IO crossed 50 percent in June 2014, this was known within hours. Not days, not months — hours.

Three conditions satisfied. Which means TfT should work. And it did work: the community mirrored the pool’s actions — miners left, the reputation collapsed, the price of bitcoin fell. The economic pressure was a retaliatory response to the threat of breaking cooperation. When GHash.IO publicly promised to limit itself to 40 percent — forgiveness restored cooperation. After a few months the situation returned to normal. That was TfT at the level of the global mining community. Without a coordination center. Without a formal contract. Just four properties working through three conditions.

Now it becomes clear why in other situations pressure doesn’t work. If a network is small and not visible from the outside — clarity is broken. If the miners are anonymous and there’s no reputation — memory is broken. If the game is played once (say, if the network is on the verge of collapse and won’t survive the next year) — iteration is broken. Anywhere even one of the three conditions is broken, Tit-for-Tat stops being the optimal strategy, and defection becomes rational.

So if we’re building a distributed system and we want cooperation without a central arbitrator to work in it — we have to design it so that all three conditions are satisfied. Iteration, memory, clarity.

This looks like a recipe. And it almost is a recipe. But there’s one nuance which none of Axelrod, Rapoport, or anyone who read their work in the 1980s could have predicted. What was left unclear If everything is so simple — three conditions, four properties, an optimal strategy — then why did we say at the end of Chapter 1 that Bitcoin has a structural flaw? After all, in it the three conditions are satisfied.
The answer: Axelrod’s three conditions are a necessary condition for cooperation. But not a sufficient one.

Bitcoin satisfies Axelrod. There is iteration in it, and memory, and clarity, and Titfor-Tat works there. That explains why the network survived in 2014. But there is one more factor that Axelrod didn’t write about, because in 1980 it was impossible to see. This factor is connected not to the conditions of the game, but to what exactly is being won in this game. To the prize itself.

In Axelrod’s tournament the prize was abstract — points. The programs couldn’t exchange those points for something else, asymmetric. They couldn’t, for example, use their points to buy votes in determining the future rules of the tournament. They couldn’t buy their reputation.

In Bitcoin the prize is real money. And this money can be used, among other things, to influence the system itself. To buy more equipment. To capture a larger share. To push through certain changes in the protocol. To direct the industry in a particular direction.

This creates a different problem. Not the problem of the absence of the three conditions — the three conditions are satisfied. But the problem that the very prize in the game contains, inside itself, an asymmetry that was not in the 1980 tournament. The prize gives the ability to change the rules of the game. And that is a class of attack which Axelrod did not model.

It’s exactly this flaw — structural, subtle, almost invisible — that is the reason Bitcoin, for all its remarkable properties, remains the Darby phase, not the Murdoch phase. It solves the problem of cooperation between participants within the framework of the current game. But it does not solve the problem that the money earned in this game can be used to change the game itself.
But before moving further, it’s worth pausing for a minute. Because we’ve derived something important.

Cooperation without an arbitrator is possible. This is not a utopia and not mysticism. It is a mathematical fact, proven in 1980 in a tournament that fourteen programs took part in. It requires three conditions — iteration, memory, clarity — and one strategy made of four lines of code.
And if we want to build systems in which millions of people, without coercion, act in common interests, we now know what to build from.
That’s the first piece of good news in this book.
The next chapter is about the bad news.
A Gene You Can’t Repair From Inside the Cell

Imagine an organism. It has DNA. The DNA codes for proteins. The proteins assemble cells, the cells assemble organs, the organs make the organism. If there’s an error in the DNA — say, one letter is wrong — that error is reproduced in every cell, because every cell copies the same DNA. The consequences can range from imperceptible to catastrophic, but one thing is clear: no cell inside that organism can fix the DNA error. For that you need someone outside, with different tools.

That’s exactly Bitcoin’s situation right now. It has its original construction — Proofof-Work with anonymous miners and an open protocol. That construction solved Satoshi’s specific problem — to create digital money with no bank in the middle. And it solved it brilliantly. But it has one side effect: anything earned inside the system can be used outside it, and the system has no mechanism to defend itself against how that earning changes the system itself.

I’ll try to show this on three different layers. First — on the layer of computational power, where money earned from mining buys still more mining and concentrates in a few hands. Then — on the layer of ownership, where the same money, having passed through exchanges and funds, comes back as large institutional positions. And finally — on the layer of development, where the same money pays the engineers who write the protocol itself.
Three layers. The same mechanism. And in each of them — a structural contradiction between what Bitcoin promises in its original construction and what actually comes out.
Layer One: Who Counts
Let’s start with mining.

When Satoshi launched Bitcoin in 2009, he seems to have sincerely thought that mining would be done by thousands of people on home computers, each one independently. “One CPU — one vote,” he wrote in the white paper. One processor, one vote. Every participant in the network defends it with their small bit of power, and no one has an advantage over anyone else. In 2009–2010 that’s how it actually worked — Satoshi himself mined on an ordinary laptop, taking the whole block reward. That picture died very quickly. In 2010 someone figured out that graphics cards could be used for mining — they hash dozens of times faster than processors. In 2011 the first FPGA miners appeared, several times faster again. In 2013 Bitmain released the first ASIC — an integrated circuit honed for one single operation, SHA-256 hashing. The ASIC was a thousand times more efficient than a GPU. Home computers were out of the game. So were graphics cards. Only ASIC farms remained.

By 2016 most mining had moved to China, where electricity was cheap and local authorities weren’t interfering yet. By 2021 China had banned mining, and the industry relocated to Texas, Kazakhstan, Russia, Iran, Iceland. By 2024 — after another “halving,” when the block reward was cut in half from 6.25 to 3.125 BTC — the small operators were squeezed out for good. Only the large industrial farms survived: the ones with long-term contracts for wholesale electricity, their own cooling infrastructure, and teams of engineers.
As of April 2026 the picture looks like this.

At the very top — mining pools. These are associations of miners that combine their computations and split the reward. Of all the world’s miners working on Bitcoin, Foundry USA serves about 29 percent. AntPool (owned by Bitmain, the largest ASIC manufacturer) serves another 21 percent or so. ViaBTC — about 11. F2Pool — about 10. SpiderPool — about 7. MARA Pool and SecPool — 6 each.
The first two pools together control roughly half of all Bitcoin hashrate. The first four — about seventy percent.

This is a fundamentally important number, and it’s worth pausing on it for a minute. When a pool controls a certain share of the hashrate, it essentially decides which transactions go into the block. The pool doesn’t actually mine the blocks itself — that’s done by the miners connected to it. But the pool builds the “block template” — the list of transactions the miner then tries to hash. If the miner happens to find the right hash, the block is published with the transactions the pool selected.

In other words: four organizations — Foundry, AntPool, ViaBTC, F2Pool — decide which transactions get into seventy percent of all Bitcoin blocks. This isn’t a threat to the network in the sense of “they could destroy it.” It’s much more subtle: they can slowly, transaction by transaction, decide who pays more for the right to enter a block, whose transactions get processed first, and whose get stuck. They can (and sometimes do) exclude transactions from addresses under sanctions — for example, addresses on the U.S. Treasury blacklist. They can (and this has already happened) prioritize certain kinds of transactions that bring in higher fees.

And here’s the thing — they can do all of this without breaking a single protocol rule. They’re simply taking advantage of the fact that they have a lot of hashrate. And they have a lot of hashrate because they earned it on previous blocks and reinvested into more equipment, cheaper electricity, and better engineers.

The game rewards winners with money. Money buys more equipment. More equipment gives more hashrate. More hashrate — more wins. The cycle is closed. Notice that this cycle violates none of Axelrod’s conditions. The three conditions — iteration, memory, transparency — are still met. New blocks come out every ten minutes (iteration). Everything is recorded in the blockchain forever (memory). The hashrate of every pool is publicly visible (transparency). Everything’s in order. But inside this perfectly functioning architecture a process of concentration is going on that isn’t accounted for by the rules of Tit-for-Tat. Because TfT is a strategy for equal players. It says nothing about what to do when one of the players is twenty times bigger than another. In Axelrod’s tournament all programs had equal starting conditions. In real Bitcoin — they don’t.
Layer Two: Who Owns
Now let’s look at another level.

Bitcoin isn’t only miners — it’s holders. People who simply own coins and store them on their own wallets or on exchanges. In theory, since every bitcoin is identical, distribution should be uniform. In practice — it isn’t.

In January 2024 the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) approved spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) for the first time. This was the culmination of years of pressure from large asset managers — BlackRock, Fidelity, Grayscale — who wanted to be able to sell bitcoin to their institutional clients through ordinary brokerage infrastructure, without having to deal with crypto exchanges and cold wallets. BlackRock is the world’s largest asset management company; it has on the order of 11 trillion dollars under management. That’s more than the GDP of any country except the United States and China. When BlackRock launched its Bitcoin ETF under the ticker IBIT on January 11, 2024, money poured in like a river.

As of April 2026 — two years later — IBIT holds roughly 800,000 bitcoins, which corresponds to about 63 billion dollars at the current price. That’s about 49 percent of all assets in all U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs combined. In the first quarter of 2026 alone, IBIT took in net inflows of 8.4 billion dollars.

But IBIT isn’t the only large holder. The company Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy, a business-analytics firm that then reinvented itself as a pure Bitcoin treasury) as of April 17, 2026 owns 815,000 bitcoins with a total acquisition cost of 61.56 billion dollars. That’s about four percent of all the Bitcoin that has ever existed. No single entity in history has held that kind of share — except, possibly, Satoshi himself, whose coins haven’t moved since 2010.

If you add up everything held by U.S. spot ETFs, you get about 1.31 million bitcoins — roughly 6.2 percent of total supply. Add Strategy — you get more than ten percent. Add the large exchanges (Coinbase, Binance), corporate treasury positions, large private holdings — and it turns out that several dozen entities account for a quarter of all Bitcoin.
What does this mean in practice?

It means that if BlackRock decides one fine day, on a regulator’s order, to freeze IBIT’s assets — eight percent of all Bitcoin instantly becomes illiquid. That’s a market shock of a magnitude Bitcoin hasn’t seen yet. It means that if Strategy faces a margin call on its loans (and it has been borrowing to buy bitcoin), it could be forced to liquidate 815,000 coins — which would crash the price several times over in an instant. It means that if the U.S. government decides to regulate Bitcoin with new legislation, the main channel of influence is no longer decentralized miners in Kazakhstan but BlackRock in New York, where one phone call to the right office can change the behavior of trillions of dollars.

The paradox is that Bitcoin was conceived as a network resistant to centralized pressure. Decentralization was not a side effect, it was a central requirement. And yet sixteen years later we have a construction in which a few large institutional players control such a share of supply that they are structurally able to influence price, liquidity, and the regulatory agenda more than the rest of the market combined. How did this happen?

The same way it happened with mining. Each individual movement of money was voluntary and individually rational. A pension fund wanted exposure to Bitcoin but couldn’t hold the coins directly because of regulatory restrictions — bought IBIT. A family office wanted diversification — bought IBIT. A corporation wanted a hedge against inflation — bought IBIT. No one was coerced, no one was manipulated. Each individual decision looked sensible.

But the aggregate result of millions of such individually rational decisions is gigantic concentration. Which now itself becomes a factor in the equation. Because the more bitcoin BlackRock has, the more voice BlackRock has in any public discussion of what Bitcoin should be in the future. And that voice isn’t the same as an ordinary holder’s. It’s a voice that gets listened to at the SEC, in Congress, at the Federal Reserve. Layer Three: Who Writes The third layer is the most invisible, but the most important.

Bitcoin is code. That code is written by people. There aren’t very many of them. According to a 2024 BitMEX Research report, on all of Bitcoin — which at that point was worth about a trillion and a half dollars — 41 developers were actively working: those who made at least five commits to the main Bitcoin Core repository over the year. Forty-one people, on a trillion and a half.

Of those forty-one, about two-thirds live in the U.S. and Europe. Three developers — in Latin America (Argentina, Brazil, El Salvador). Four — in the rest of the world. That’s Tier 1 statistics, drawn from public commit data.
Who funds them?

Bitcoin has no foundation. No central organization. No proverbial treasury that pays salaries from. That was all by Satoshi’s design — so that nobody could halt development by pulling funding. But programmers have to work, and they get paid through various sources.

Blockstream. A company founded in 2014. Among its founders — Gregory Maxwell, Pieter Wuille, Matt Corallo, Jorge Timón, Mark Friedenbach (all active Bitcoin Core developers), as well as Adam Back (the inventor of hashcash, on which Satoshi built Bitcoin’s PoW) and venture investor Austin Hill. Since its founding, Blockstream has raised more than half a billion dollars in investment in total — $76 million by 2017, $210 million in a Series B in 2021, another $210 million in convertible notes in 2024. The company clearly has several key Core developers on its payroll. Adam Back, its president, explains it this way: the company has an interest in seeing Bitcoin supported, developed, and scaled.
Chaincode Labs. A research center in New York that funds several more key developers.

MIT Digital Currency Initiative. An academic cover at the MIT Media Lab; it started up around 2015 in response to the funding crisis among Core developers after the collapse of the Bitcoin Foundation.
Brink, OpenSats, Spiral, Human Rights Foundation. Nonprofit grant programs. Large exchanges — Coinbase, OKCoin, OKX. Periodically issue grants.

The total annual funding for all Bitcoin Core development is estimated at 150–200 million dollars a year — for a network worth more than a trillion. By comparison, the Ethereum Foundation in 2024 spent about 50 million on development, with a market cap ten times smaller than Bitcoin’s. Polkadot — 16 million, with a market cap a hundred times smaller. Per dollar of capitalization defended, Bitcoin underfunds development by an order of magnitude.

And — here’s where it gets subtle — a disproportionately large share of the modest funding that does exist flows through Blockstream. A company that has its own commercial products: Liquid (a sidechain for financial institutions), the Lightning Network (an L2 for fast payments), mining hardware, institutional services. The interests of these products sometimes coincide with the interests of an ordinary Bitcoin user, and sometimes they don’t.

A classic example is the 2023–2024 debates over the Ordinals protocol, which made it possible to write arbitrary data (images, NFT collections, even books) onto the Bitcoin blockchain. Technically this was done through Taproot — a protocol upgrade that Core developers shipped in 2021 for other purposes, but which Casey Rodarmor used in early 2023 in an unexpected way. Ordinals quickly took up a significant share of block space, driving up fees and changing the network’s economics.

One of the senior Core developers, Luke Dashjr, submitted a pull request that would have technically restricted Ordinals. Another maintainer, Ava Chow (a former Blockstream employee), closed the PR, citing “lack of consensus and creating noise.” The community split. Some considered Ordinals a creative use of the network. Others — parasitism on block space meant for monetary transactions. The decision was, formally, made by one person. That decision could not be reversed by anyone except the maintainer himself or another maintainer with equal rights.

Ordinals didn’t break a single Bitcoin rule. But they radically changed how the blockchain is used. And that change happened not through a vote of miners, not through a referendum of holders, but through the individual decision of a few developers with commit access. Who get paid by specific companies. Who have their own business interests.

Formally the network remains decentralized — it has no CEO, no foundation, no board of directors. In fact, a narrow circle of people, financially tied to a limited set of companies, makes decisions that affect trillions of dollars of capital and millions of users.

And again — this is no one’s evil intent. It’s just a consequence of how the development economy is set up. Bitcoin doesn’t pay developers out of its blocks. They are paid by external companies. The companies have interests. The interests concentrate. The developers fed by those companies cluster around the tasks those companies consider priorities. Regardless of how well those tasks line up with Bitcoin’s tasks as a public good.
The Three Layers Together

If you look at the three layers at once, a common structure is visible. On the mining layer — money earned in previous blocks buys more hashrate. More hashrate gives more influence over which transactions go into blocks. On the ownership layer — money earned from mining or from price appreciation buys more coins through institutional instruments. More coins gives more voice in the public discussion of Bitcoin’s future.
On the development layer — money earned at exchanges, at ETFs, at mining infrastructure, funds developers. The developers who receive that money decide where the protocol moves.

On each of the three layers, the same mechanism is at work: an internal win is converted into external influence. And that influence, in turn, can be used to change the conditions of the next rounds of the game in one’s own favor.

This is where Axelrod’s model breaks. Not because Tit-for-Tat is a bad strategy. TfT is still optimal for the situation it describes. But it describes a situation in which points cannot be converted into the right to change the rules. Bitcoin is a situation in which they can.

Axelrod in 1980 couldn’t have foreseen this, because in his tournament there was no money. There were abstract points that couldn’t be used for anything except tallying up the winner. Whereas in a real economic system, the winnings can always be converted. The only question is into what, and how much.
Under the Hood. GHash.IO Once More

In the first chapter I told the story of GHash.IO in the summer of 2014 — a pool that for a day crossed the 55-percent threshold of Bitcoin hashrate and didn’t catastrophically attack the network. In the second chapter I used that story as an example of how Tit-for-Tat works in reality — the community mirrored the threat, the pool retreated, everything ended well.
Now — the whole truth.

GHash.IO did not destroy Bitcoin. But it did use its majority position for a specific attack on a specific service. In the autumn of 2013, when GHash.IO’s share was already significant but not yet 51 percent, the pool conducted a series of double-spending attacks against the online casino BetCoin Dice. The discussion of this on the BitcoinTalk forum, in thread number 327767, is still publicly available. The idea is simple: GHash.IO accepted losing bets at its addresses, and when it lost — it mined the same transaction with its own (winning) address into a different block, turning the loss into a win. The digital version of what in a physical casino is called “replaying the round when the ball didn’t stop where it should have.”

BetCoin Dice took real losses. The investigation established that. GHash.IO didn’t formally acknowledge any public contrition, but there were reputational consequences: the pool stopped accepting deposits at its addresses, and the community started watching it more closely. This story is one of the reasons that, six months later, when GHash.IO once again grew toward the critical share, the pressure was so quick and so strong. People remembered.

This is an important correction to the picture usually painted in the Bitcoin community. People often say: “Bitcoin has never had a 51-percent attack.” That’s true only at a certain level of strictness. If you understand a 51-percent attack as “a complete rewriting of blockchain history months back, with double spending of all major transactions” — yes, that hasn’t happened. If you understand it as “use of a majority position to extract gain at the expense of other participants in the network” — it has. And it has been documented.

This is a critical detail for our subject. Because it shows: the mechanism of “converting winnings into the right to change the rules” is not a theoretical threat. It has already gone off. It just went off on a limited scale, because the pool, understanding that a full breach would kill the entire network (and its profit along with it), stopped at local exploitation.

Local exploitation is bad news in another sense. It means that a system in which the holder of a majority of computation can exploit the minority, even when not destroying the whole construction, is structurally unstable even when Axelrod’s three conditions are met. Because TfT equilibrium presupposes that the participants play more or less on equal footing. The moment a majority player appears who can carry out a “pinpoint attack” — take something from someone but not break the system as a whole — they will do it. Rationally. In keeping with their incentives. In full accordance with game theory.
And there’s no defense against this inside Bitcoin’s mechanics.
Under the Hood. Monero, August 2025

The second example is a very recent one. In August 2025 — that is, less than a year before these lines are being written — something happened that confirmed what I was just talking about, but on a far larger scale. And it was done not by one of the major exchanges and not by a hacker group, but by the project this book is, in principle, written about — Qubic.

To retell the whole story here is not the place — that’s the topic of chapter fifteen. But the brief fact is this. Monero is a network similar to Bitcoin, also Proof-of-Work, but with a different algorithm (RandomX, optimized for ordinary processors rather than for specialized ASICs). Monero’s market cap at that moment was about 6 billion dollars. Qubic’s market cap — about 300 million. A ratio of 1 to 20.

Over three months — from May to August 2025 — Qubic, through a mechanism we’ll talk about in detail in chapter 8, started paying Monero miners three times more than they were getting by mining Monero directly. No hack. No hacking. Just a different economics: “connect to our pool, we’ll route your computational work in such a way that you earn more.”

The miners looked at the numbers. Reconnected their equipment. On August 11, 2025, in a window of 122 blocks, Qubic owned 63 blocks out of 122 — 51.6 percent of the hashrate. The Monero network was under the control of a network twenty times smaller in market cap.

What happened next is a separate story. Qubic did not destroy Monero. But the technical possibility of destruction was there, and in a public statement on August 3, 2025 the Qubic developers spelled out exactly what they could have done if they’d wanted to: double-spending against exchange deposits, rewriting block history, censoring transactions, crashing the price to zero. They didn’t. They decided to stop. But they could have.

For our chapter — and specifically, for the question of why Bitcoin can’t fix itself — this is the key episode. Because it proves empirically, not theoretically: any PoW network can be attacked by offering miners a better economics. The Qubic developers, summing up the experiment, formulated this as one of three proven theses: “Incentives Dictate Consensus: Any Proof of Work blockchain can be attacked and controlled by providing superior economic incentives to its miners.”

This is a critical statement. It isn’t saying “Bitcoin is weak” — Bitcoin is strong, which is precisely why it’s more expensive to attack. It’s saying “no PoW network is structurally protected.” The protection is just money. More money — more protection. Someone with bigger money can buy that protection out. And money, let me remind you, is exactly what accumulates with those who have already won the game.
The circle is closed.
What This Means for Our Story
Let me bring it all together.

The first chapter ended on the point that Bitcoin assembled a revolution — but in doing so left “Murdoch’s gas” in the air, computational cycles that nobody needs. That was bad news about the use of a resource.

The second chapter gave good news: cooperation without an arbitrator is possible if Axelrod’s three conditions are met, and Bitcoin on the whole meets those conditions. The third chapter — that is, this one — says: the bad news is deeper than we thought in the first chapter. Bitcoin not only uses its resource inefficiently. It is also structurally incapable of fixing itself, because the money earned inside is constantly being converted into power outside, and that power comes back inside as the ability to change the rules. Concentration of mining. Concentration of ownership. Concentration of development. Three layers, the same dynamic.

You could say that all of this is just the general problem of capitalism, and Bitcoin isn’t unique in it. That would be true if Bitcoin hadn’t promised the opposite. And it did. It promised that every processor would be one vote. That mining is decentralized. That nobody controls the network. That the money it produces is neutral and resistant to any politics. Sixteen years on, all of that is either already untrue or becoming untrue right in front of us.

And not because Satoshi was wrong. He wasn’t wrong — he solved a specific problem, and he solved it. It’s just that his solution is the Darby phase. The first great breakthrough. It opens doors that were locked before. But it has a structural limit you can’t step over from inside. The Murdoch phase is already a different engineering problem, with different conditions.
And here we come to the main question of this chapter.
The Fourth Condition

Axelrod in 1980 described three conditions under which cooperation is possible: iteration, memory, transparency. He didn’t write about a fourth, because in his tournament that condition was satisfied automatically — the programs played in a closed system in which winnings could not be converted into anything external. In the real world this condition may or may not hold — and that is the defining difference between systems that stay cooperative and systems that drift toward oligopoly. Let me try to state this condition explicitly:
The system has to be set up so that winnings inside the game cannot be converted into the right to change the game itself.
