Or shorter: the boundary between “the prize” and “the rules” must be impossible to cross from inside.

In Axelrod’s tournament that boundary was absolute — points and rules lived in different worlds. In Bitcoin that boundary is a permeable membrane. Internal money constantly seeps outward, acquires external influence, and comes back in already as pressure on the rules. Gradually. Year after year.

This fourth condition isn’t an improvement on Axelrod. It’s an addition. The three original conditions determine whether cooperation will be the equilibrium between players. The fourth determines whether that equilibrium structure will be preserved in time, or whether it gradually drifts toward a new equilibrium in which a few play and many submit. It’s about the durability of durability itself.

If we want to build a system that satisfies not only Axelrod’s three conditions but also the fourth, we need an architecture built differently. Not “an improved Bitcoin.” Not “Bitcoin with a patch against concentration.” A fundamentally different construction, in which the very mechanism of winning is built so as not to produce concentration. This is a non-trivial engineering problem. The naive solution — to forbid the sale of bitcoin to large investors — doesn’t work, because it destroys the first property (a free market). The naive solution — to make the developers receive a salary from the protocol — works partially, but runs into the question of who decides whom to pay. The naive solution — to forbid mining pools — doesn’t work, because it destroys the ability of small miners to participate in the network.

What’s needed is an architecture in which the answer to all of these questions is built into the very mechanism by which the network operates, rather than being decided by a vote or by an authoritative directive. Where the mining process itself produces decentralization rather than concentration. Where the ownership process itself prevents oligopoly among large holders. Where the development process itself depends on the entire community rather than on a narrow group of sponsors.
Such an architecture exists. It’s called Qubic. And how it works is the subject of this book from chapter six to the end.

But before we talk about how it works, we need to talk about the man who made it. Not because the project’s history is incomplete without the man’s history — but because this man saw Bitcoin’s structural defect not in 2025, when it became obvious to everyone, and not in 2020, when it began to show up in the data. He saw it in the early 2010s, when Bitcoin was still young and nobody doubted that it would remain decentralized forever. He saw it — and that’s why he was able to build two crypto networks that came out at the very top of the all-time ICO ranking: the first, in first place; the second, in second. More than a million percent ROI on one, four hundred thousand on the other. And from those two networks he took away an understanding of exactly how crypto projects die from inside.
His name is Come-from-Beyond, and he really did come from beyond.
P A r T i i The Man

This story may differ in micro-details from how its protagonist himself would tell it. Some things he has never publicly confirmed, some he has confirmed years later and in passing, some he has deliberately left in the air. I assembled it from forum archives, late interviews, throwaway remarks, technical traces in the code of three networks, and the few facts I could verify myself. Somewhere I’m probably wrong. If he ever reads this and says “not quite,” then it’s not quite. But the general outline is this. There’s a peculiarity about people who later turn out to be right: they see something earlier than others, and at the moment they see it, nobody believes them. Galileo, looking through his telescope at the moons of Jupiter. Semmelweis, demanding that surgeons wash their hands. Turing, asserting that one day a machine would play chess better than a human.

The hero of this chapter is no Galileo and no Turing. He didn’t discover any laws of nature. He was simply one of the thousands of programmers reading the BitcoinTalk forum in 2010 and trying to figure out what strange thing this notorious Satoshi Nakamoto had just launched. The difference is that most of those thousand programmers saw a miracle. He — a year or two later — saw a crack.

That’s an unusual ability. To see a defect in something everyone else admires, and not say “but it works, so everything’s fine.” To say “yes, it works, but right here there’s going to be a problem — not tomorrow, but in ten years.” And to start building something else while everyone around you is still celebrating.

I named this person at the end of the previous chapter: Come-from-Beyond. A handle taken back in the early 2000s. As with Satoshi, the handle here isn’t a way to hide — it’s a way to sign. That’s a separate and curious parallel we’ll come back to. This chapter is about what this person was doing before Bitcoin entered his field of view. What his background was. Why he ended up in the right place at the right time with the right set of tools to see Bitcoin’s flaws sooner than anyone else in the industry. And why by 2013 — when he first stepped on the stage himself — he already had everything he needed to build something fundamentally different.
A Programmer From the Nineties

If you trace the footprints backward, the earliest ones Come-from-Beyond left go back to the late 1990s. An Eastern European teenage programmer working on a large game project that never shipped. In one of his remarks many years later he’ll mention that this project was twenty-five years ago — that is, somewhere around 1999. “It was written for one of my first big games which never released. ~25 years ago.” A big game, group work, didn’t make it to release. The classic fate of early 3D games of that era. To understand the context, it’s worth saying a couple of words about what programming looked like in Eastern Europe at the turn of the millennium. By the end of the 1990s, in the countries of the former socialist bloc, a generation had appeared with a computer at home, more or less stable internet, and access to any textbook or source code you could find. At the same time, this generation had almost no institutional career infrastructure — no Silicon Valley nearby, no venture capital, no internship programs at big companies. People taught themselves, worked remotely for Western clients or for local employers, and invented their own problems.

This turned out to be a very productive environment — in the sense that it produced people accustomed to solving problems that nobody pays for, without external validation, for their own interest. A habit rare in more settled ecosystems. Come-from-Beyond was one of these. He played Ultima Online — one of the first big mass online games, in which hundreds of players simultaneously roamed a shared virtual world — and quickly discovered that some of the in-game tasks (gathering ore, fishing, hunting hides) lent themselves to automation. In 2024 he’ll mention in passing that “My first farming bot in UO was doing it that way.” Which is to say that as a teenager he was already writing programs that played the game for him.

To a modern eye this sounds like a small thing. But it’s worth thinking about what this person was doing to make such a bot work. UO had no open API. The bot had to emulate mouse and keyboard input, recognize images on screen, react to changes in game state in real time. That’s a real engineering problem — and in 1999–2000 it was nontrivial even for adult professionals.

The next footprint left behind is more formal. In 2003, in one of the regional technical publications (back then there were such things — computer portals in local languages, with or without a paper supplement) an article was published called “Methods for Detecting Plagiarism in Programming.” The author — him, then still under his ordinary name, without the crypto handle. The article worked through the technical side of the question — how, looking at source code, you can determine that someone copied it from someone else, even if the variables were renamed and the comments rephrased. A topic relevant to educational institutions and to the protection of intellectual property in the software industry.
This article matters to us for two reasons.

The first — it proves that his first published work goes back to the early 2000s. By the time Bitcoin appears on the scene, he has ten years of programming practice behind him and at least one printed work on a professional topic.

The second reason is the subject of the article. Plagiarism in programming. How do you know that this code is yours and not someone else’s stolen from you. What structural traces remain in a program that give away its author. The question of how to identify an anonymous creator by the style of the code is one of those questions that, when an anonymous Satoshi Nakamoto appears on the scene in 2008, will unexpectedly take on extreme relevance. And, amusingly, many years later he himself will refer back to this 2003 article of his in one of the most enigmatic phrases in this whole story. But it’s too early for that now.

In parallel with this, by his own later admissions, in the very early 2000s he started thinking about something else, much more ambitious than games and plagiarism. In one of his early exchanges he’ll say that Aigarth — a project he has been working on, with varying intensity, since the very beginning of the 2000s, for about twenty years by 2023. What exactly Aigarth is we’ll work through later. For now it’s enough to say: the task he set himself at twenty was bigger than crypto, bigger than Bitcoin, bigger than the entire industry that came afterward. Crypto would be infrastructure for Aigarth, not the other way around.

This is an important angle. He didn’t come to crypto “to make his own coin.” He came to crypto with a much older and bigger problem, for which he needed infrastructure that couldn’t be built without crypto.
Meeting Bitcoin. 2010
Satoshi published the white paper in October 2008. In January 2009 he launched the network. In December 2010 he disappeared — leaving only a million mined coins and not a word about who he was.

Somewhere in that interval, Come-from-Beyond first opened BitcoinTalk. He doesn’t name an exact date, but many years later, in 2025, in a conversation with someone in the community, he’ll mention that he had used the technique of finding sockpuppets (fake accounts of one and the same person under different names) on BitcoinTalk “like 15 years ago.” Fifteen years from 2025 is 2010. That is, by the time Satoshi was still active and posting in the forum, he was already reading that forum closely enough to be doing account forensics.

How many bitcoins he had at this point and how they appeared — he has never publicly disclosed. Possibly he mined some himself in the early days, when CPU mining at home still made sense and one block reward was fifty coins. Possibly he bought some later. Possibly both. Someone hunting for sockpuppets on BitcoinTalk in 2010 is unlikely not to have tried running on his machine the thing that was being discussed there. But let that stay open — it’s one of those details he left in the air, and I’m not going to expose him.

Formal registration on the forum came later. In October 2011, Litecoin appeared — the first major variation on the Bitcoin theme, created by ex-Google engineer Charlie Lee. Litecoin had poor technical documentation, and Come-from-Beyond, wanting to dig into the details and not finding answers in open sources, was forced to register on BitcoinTalk to ask a question. He himself will later describe this as “an act of bravery for a lazy programmer.” His account got the number 46556; the profile is registered before November 22, 2011, which is publicly verifiable to this day — the profile page is open, anyone can go and check.

This single event — a technical registration to ask a question about Litecoin — will eventually grow into fifteen thousand messages over the years that follow. The BitcoinTalk archive holds them all. If anyone has the patience, they can reconstruct one specific programmer’s evolving views on the crypto industry literally week by week. By the end of 2011 he is already deeply involved. Not a public figure, not an author, not an activist. Just a very attentive observer who already has his own view of where this industry is going — and where its problems are.
What He Saw

The previous chapter ended on the point that this person saw Bitcoin’s problems in the early 2010s — at the moment when nobody in the industry doubted its eternal decentralization. What exactly did he see?
Let’s break it down step by step.

By 2011 Bitcoin had been running for two years. The network held, transactions went through, miners were getting more numerous. The price was volatile, but the trend was upward. On the BitcoinTalk forum, optimism reigned: a solution had been found to a problem that had been considered unsolvable. Digital money without a bank. Freedom from state issuance. Decentralization for the ages.
Come-from-Beyond, on top of the problems described in chapter 3, saw the most interesting thing of all:

Bitcoin uses its computational power irrationally. In a world where distributed computation could be solving real problems — training neural networks, modeling the climate, verifying cryptographic constructions — Bitcoin’s miners are computing useless hashes. This isn’t a bug — it’s by design. Satoshi chose a solution that worked, and it worked brilliantly. But the solution was single-purpose. Compute turned into protection and nothing else.

Come-from-Beyond, working on Aigarth — a project that needs distributed computational substrate at industrial scale — looked at those hundred and seventy terawatthours a year (the figure for 2026; in 2011 it was counted in gigawatt-hours) and saw, literally, his infrastructure being burned on guessing random numbers. For him this wasn’t an abstract injustice. It was personal. He needed a computational substrate for the AI project he had been thinking about for ten years. Bitcoin was taking that substrate and burning it for nothing.
So: four problems, seen at once. Any one of them, on its own — noticeable. All together — no longer just a defect, but a structural diagnosis.

Most people, on seeing such a diagnosis, do one of two things. Either they close their eyes and keep using what’s there, because it works. Or they write a long forum post, take a wave of downvotes from the enthusiasts, and walk away disappointed. Come-from-Beyond did a third thing. He silently kept accumulating early coins, to have capital and independence, and started thinking about how to build it differently. The Satoshi Question This is a fitting place to stop for a minute and say a word or two about a question that any attentive reader will inevitably raise.
Is Come-from-Beyond Satoshi Nakamoto himself?

The question is a serrrrious one and deserves a book of its own. Dozens of researchers in the cryptological world are working on exactly this question right now — you get the idea. (Attentive readers of the Qubic Church website will smile here.) Mathematicians and linguists analyze stylistic coincidences, conspiracists draw diagrams, enthusiasts dig through the BitcoinTalk archive, and the professional tabloids periodically publish articles under the headline “We’ve Found Satoshi!” Discovering a week later that they were wrong, they wait for the next week and publish another article just like the first. The Satoshi-hunting industry in this sense is its own separate, sustainable ecosystem in which you can genuinely make a career.
For this book I’ll limit myself to two things.

First. There are firmly established facts that noticeably narrow the space of possible interpretations. Come-from-Beyond was in the BitcoinTalk community as early as 2010 — that is, when Satoshi was still active. He has a 2003 publication behind him about methods that he himself will later jokingly refer to in the context of “Satoshi framed me, he knew about this my article” and decided to use the method I described. He created BCNext — the identity under which the NXT project was launched in 2013 — and many years later cryptographically confirmed that BCNext is him by signing a message from the NXT genesis account. He himself openly admits that for ten or fifteen years he has been deliberately leaving false clues for the curious — because “Waiting 10-15 years for good trolling is worth it.”

Second. There’s a sensible way to formulate an answer that stays accurate under any interpretation. Satoshi was not so much a person as a function: create a decentralized system without an owner and disappear, so that the system can live without you. Come-from-Beyond is a creator by that same function. Whether he was personally there in 2009, whether he worked with whoever was there in 2009, or whether he simply learned to play that same role a decade later — the difference between these three options can’t be cleanly separated by the data publicly available today. But the function itself is the same with him. Create and step aside. Build without an owner. Disappear as a center of control, leaving the system to self-reproduce. Let’s make a working assumption for this book: Come-from-Beyond is some part of Satoshi. Not necessarily the very person who sat at the bitcoind console in 2009. Possibly that one. Possibly the one who was nearby. Possibly the one who came later and took up the same functional niche. Possibly came from beyond :cfbtroll: This assumption is enough for what this book is about. We don’t ask the question further. Back to business.
Why This Particular Person

There’s a question this chapter has to answer directly: why was it Come-from-Beyond, and not some other thirty-year-old engineer of the same generation, who saw in 2011 what would only become obvious to everyone else by 2024?
Short answer: because at the same time he had the right technical background, the right discipline of thinking, and he was… a genius.
Let’s break it into parts.

Technical background. By 2011 he had been writing code for ten years in different modes: game engines, bot infrastructure, source-code analysis tools, server applications. That means he had an intuitive grasp of what happens when a distributed system starts to scale. How many people among the early Bitcoin enthusiasts actually understood how the network would behave when the hashrate grew by a billion times? Very few. The answer required either experience working with systems that had gone through this, or the mathematical habit of extrapolating curves into the future. Comefrom-Beyond had both. Cryptographic literacy. His first publication — about methods for detecting plagiarism in code — is, when you get down to it, a problem about how to identify an author by the structural fingerprint left in an artifact. That’s a close cousin of cryptographic problems. The very subject matter in which, by 2008, the entire logic of the Satoshi paper would take shape: hashes, signatures, proofs of key possession. He wasn’t a cryptographer of the academic sort, but he was a person to whom the basic ideas of cryptography didn’t look like magic but like specific engineering work.

Game theory. This aspect is less public, but from my own observations — the technical decisions in NXT, the formulations in early forum discussions, the structure of Qubic — it’s clear that by the early 2010s he was already thinking about distributed systems in this frame. Tit-for-Tat as an idea had been in the air by then for thirty years. Whether he read Axelrod or arrived at the same principles himself, observing repeated interactions in games — unknown; he doesn’t say. What matters is something else: the thinking tool was in his hands. He was looking at Bitcoin not only as code but as a game in which several types of players with their own interests interact under known rules. That’s exactly the angle from which the cracks become visible.

The absence of an external contract. And this is, perhaps, the most important. In 2011, unlike today’s crypto stars, none of the early participants was a “professional crypto founder.” There were no positions, no venture funds specializing in blockchain, no media machine feeding off explaining cryptocurrencies to ordinary people. Comefrom-Beyond was simply interested in the technology and was mining coins. That freed him from a huge layer of cognitive biases that would later make other early participants defend Bitcoin as their personal article of faith.

He had no incentive to defend Bitcoin. He had no incentive to break it either. He had an incentive to honestly assess whether this was working sustainably or not, and if not, to think about what to do next.
He thought. And he started doing.
Two Pseudonyms and One Hint
There’s one more motif that we’ll only sketch here and unpack later.

In 2008–2009, Satoshi Nakamoto appeared on the scene. An anonymous pseudonym that released a working system, replied to community messages over the course of two years, and quietly walked away in early 2011, leaving the project to live a life of its own. In September 2013, on that same BitcoinTalk forum, a user named BCNext appeared. He published an announcement of a future project called NXT, made several posts over the course of two months, and on November 8 of that year fell silent for good. NXT would launch on January 3, 2014. Many years later Come-from-Beyond would cryptographically confirm that BCNext is him, by signing a message from the NXT genesis account. A second identity that turned out to be a continuation of the first line. And there was one more account that’s worth mentioning, even though it’s too early. In 2013 a user named Maria appears on BitcoinTalk. A few short posts. One of them is signed “Maria Bitcoin Founder.” A phrase that in 2013 sounded like someone’s bad joke. The account would get lost in the stream of forum messages, and for ten years no one would remember it.
Maria will return to us in another guise, but later. For now what matters is the general pattern.

What we have in front of us is a person who has already once, in publicly confirmed form, repeated the very structure in which Satoshi was made. Create under a pseudonym, launch a working product, step aside, leave the system to live. This isn’t a one-off coincidence anymore, it’s a regularity beginning to form. And if we accept the working assumption we arrived at on the previous page — that Come-from-Beyond is some part of Satoshi — then the regularity becomes a rule. The same method, applied either by different people or by the same person across different projects, gives the same result. Good engineering is done without a name. Good systems live without a creator. Everything else is detail, which we’ll work through in the chapters to come. By 2013 Now let’s look at where Come-from-Beyond stands at the end of 2012 — at the moment when he’s ready to make his first full step onto the stage.

Behind him are ten-plus years of engineering work. A published article on software code analysis. Practical expertise in distributed systems, gained in the gaming industry and the bot environment. Early participation in the Bitcoin community since 2010. Enough early bitcoins to have capital and independence. An understanding of Bitcoin’s problems formulated two years before they showed up in public. A multi-year parallel project (Aigarth), for which a Bitcoin-like network is infrastructure, not an end in itself. Cryptographic literacy. An understanding of game theory. The discipline that won’t let him build a coin with a twenty-percent stake for himself. The habit of disappearing once a project is finished.

“Qubic is my first project, envisioned before Nxt and IOTA,” he’ll say in 2024. But Qubic is too ambitious a project for 2013. The technology isn’t ready. The infrastructure isn’t ready. The community isn’t ready. Doing Qubic in 2013 means failing for sure. So he does what any smart engineer with a long-term task does: he breaks it down into intermediate steps. First — show the world that Proof-of-Stake works. That’ll cost him — by his own estimate — five minutes for the algorithm and two months for the code. Under this, the NXT project will open, on behalf of the BCNext identity. The first pre-ICO in history will launch, the first community of long-term holders in history will gather, it will become at its peak the third cryptocurrency in the world by capitalization, deliver the first place by ROI in the entire history of the crypto industry — 1,265,555 percent according to Cointelegraph — and be replaced through Ardor with a one-to-one airdrop. That’ll take him about ten years.

As the next step he’ll start work in 2014–2015 on a second project — IOTA — where he’ll try to solve the problem of “how to make a blockchain without a chain of blocks.” That’ll work too. The world’s second-place cryptocurrency by ROI according to that same Cointelegraph ranking — 424,084 percent. That’ll take him another five years or so and end in a painful internal conflict with co-founders. He’ll leave. And only in 2022, drawing on the experience of two previous launches, with evidence behind him that his engineering decisions are accepted by the market and make people millionaires, with the technical and infrastructural readiness that didn’t exist in 2013, will he finally launch Qubic. The project he had been envisioning for twenty years. The project in which he tries to bring it all together: useful mining, AI training, an economy without a controlling owner, infrastructure capable of withstanding scale and not starting to drift toward oligopoly.

Two networks before Qubic — first and second place by ROI in the entire history of crypto ICOs. Twenty years of work on one big idea. The habit of leaving when a project is done. A method in which the creator disappears so that the system can live on. By 2013, he already has everything he needs.
Time to step onto the stage.

Up to this point I’ve been assembling the story out of scraps. Out of fifteen thousand messages on BitcoinTalk, late interviews, throwaway remarks, three sets of technical fingerprints. Starting in 2013 it gets easier to assemble: public records, verifiable ICOs, known names, open court documents in Norwegian. The man who in the previous chapter was a shadow on the forum now starts making things that stay. Three things. Three cryptocurrency networks, each with its own history, its own team, its own peak, and its own end. Looked at from the outside, these are three different projects with different architectures and different fates. NXT launched in January 2014, became the world’s third cryptocurrency by capitalization, and was smoothly replaced by a successor. IOTA launched a year later, drifted away from its principles, and left behind public lawsuits in Norway on which its creator spent more than a million dollars of his personal money. Qubic launched in April 2022 and, as of early 2026, is still running.

Looked at from the inside — from Come-from-Beyond’s side — these aren’t three projects. It’s one project, broken into three stages, stretched over thirteen years, and it will end one more year from now, in April 2027.

Imagine an architect who has to build a bridge across a chasm no one has crossed yet. The technology for building such a bridge doesn’t yet exist. So the architect builds two smaller crossings along the way — not for the sake of the crossings, but for the sake of experience. To learn how the material behaves. To train the workers. To convince the people on the other shore that bridges, in general, can exist. The crossings turn out to be useful — people walk across them, they become local infrastructure, the newspapers write about them. But the architect knows that this isn’t the main thing. The main thing is still ahead.

This chapter is about three such constructions. Two are already done. The third is in progress. The fourth construction, if you take this metaphor further, is the architect’s departure at the moment when the bridge is built and tested. By his plan, that’s supposed to happen on April 13, 2027. But the fourth — at the end.
NXT. January 2014 — the first crossing

On September 28, 2013, on the BitcoinTalk forum, a user under the handle BCNext appears and publishes a short announcement. The announcement says: a new cryptocurrency will soon be launched, built entirely on Proof-of-Stake — no mining, no electricity burning, no ASICs, no Bitcoin lineage. The programming language is Java, not C+ +. Distribution: the first ICO in crypto history — anyone interested sends BCNext bitcoins, and in exchange, at the moment of launch, receives a proportional share in the new network.
The announcement is short, no whitepaper. A few technical clarifications. A promise that the network will be launched “in the coming months.”

By that time, the crypto community treated the idea of Proof-of-Stake roughly the way they treated perpetual motion. Everyone understood that theoretically it should be possible, but every known attempt — Peercoin in 2012, several smaller experiments — either turned out to be a hybrid with Proof-of-Work or had structural problems like “nothing at stake” (where, at the moment a network forks, it’s profitable for a miner to vote for both branches at once, and the network loses the ability to come to agreement). Building a clean, working, stable 100% PoS was an open research problem several teams had been working on for years.

BCNext spent on solving it, by his own later admission, five minutes on the algorithm itself and two months on the code. “In 2013 we didn’t have non-flawed PoS yet and the idea looked cool, so BCNext spent 5 mins to invent working 100% PoS algo and extra 2 months to code it. Then he has gone for good because Nxt was a side-chick” — he’ll write in January 2023. Another remark of his, more than a year later: “Don’t worry, in Nxt I warned in advance that Nxt had been a side-chick and I implemented PoS because of Spanish shame which I was feeling, observing whole crypto industry being unable to implement such easy thing.”

“Spanish shame” (vergüenza ajena) is shame for someone else, for the way they’re embarrassing themselves. He acted like a man who looks at collective helplessness and, with a sigh, silently does the work himself.

The entire NXT codebase: three thousand lines of Java. “Nxt was 3k lines,” as Comefrom-Beyond will put it briefly in October 2020. For comparison: by 2026, the average Layer-1 cryptocurrency runs to hundreds of thousands of lines. NXT was the most compact fully functional crypto network of its time and probably remains one of the most compact to this day.

LAUNCH AND RESULTS. The ICO ran from September 28 through the end of November 2013. Twenty-one bitcoins were collected — about 14,000 dollars at the exchange rate of the time. Distributed proportionally among 73 participants. A few years later, that initial sum would turn into a market cap measured in hundreds of millions. On November 8, 2013, BCNext makes his last post under that account.

On January 3, 2014, at 02:08 UTC, the first NXT block is created. The network is live. What follows is something nobody expected. NXT works. Pure Proof-of-Stake, no mining, no electricity burning, no Bitcoin dependency, climbs the rankings, and at its peak becomes the world’s third cryptocurrency on CoinMarketCap — beneath only Bitcoin and Ripple. “Nxt was #3 on CMC, right below Bitcoin and Ripple (which isn’t actually a cryptocoin)” — Come-from-Beyond’s exact phrasing years later. As he himself put it elsewhere, summarizing his record: “Invented and implemented first working 100% Proof-of-Stake. Conducted first ICO (and all the others followed). Created the first coin which wasn’t a clone of Bitcoin.”

By 2017, at the peak of the next crypto cycle, NXT will enter the Cointelegraph ranking “Top 10 ICOs by ROI in History” — and take first place there with a return of 1,265,555 percent. More than one million two hundred thousand percent. Twelve and a half thousand x. The source matters precisely because it’s third-party: Cointelegraph ranks the history of crypto ICOs by open data, and NXT comes out higher than Ethereum, higher than everything else.

In April 2014, Come-from-Beyond’s contract formally ends. BCNext leaves — silently, as promised. This departure had been announced in advance. The community had been warned: as Come-from-Beyond will summarize it years later, “in the very beginning of Nxt I warned community that it’s my temporary project.”

Many years later, Come-from-Beyond signs a message from the NXT genesis account. Only BCNext could have the private key to that account, because BCNext is the one who created the first block. When the signature from that key is set down by Come-from-Beyond, that’s a cryptographic proof: BCNext and Come-from-Beyond are the same person. The first promised departure turns out, at the same time, to be the first publicly confirmed link between pseudonyms. In the NXT community this link is by now treated as a settled fact — established and not requiring further discussion. The network itself keeps running. By 2018 Come-from-Beyond, together with the company Jelurida (which by then had become NXT’s main maintainer), launches a new project — Ardor — and does an airdrop to all NXT holders at one-to-one. Anyone who held NXT receives an equivalent amount of the new coin for free. As Come-from-Beyond will summarize the move in 2024: “Nxt was replaced by Ardor which did 1:1 airdrop to all nxt holders, then Ardor pivoted to B2B sector, anyway, in the very beginning of Nxt I warned community that it’s my temporary project.”

NXT, meanwhile, doesn’t go anywhere. It keeps running in parallel with Ardor to this day. “Nxt is still running,” Come-from-Beyond observes in May 2023. In 2026 — also still working. The first network into which CfB invested his first departure outlived thirteen years. Holders who didn’t manage to sell at the peak got Ardor for free in the airdrop. As he’ll note separately: “Every nxt holder got corresponding amount of ardor and earned good profits.” This wasn’t abandonment — it was orderly succession.
What NXT did first
To get a sense of the scale, it’s useful to list how many “firsts in history” are recorded in those three thousand lines of Java.

The first working 100% Proof-of-Stake. “Nxt wasn’t improved version, it was 1st, never seen implementation of pure PoS,” in Come-from-Beyond’s own phrasing. Not a hybrid, not an experiment — a working, stable one that lived through every market cycle. All later PoS networks — Ethereum after the 2022 merge, Cardano, Solana, Polkadot — appeared later and in many ways inherited ideas first realized in NXT. The first ICO in history. The model “collect bitcoins, distribute the new coin proportionally at the moment of launch” was first done specifically for NXT. Ethereum in 2014 ran an ICO on roughly the same scheme. The whole subsequent enormous wave of 2017 ICOs that crashed the market and triggered a regulatory wave — all of them trace structurally back to the NXT model.

The first cryptocurrency not in C++. Before NXT, every cryptocurrency — Bitcoin, Litecoin, Dogecoin, the rest — was a fork or a variation of Bitcoin’s C++ code. NXT was written from scratch in Java. As Come-from-Beyond noted in late 2023, having stumbled on an article about it: “Spotted an article I’ve never seen before, looks like Nxt was the first non-C++ crypto.” That sounds like an accountant’s detail, but it actually means NXT was the first cryptocurrency built not as a variation of Bitcoin but as an independent architecture.

The first NXT Asset Exchange — an on-chain exchange. The ability to create and trade tokenized assets directly on the network, with no intermediary. A concept that in 2020 will explode in the form of DeFi on Ethereum and bring billions in turnover. The NXT Alias System — a name service on the blockchain. Mapping short readable names to addresses. Roughly what the Ethereum Name Service (ENS) will do in 2017 was already working in NXT in 2014.

All of this — without a whitepaper. Without a scientific paper, without a formal protocol specification. “None of my projects had whitepapers, I’m an engineer, not a writer,” Come-from-Beyond will say in March 2024. And separately, in December 2023, with a characteristic intonation: “Superstition, Nxt had no whitepaper and made many people millionaires. Do you need WP or become rich?”

But the main thing about NXT’s history isn’t what was done there for the first time. The main thing is that this project, from the very start, was flagged as intermediate. “I did quit Nxt coz of it being just a detour, because PoS was trivial and still cryptocommunity wasn’t able to implement it” — that’s how he’ll put it in October 2023. Detour: the side road, the way around.
The first crossing was built to show that it was possible. The material held up. The workers got trained. People came to believe that bridges exist.
He could move on to the next.
IOTA. 2014–2019 — the second crossing

If NXT was proof that Proof-of-Stake works, IOTA was an attempt to solve a problem that PoS doesn’t solve: how to build a network that has no chain of blocks at all. The whole architecture of Bitcoin (and NXT, and every PoS network that came after) is built as a linear sequence of blocks added to a single main chain. This has two problems. The first is a fundamental fee per transaction, because space in a block is limited and there’s an auction for it. The second is a fundamental ceiling on throughput, because fixed-size blocks appear at a fixed rate. Attempts to scale run into one or the other.

The alternative that began to be discussed in academic circles by 2013 was to give up the linear chain and instead use a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each transaction itself confirms several earlier ones; the network grows like a tree, not like a rope. Theoretically this gives throughput that grows with the number of participants and removes competition for block space — which is to say, fees.
Theoretically. In practice, by 2014 nobody had launched a DAG network. There were papers, there were ideas, there were some mathematical models. There was no working network.

IOTA was the first. The author of the mathematical description — the whitepaper called “Tangle” — was Sergei Popov, a mathematician by training. As Come-from-Beyond will put it in August 2021, “Popov wrote Tangle whitepaper.” The engineering implementation, that is, writing the working code, was handled by Come-from-Beyond and several other people. IOTA itself didn’t have a whitepaper — it had the Tangle whitepaper, signed by Popov. “IOTA had no whitepaper, only Tangle did,” he’ll clarify in July 2024.

In August 2021 he’ll clarify another detail, important for what happens next: at the moment IOTA’s genesis block was created, David Sønstebø — the man who in a few years’ time will be referred to in the public sphere as “IOTA co-founder” — was not a member of the team. He joined later. At the moment the network launched, he was not in it. This isn’t a contested interpretation, it’s a factual statement: “Dom is not a founder, he wasn’t even a member of IOTA team when genesis was created.”

IOTA launched in June 2016. By the peak of the next cycle, late 2017 to early 2018, it will enter the same Cointelegraph ranking as NXT. Second place. Return of 424,084 percent. Four thousand two hundred forty-one x. Higher than Ethereum’s. Lower — only than NXT’s.
Two networks from one person — first and second place in the entire history of crypto ICOs by return. Cointelegraph, not Come-from-Beyond, was the one who counted. It’s a public ranking.
What happens next

In 2017–2018, the IOTA Foundation (IF) is set up around IOTA — a German non-profit registered in Berlin. The goal: structural project governance, grant infrastructure, corporate partnerships. On paper, everything looks like every serious crypto project of that period.
In practice, by Come-from-Beyond’s account, what starts next is what in his conversations five years later will be called by one word — collapse.

“In IOTA everything stopped working as intended after IOTA Foundation was created. They took all resources for meaningless partnerships, so I quitted IOTA and decided to run Qubic standalone, instead of running it on IOTA” — phrasing from July 2024.

And in fuller form, July 2025: “IOTA collapsed because of people embezzling money and resources for own benefit. They literally took money and devs dedicated to core development to develop and promote side-projects related to IOTA, they invested into.” I won’t retell the details. They’re partly public — in open court documents in Norway, where in 2019–2021 the main bulk of the legal dispute was moved. Part is closed. Part is in correspondence that will never become public.
A few facts that are recorded and verifiable:

Come-from-Beyond left IOTA around 2019. The departure was public, with a stated reason — as he put it himself, “IOTA Foundation collapsed into gang of those worrying only about money, not achievements.” The network itself wasn’t destroyed. He didn’t use his role as a core developer to bring IOTA down from the inside, although he had every technical means to do so.

In parallel, his access to the Jinn documentation was cut off — Jinn being a project to develop a proprietary ternary processor, conceived as the hardware layer for IOTA (and for Aigarth, but more on that later). “David holds Jinn IP hostage, so I had to invent algo constructing Jinn circuits without human assistance. Now it’s being used in Qubic mining” — short phrasing from December 2021. Jinn Labs, the team that had been working on the chip, was fired by Sønstebø.

On the Norwegian lawsuits Come-from-Beyond spent, by his own public admission, a seven-figure sum in dollars — more than a million dollars of his personal money. By August 2021 he had already won at least one case — against IOTA AS and the IOTA Foundation. As he puts it: “The current won lawsuit wasn’t against D&D, it was against IOTA AS and the IOTA Foundation.”

From the standpoint of our story — the story of the “create and leave” method — one detail matters. The departure from IOTA was not a planned departure, the way BCNext’s was from NXT. It was a forced departure at a moment when a project conceived as an incubator for Qubic had been captured from within and was no longer fit for its original purpose. Come-from-Beyond doesn’t leave because the work is done. He leaves because the work can no longer be done here. That’s a different kind of departure — but on the result of the method it acts symmetrically. The idea evacuates, the network keeps living its own life, its builders commercialize it further as best they can. Jinn and the algorithm that will become the heart of Qubic Here we have to pause on one technical detail, because it’s the most important point of connection between two chapters of this book and the explanation for why Qubic is built the way it is.

Jinn was a ternary (trinary) processor, conceived as a hardware accelerator for IOTA operations and, in the longer term, as the execution layer for Aigarth. Ternary logic is rare in modern computing but theoretically more efficient for certain classes of tasks, including a number of neural-network operations. Jinn existed as a project of the Jinn Labs team starting in 2015, had its own IPO (JINN token holders received a share in the future product), and had working prototypes.

When Sønstebø cut off Come-from-Beyond’s access to the documentation and fired the team, physically making the next version of the chip became impossible. But the software task — “how to describe the schematic of such a processor automatically, without manual engineering work, given only a specification of what it has to compute” — remained.
Come-from-Beyond solved that task over the next year and a half.

The algorithm he came up with takes a description of a desired function — for example, a small artificial neural network — and automatically assembles, out of elementary operations, a logical schematic that implements that function. Without a human. Without an engineer manually trying out architectures. A pure search through the space of possible schematics.
“Now it’s being used in Qubic mining” — short phrase, December 2021.

This isn’t an incidental technical aside. This is the core of what’s called UPoW in Qubic — Useful Proof of Work. Qubic miners aren’t picking hashes; they’re running automatic synthesis of neural-network schematics. Each attempt is a piece of useful computational work which, in aggregate, trains something larger.

One thing matters to nail down here. The loss of Jinn forced him to invent something that would later become the heart of Qubic. If Sønstebø hadn’t cut off his access — there would have been no forcing condition. With no forcing condition — no algorithm. With no algorithm — Qubic would not look the way it looks. This is one of those rare cases where you can pinpoint the moment at which a hostile circumstance becomes the precondition for the next architecture.

Adversity to architecture — trouble turning into design. Engineers in our industry rarely get to point at such a moment in their own biography. Come-from-Beyond can. In an early Qubic explainer, he summarizes what he was actually building: “Qubic began life as as an initialism-turned-acronym, QBC, which stands for quorum-based computation… Specifically, Qubic is a protocol that specifies IOTA’s solution for quorum-based computations, including such constructs as oracle machines, outsourced computations, and smart contracts.”
Qubic. April 2022 — the main thing
On April 13, 2022, Qubic’s first block is created. The network is live on mainnet. Come-from-Beyond launches what he had in mind twenty years earlier.

In this chapter I’m not going to retell Qubic piece by piece. That requires the entire next part of the book, and that part is in progress. Here — only the general outline. A few entities, five paragraphs. Just enough to make it clear what came together out of the experience of the two earlier projects.

676 computors. The Qubic network is held up not by an arbitrary number of validators and not by an open mining pool, but by a fixed pool of 676 participants, partly rotated each week according to a publicly announced rule. The number 676 isn’t random, but the explanation of its meaning is in the next chapter.

UPoW — Useful Proof of Work. The very thing discussed in the IOTA section. Miners aren’t picking random numbers; they’re doing useful computational work — automatic synthesis of neural-network schematics. In aggregate, this work trains the platform that has lived in Come-from-Beyond’s head since the early 2000s under the working name Aigarth.

Aigarth. I’ll limit myself to calling it “an AI platform conceived by CfB since the early 2000s, for which all of this cryptocurrency infrastructure is a preparatory skeleton.” What Aigarth actually is, how it’s built inside, what makes it different from ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and the other public large models of 2025–2026 — is the conversation of part five of the book. Within this chapter, only one thing matters: the cryptocurrency part of Qubic exists for the sake of Aigarth, not the other way around. The Arbitrator. In the current architecture of Qubic there’s a special role — the Arbitrator, performed manually by Come-from-Beyond himself. Its functions are bounded by the source code: he can’t print coins, he can’t change transactions, he can’t shut anyone’s wallet. But certain coordinating decisions — for example, the change of the rules for selecting computors for the next week — go through him. This role is temporary. By the announced plan, on April 13, 2027, exactly five years after the mainnet launch, the Arbitrator will be abolished. The last lever through which the creator can touch the network will be dismantled.

This is the fourth departure. If we accept the working assumption of the previous chapter — that Come-from-Beyond is some part of Satoshi — this is the fourth public departure in the same chain. Satoshi in December 2010, BCNext in April 2014, Comefrom-Beyond himself out of IOTA around 2019, and the fourth — April 13, 2027, the Arbitrator of Qubic.
Three have already happened. The fourth is announced, dated, and written into the protocol.

If it happens as planned — the method is confirmed for the fourth time. If it doesn’t — the method isn’t confirmed. That’s a falsifiable prediction with a specific date attached. Engineers’ biographies don’t often contain such things.

It’s worth noting that Qubic is a return to the original concept. The very same quorum-based computation that was QBC inside IOTA was pulled out, rethought, strengthened by experience, and made standalone. Twenty years of work on one big idea came together into one network.

One more characteristic detail, of the kind that doesn’t show up in reports. Qubic didn’t start with an empty audience. At launch, the project already had a community — the same people who held NXT, then came into IOTA, and now came into Qubic. Comefrom-Beyond described this himself in November 2023 with a vivid metaphor: “Ever seen game guilds which play different games together? They go from game to game as a formed guild without a founder. We came to Qubic from IOTA, were in Nxt before that.” That means Qubic didn’t have to explain from scratch who Come-from-Beyond was and why his engineering judgment was worth trusting. A group of people who had convinced themselves through their own experience were already walking with him. And this, by the way, separately explains why the early Qubic community is structurally different from those of random 2022 crypto projects: it has a disproportionate number of people with thirteen years of crypto experience and the memory of two prior transitions.

Come-from-Beyond ranks his three projects himself, briefly and without false modesty: “Kaspa, IOTA, Qubic. Qubic is the best so far.” (Kaspa in this list is a network not made by him; he mentions it as a comparison, because its developers use part of his early DAG research. What matters is not Kaspa but the other two elements — IOTA and Qubic. By his own assessment, Qubic is above IOTA.)

He came to the Qubic launch not just with an idea. He came with thirteen years of experience launching working crypto networks, with a doubly confirmed track record, and with an algorithm that nobody but him could have invented, because nobody else had lost Jinn.
Under the hood: the pattern of three projects
If you put the three projects side by side, seven shared traits become visible. Not one or two — seven, repeating systematically enough that you can’t write them off as coincidence.

First, the pseudonym as a signature. BCNext for NXT. Come-from-Beyond for IOTA and Qubic. In both cases the handle isn’t a way to hide. It’s a way to sign, and at the same time to separate the man from the project. BCNext isn’t a mask, it’s an identity that has its own private key and its own cryptographic tie to the NXT genesis block. Come-from-Beyond isn’t a mask, it’s the identity under which all public activity since 2011 has been carried out.

Second, compact code. NXT — three thousand lines of Java. Qubic core — also compact; Come-from-Beyond hasn’t named exact figures publicly, but by indirect signs and by the way he talks about it, it’s the same orders of magnitude. IOTA — here it’s harder, because the source code was picked up and reworked by the IOTA Foundation after Come-from-Beyond’s departure, and judging the size of the original by the current state of the network would be incorrect.

Third, no whitepapers. “None of my projects had whitepapers, I’m an engineer, not a writer.” Two of the three networks — first and second in the history of crypto ICOs by return. This isn’t an oversight, it’s a principle. Working code matters more than a document. A document describes the intent; the code implements it. If the code works, the intent is verified; if the code doesn’t work, no beautiful document will save it. Fourth, warning the community in advance. NXT was openly declared a “temporary project” at the very start. IOTA — when the conflict with the Foundation became visible, Come-from-Beyond announced his departure and its reasons publicly. Qubic — regularly, almost weekly, in his public correspondence Come-from-Beyond reminds people of the risks and that Qubic holders have to make decisions for themselves. This isn’t modesty; it’s a disclaimer written into the methodology.

Fifth, leaving at the right moment. BCNext — in April 2014, when NXT was launched and working. Come-from-Beyond out of IOTA — around 2019, when it became clear that the Foundation had captured the project. The planned abolition of the Qubic Arbitrator — April 13, 2027. One departure was planned. One was forced. One is still ahead. But in all three cases the structure is the same: the creator steps back, the network continues. Sixth, track record. Two of the three networks — first and second place by ROI in the history of crypto ICOs according to a third-party Cointelegraph ranking. 1,265,555 percent and 424,084 percent. Come-from-Beyond comments on this briefly: “Check Nxt and IOTA price chart, you can spot places where we were getting rid of useless holders. Do you think getting top ROI 2 times is a coincidence? I’m an engineer and engineering laws work same way everywhere.”

This is an important quote, and two things in it are worth attention. The first — “we were getting rid of useless holders.” This refers to periodic events — including FUD, provocations, price corrections — that wash low-conviction holders out of the project before the project goes mainstream. These aren’t accidents, they’re a deliberate part of the strategy. This explains why Come-from-Beyond himself sometimes broadcasts publicly skeptical things about his own projects. It’s not a paradox — it’s a filter. The second thing — “engineering laws work same way everywhere.” He doesn’t say “I got lucky.” He says “I’m an engineer.” That’s a direct answer to any argument of the form “crypto is a lottery.”

Seventh, the community as a guild that travels. It was already mentioned in the Qubic section — I’ll just repeat the formula: NXT → IOTA → Qubic holders move through projects the way a gaming guild moves through games. This structurally lowers the launch cost of each subsequent project: part of the trust carries over from the previous one. Not all of it; each project still has to prove technical merit from scratch. But the basic trust in the engineer himself — carries over.

And an eighth trait, separate, not about the projects but about role separation. In all three cases Come-from-Beyond is the engineer, the inventor, the architect. The commercializing is done by others. In NXT — the company Jelurida, which picked up support after BCNext’s departure, made Ardor, took it B2B. In IOTA — the IOTA Foundation, which took the project and steered it on its own course (in Come-from-Beyond’s view, into a dead end, but that’s now its own responsibility). In Qubic — a distributed community of developers and ecosystem projects who, as of 2026, are building applications, exchanges, bridges, and services on top of the core protocol. Inventor and commercializer are two different roles, rarely combined in one person. With Come-from-Beyond, that discipline of separation is now written into his biography three times. Seven traits, reproduced across three projects. Different architectures, different markets, different years, different teams. The same person, the same method, the same result.
Time to move on

By April 13, 2022, Come-from-Beyond had everything he didn’t have in 2013. Twenty years of thinking about Aigarth. Two launched crypto projects, one fully stepped away from, one forcibly left in someone else’s hands. Two confirmed places in the historical top by return on investment. The algorithm for automatic schematic synthesis, born out of the loss of Jinn. A community that had come along with him from the previous projects. An industrial maturity that didn’t exist thirteen years earlier. And — the main thing, perhaps — proof to himself that the “create and leave” method really does work. Twice. In projects with different architectures and different fates. With a result that an outside third-party ranking nailed down in the top two slots.
Qubic launched. The third project by sequence, but the first by intent. The very one for which everything else had been done.

And here, in 2026, standing midway between launch and the planned departure of the Arbitrator, you can take a step to the side and ask the question this part of the book has been answering at length: who is Come-from-Beyond, and why is it worth believing he knows what he’s doing. The answer, assembled from the two previous chapters, comes out like this: an engineer with twenty years of experience, who has twice proven his method, who publicly announces his departures in advance, who has been working on one big task (Aigarth) since the early 2000s, who uses cryptocurrencies as infrastructure rather than as the goal, and who has scheduled his fourth departure on a specific date. If that departure happens — the method is confirmed for the fourth time. If it doesn’t — it isn’t. That’s an honest falsifier.

But the next question is a different one. Not who and not why, but how. How exactly is the Qubic network built so as to be capable of living without its creator? Why 676 participants — and not 700 and not 1,000? How are they replaced every week, who selects them, and by what rules? What happens to the QU coins inside, how are they emitted, and where do they disappear to? How exactly does UPoW work, and how does useful computational work turn into protection of the network from attacks? And the main thing — how is the moment of transition arranged, when the Arbitrator is abolished and the last point of human governance disappears from the protocol? These questions aren’t about the man. They’re about engineering. And answering them requires going inside the protocol.

In the first chapter of this book we talked about the cascade of coal as a metaphor for the development of technologies. Darby in 1709 obtained the first iron smelted on coke, but didn’t know what to do with the gas going off into the air. Murdoch in 1792 figured out how to collect that gas into a pipe and use it separately to light streets — and that moment was the start of a completely new industry that within a century replaced the city’s infrastructure. The qualitative leap — from “burn coal for heat” to “collect what gets released in the process and put it to work.”

Bitcoin in this metaphor is Darby. The first fire. An incredible achievement that opened an era, but single-purpose: all the computational power released as the network does its work is burned to no purpose, like the gas going up into the sky over Darby’s blast furnace in Coalbrookdale at the start of the eighteenth century. Qubic in this metaphor is Murdoch. The moment when people start collecting the gas into a pipe. The Coalbrookdale of the digital age — that, probably, is what historians of technology will call this phase a hundred years from now, if there’s anyone left to do it. That phase is already arriving. About its inner workings — the next part of the book. Its first chapter is about the 676 voices that hold the network up.
Mechanics
P A r T i i i The Mechanics

The number 676 isn’t aesthetic. It isn’t pretty. It isn’t symbolic. It’s the exact number of participants who simultaneously make up the main load-bearing structure of Qubic at any given moment in time. Six hundred and seventy-six computers, connected into a single network and voting every few fractions of a second on one and the same question: “what will be the next state of the whole system.”

If you want to picture this construction in a single image, picture a parliament with 676 seats. The parliament has a rule: to pass any decision, you need to gather no fewer than 451 votes in favor. Four hundred fifty-one is just over two-thirds of 676. Less than that — the decision doesn’t pass.

The parliament has no speaker with special powers. It has no factions with privileges. No party discipline. No lobbyists whose role in the corridor differs from the role of deputies on the floor. Each of the 676 has exactly one vote, and that vote can’t be bought, bought out, pooled, or converted into two votes, no matter how much work that deputy did over the past week.

Once a week, the composition of the parliament partially changes. Not entirely — gradually, by a fixed rule. Those who showed the worst result over the past week yield their seats to those who, over the same week, performed more useful work and are now claiming entry. The number of deputies replaced at one time is rigidly capped — it can’t be inflated by a one-off decision, and it can’t be reset to zero. The parliament refreshes on a regular rhythm, the way leaf cover turns over, only not in autumn but every seven days.

That, at the level of a rough analogy, is how the Qubic network is built. The analogy, as always, has a limit beyond which it shouldn’t be stretched. 676 computers don’t argue, don’t deliver speeches, don’t vote against their convictions under pressure. They execute a precise sequence of cryptographic operations in which a “vote” is a signature and a “decision” is the new state of the network being accepted. But the basic principle — a fixed small circle, a two-thirds threshold for any change, regular partial rotation — is exactly the one described above. That’s the frame to start from. There’s another, more organic metaphor worth mentioning here once and returning to closer to the end of the book. Beneath the mushrooms in a forest ecosystem lies the mycelium — a network of fine threads stretching tens of meters in every direction. Mycelium has no center. It has no owner. Individual sections of it die off and regenerate continuously; the whole, meanwhile, goes on existing longer than any of its fragments. When I first saw a diagram of Qubic’s 676 computors next to a diagram of mycorrhiza, I was struck by the topological similarity. This isn’t mysticism, and it isn’t poetry; it’s simply a statement of the fact that distributed systems without a center — biological or engineered — converge on the same architectural solutions.

This chapter is about the mechanics. How the 676 actually vote. Why any decision requires a threshold of 451, rather than, say, 339 (a simple majority) or 676 (unanimity). What a tick is — the basic time unit of the network in which all of this manages to happen. How the weekly rotation of membership works, and why it’s precisely this rotation that makes the network structurally resistant to capture from within.

In the previous chapter I compared Qubic to Murdoch in 1792 — the man who first collected the gas being wasted from blast furnaces and channeled it into a pipe. The 676 voices aren’t Qubic’s “gas pipe” itself. The gas pipe is the next chapter after this one, on useful computational work. But for the pipe to hold and not be captured — first you need a construction that holds it. Floor, walls, foundation. Coalbrookdale of the digital age, day one: assembling the frame.
Let’s start with the threshold of 451.
A Quorum of 451 out of 676

If a parliament has 676 seats and any decision requires a minimum of 451 votes in favor, then what a hypothetical coalition capable of coordinating would hold is not a majority of seats but a supermajority. A majority is when 51 out of 100 back you. A supermajority is when two-thirds back you. Formally: 2/3 of 676 is 450.67. Round up, because a vote is a discrete quantity: there are no fractional votes. You get 451. Where did the two-thirds logic come from in the first place, rather than, say, threequarters or a simple majority of 50% + 1? Two-thirds is the classical threshold in distributed systems where some participants may behave dishonestly or simply fail. It came from a field that computer researchers began developing in the late 1970s under the name “the Byzantine generals problem.” The name is conventional; it’s taken from a parable about a group of Byzantine generals who, having surrounded a city, must agree on a common plan (storm or retreat) through messengers, knowing that some of the generals may be traitors and will pass on contradictory messages. The essence of the problem: at what maximum number of “traitors” in the group are the honest participants still able to arrive at a single correct decision? The mathematical answer turned out to be hard. If traitors can number up to onethird of the group, the honest two-thirds can work out a common decision that the traitors are unable to derail. If there are more traitors than one-third — no protocol trick can save the situation; the group is in principle incapable of guaranteed agreement. Two to one is the mathematical boundary of a distributed system’s resilience to dishonest or failed participants.

A natural question may come up: why not get by with a simple majority, that is, 51%? In ordinary voting in a live parliament, where everyone voting is in the same hall and can ask one another to repeat themselves, a simple majority works fine. In a distributed network, connected only by messages, things get more complicated. Imagine for a second the following scenario. 339 computors sent in their votes for one version of the new state; another 337 voted for a different, conflicting one. Who’s right? If there are 226 malicious participants in the network, a situation is theoretically possible in which those 226 sent half the network one vote and the other half the opposite vote. Each part of the network sees a local majority for its own version and accepts it as canonical. The network splits into two parallel worlds, each of them confident of its own rightness. This is the classical “Byzantine” problem in action. The two-thirds threshold eliminates this possibility: under any arrangement, if 451 participants voted the same way, a second group of 451 in the network physically cannot exist, because 451 + 451 = 902 > 676. Therefore, any decision that gathered 451 votes is unambiguously canonical. An alternative branch, having pulled together the same level of support in parallel, doesn’t exist by arithmetic.

This boundary is wired into the Qubic protocol literally. Of the 676 computors — those same “parliamentary deputies” — up to 225 participants can be unavailable, broken, caught in a network partition, or colluding against the network at the same time. That’s less than one-third. The remaining 451 are already a supermajority; they continue to make decisions, and any decision they make is canonical for the network. But if 226 or more go against the network, then the network, by protocol, cannot reach consensus; it freezes, waiting for a workable mass to be restored. It doesn’t start accepting “alternative” blocks, doesn’t split into warring branches, doesn’t drift into a state from which it would later need to vote on its own rescue. It stops. This is, in a sense, a safety technique opposite to Bitcoin’s: Bitcoin keeps working even under a strong concentration of hashrate, just with degraded protection. Qubic either works with guaranteed protection, or doesn’t work at all.
Now an important, subtle, often misunderstood detail.

Each computor has exactly one vote. Not “one vote per unit of capital.” Not “votes proportional to a computer’s power.” Not “the more I earned in the previous epoch, the more votes I have in this one.” One participant — one vote. It’s a protocol rule that can’t be circumvented, no matter how many resources one participant has accumulated. This, if you step back a moment, is the main structural difference between Qubic and systems in which the weight of a decision is proportional to the resource invested. In Bitcoin, a large pool that has concentrated a big share of the hashrate gets a proportionally larger probability of determining the contents of a block; the more equipment you have, the more weight you have. In classical Proof-of-Stake, a large coin holder gets a proportionally larger probability of becoming a validator; the more money you have, the more weight you have. In both models, accumulated resource is converted into the right to participate in shaping the rules of the next step. In Qubic this conversion is forbidden by the protocol. A computor with a huge fleet of servers and a computor with the minimum configuration that still lets it hold its seat have, in every vote, equal weight — one vote. The only thing many resources buy you is a chance to stay among the 676 and not be displaced in the next epoch. But while you’re in the 676, your weight is exactly the same as anyone else’s.

Here, I think, the attentive reader will recall one of the conditions from chapter three. We formulated it back then in these words: a win in the game must not give the player the ability to change the rules of the game itself. The formulation was abstract; this is its concrete engineering embodiment. Within a single vote, no accumulated advantage converts into votes. Let’s figure out what, exactly, gets voted on. The Tick: The Moment at Which the Network Makes a Decision In ordinary life we think of time as continuous. Week passes into week, day into day, with no clear seams. Distributed networks can’t do that. For 676 computers scattered across the planet to arrive at a common decision about “what is the network’s current state,” they need a common discrete time grid. They need moments when all of them simultaneously look at the world and simultaneously vote.
In Qubic this unit is called a tick.

A tick is one completed round of voting. Roughly the following sequence happens in each tick. First, one of the 676 computors is selected to play the role of “leader” for this tick — it gathers the transactions that came in over the previous micro-interval, orders them, and proposes the resulting bundle as the network’s next state. Then its proposal is broadcast to all the other 675. Each of them, on receiving the proposal, checks it against the protocol — the transactions don’t contradict each other, the leader had the right to propose anything, the signatures are correct — and votes “yes” or abstains. When 451 “yes” votes are collected, the proposed state is accepted as canonically new. The network has taken one step. The next tick begins.

It’s worth emphasizing that the “check” here is not a formality. Each computor holds a complete current picture of the network: which addresses exist, how many coins are on each one, which obligations are already pending, which transactions were accepted in previous ticks. When a proposal from the current leader reaches it, it itself, with its own code, applies all the proposed transactions to its own state and sees whether it gets the same result the leader claimed. If it does — it votes “yes.” If not — it doesn’t vote. For a malicious leader there’s simply no way to push through a false proposal: 675 independent verifiers will run his calculation through themselves at the same time and independently see the discrepancy. The only proposal that survives is one that’s objectively correct by the rules of the protocol.
Two key points of this mechanic are worth singling out.

First — the leader role isn’t fixed. It rotates by a deterministic rule known to all 676 participants in advance. This isn’t an “auction for the right to propose a block,” as in Bitcoin, where the contents of a block are formed by whichever miner first happened to solve a cryptographic puzzle — and that means, with high probability, a large pool. In Qubic, for each tick the leader is known in advance and changes for the next tick. No computor can stably control the flow of proposals; the most it can do is be the leader in its own tick, and in the next one the next computor in the order replaces it. Over a thousand ticks, each of the 676 computors gets to be leader roughly the same number of times.

Second — the decision requires the agreement of a supermajority, not the leader. The leader doesn’t make the decision. The leader proposes. The decision is made by 451 votes. If a leader tries to propose something incorrect — a transaction that breaks the rules of the protocol, or a block with a double spend — then 451 honest computors simply won’t vote in favor. The proposal won’t pass; one tick later, its place will be taken by a proposal from the next leader, and the network’s work will continue. A spoiled leader can’t hold up the network for longer than one tick.

If you translate this into the language of more familiar distributed systems — in Bitcoin every block is formed by exactly one miner (more precisely, by exactly one pool), the one that got lucky finding a hash with the required prefix. The rest of the network can accept that block or reject it, but it’s always one entity that forms it. In Qubic every decision is formed collectively: the leader only puts forward a hypothesis; the supermajority approves it. The difference is in where the decision is concentrated. In Bitcoin — at the point of formation. In Qubic — in distributed voting across the whole network. The exact frequency of ticks — exactly how many of them happen per second — is set by a protocol constant and described in the Qubic technical specification. What matters for this chapter is one thing: there are many ticks per unit of time, the count runs into single digits per second and higher, and each tick is a full round of voting by 676 participants. On the scale of a single day, the Qubic network makes tens or hundreds of thousands of collective decisions, each of which has gone through the quorum of 451.
Now to the most interesting part. Imagine you wanted to capture such a network. What would you need to do?

Rotation: Why the 676 Can’t Be Captured from Within To control the Qubic network, it isn’t enough to buy more equipment than your competitors. It isn’t enough to rent more cloud than the strongest computor. It isn’t enough to band together into a pool. None of these moves will increase your weight in voting — all 676 votes are equal.
What you need is to take as many of the 676 seats as possible. Ideally — 226, to paralyze the network (by making a quorum impossible), or 451, to start forming your own decisions.
This is where the weekly rotation mechanism comes into play.

Time in Qubic is broken into weekly intervals called epochs. An epoch is a unit larger than a tick. Within a single epoch, the composition of the 676 computors is fixed: whoever made it into the epoch works in it until the end. At the boundary between two epochs, part of the composition is replaced: the worst by the results of the past epoch yield their seats to the best of the candidates who have submitted an entry application. “Worst” and “best” — by a single metric: the volume of useful computational work performed over the epoch. As to what “useful work” is in Qubic and why it’s even possible, that’s the next two chapters of the book; here it’s enough to know that each computor, at the close of an epoch, has an unambiguous numerical assessment of its contribution, and that assessment is what decides whether it stays or leaves.
An important structural fact: no more than 225 participants can be replaced at the same time in one epoch transition.
Not 300. Not 400. Not 676. The maximum is 225 out of 676. It’s a protocol constant. Let’s see what follows from this.

Imagine you’re a coordinated group that wants to capture Qubic. You’ve prepared 676 of your own computors, optimized them for maximum performance, and you’re ready to take all 676 seats with your nodes. How many epochs — that is, weeks — will it take you?

In one epoch transition, you can bring at most 225 of yours into the network. Fine; after the first Wednesday you have 225 seats out of 676. The remaining 451 are still the old ones, not yours. At the next epoch transition — at most another 225. Total: 450 out of 676. Still not 451. At the third transition — another 225. Total: 675. At the fourth — one last one. Four weeks minimum, even under absolutely ideal conditions for you, when you take exactly the maximum allowable number of seats every epoch.

But even this is the most favorable scenario for you, and it assumes that in each of four epochs in a row all 225 available seats were filled by precisely your candidates and no one else. It requires that, in performance, your 225 computors be better than all the other honest candidates in the world, simultaneously, week after week. If even in one of those epochs you lose the competition by even fifty positions, your 175 won’t give you the step you need, and the reckoning shifts. If you lose in each epoch by even a hundred positions, the takeover stretches out to two months and more, and all this time the network stays in the hands of the old supermajority.

But this is the hypothetical minimum. In reality you have no guarantee that your 225 candidates will land at the top by work performed. Other computers are working too; they’re submitting entry applications too. Your candidates compete with them not on the basis of “whose team is whose,” but on the basis of who has more useful output for the week. You have to not just prepare 676 machines but make it so that every week your machines steadily outplay all the other applicants in the world. Four weeks in a row. Without a single miss.

And now let’s recall the main thing: as long as you hold fewer than 451 seats, the network is still controlled by the old computors. Any decision goes through the quorum of 451; while you have 225, or 450, or 450 — that decision isn’t made by your people. The old network keeps working normally. The old computors keep noticing the newcomers coming in. If they notice that a coordinated pool of nodes behaving the same way is entering the network, they can react. At the protocol level, no — they have no mechanism to “block the suspicious one.” But at the level of the community watching what’s happening, yes. Qubic has a public market, public communication channels, public technical decisions about the roadmap. Over four weeks of a coordinated attack, the community will have time to see this, discuss it, and possibly respond — with a technical upgrade, a change to the selection rules, the recruitment of new honest computors. There’s also an arithmetical symmetry worth noting. 676 minus 225 equals 451. Exactly the number needed for a quorum. This is no coincidence. It’s a form of symmetry chosen consciously by the developers: even if you imagine the maximally extreme scenario in which all 225 allowable seats have been replaced in a single epoch transition and all of them are malicious, the remaining 451 old, honest computors still hold control over all decisions of the epoch. They make quorum without a single vote from the newcomers. That is, even under the maximum simultaneous invasion, the network doesn’t lose the ability to make decisions on the strength of its prior composition. This is the formulation from which the structural resilience of Qubic follows. Not “the creators hope that no one will attack.” Not “decentralization is our value.” But mathematically: under any sequence of actions permitted by the protocol on the part of an attacker, the network preserves the ability to operate as before for at least one full epoch per every 225 captured seats.
