And during that epoch, a real network of real people has time to see, discuss, and, if necessary, respond.

Here, at this point, it’s worth restating once more what we discussed in chapter three in connection with GHash.IO — the pool that in the summer of 2013 amassed 55% of the Bitcoin network’s hashrate. There the gap between concentration and unblocking the network played out within one turn of the cycle: today 55%, tomorrow a block with a double spend — technically possible. What stopped it was only public pressure, the departure of part of the miners from the pool, reputational damage. There was no mechanical brake.

In Qubic the mechanical brake exists. It requires no public pressure, no voluntary decisions by participants. It’s built into the protocol by the constant “no more than 225 replacements per epoch transition.” Even if the entire community kept silent while an attacker methodically built up its presence month after month, it would still take it no fewer than four weeks to reach 451 of its own seats, and the whole time the network would keep working normally.

This is the very structural mechanism I was building toward in chapter three when I said that mining must produce decentralization, not concentration. A mechanism of negative feedback, which Bitcoin didn’t have and which, if you leave Bitcoin as it is, won’t arise on its own.
Why 676, Specifically
The attentive reader who has read this far has surely already asked themselves: why 676? It looks, to put it mildly, unusual.

The first answer: 676 is 26 squared. A square number. A number convenient for representation as a 26 × 26 table, where each computor occupies one cell and has a row number and a column number. This indexing, as the Qubic technical specifications show, allows the protocol’s internal algorithms — those that handle the distribution of tasks among participants, the routing of votes, the exchange of intermediate data — to work significantly more efficiently than if computors were simply numbered 0 through 675. This is a computational argument, and it entered the network by way of engineering considerations, not aesthetics.
But the main answer is not in the square of 26. The main answer is that 676 turns out to be the golden mean across three conflicting requirements.

The first requirement is diversity. The more participants in the parliament, the harder it is for a single group to capture a majority. From the standpoint of this logic, the bigger 676 is, the better. 10,000 computors would give substantially greater resistance to concentration.

The second requirement is mutual verification. Each of the 676 checks proposals coming in from each of the remaining 675. In every tick. At a frequency of several ticks per second. If there were 10,000 computors, each one would have to check 9,999 others in every tick, and that would create a computational load that ordinary equipment simply couldn’t handle within a single tick. The network would slow down. From the standpoint of this logic, the smaller 676 is, the better. 100 computors would be able to check each other even faster.

The third requirement is fault tolerance. In any physical network, some nodes are unavailable at any given time — because of power outages, internet provider issues, an update that went sideways. For the network to always have 451 working computors for a quorum, 676 has to be noticeably greater than 451. If the network had only 451 computors (right at the quorum), then any one of them going down would stop the network. The more computors above the minimum quorum, the larger the margin of safety. From this standpoint — the bigger, the better.

676 is a compromise. Enough to provide diversity of participants and a reserve for some of them failing. Few enough that each computor can in real time monitor the behavior of each of the remaining 675. The square of an integer, so that internal algorithms work more efficiently. Double two-thirds (451 and 225), so that the construction has the symmetry we discussed above.

If the developers had taken 700, the 2/3 symmetry would have disappeared (700 × 2/3 = 466.67, rounding gives 467, and the formula “maximum replacements per epoch equals the difference between 676 and the quorum” wouldn’t work as neatly). If they had taken 625 (that’s 25²), you’d get less resilience at comparable computational complexity. 729 (27²) — more verification load without proportional gain. 676 is the point where mathematical, computational, and engineering requirements converge in a single number.
Two Orders of Decentralization

It’s useful to see the figure 676 alongside an analogous figure for Bitcoin. In chapter three we mentioned that by 2026 effective control over Bitcoin’s hashrate is concentrated in the four to five largest pools, which together hold around 70–75% of the network’s computational power. Foundry USA — about 29%, AntPool — about 21%, another three or four notable pools — the rest. If you imagine Bitcoin as a “parliament” in which votes are distributed in proportion to invested hashrate, then in this parliament four or five players make most of the decisions. That’s the realistic upper estimate for the effective number of consensus participants in Bitcoin in its current state. 676 to 4–5 is not “a hundred times more.” It’s a different order of magnitude. It’s a structural change in the nature of the network: from one where the big decisions are made by a handful, to one where they’re made by a mid-sized parliament. If you look at this difference through a metric that the crypto community sometimes calls the “decentralization coefficient” (Nakamoto coefficient — the minimum number of participants whose union is capable of attacking the network), then for Bitcoin in 2026 this coefficient equals 3–4. The union of the three largest pools gives the attackers 51%. For Qubic, this coefficient is by construction equal to 226. Two hundred twenty-six is the number of computors that have to be coordinated simultaneously to paralyze the network. Not 3. Not 4. Two hundred twenty-six.

The difference between “three coordinating players” and “two hundred twenty-six coordinating players” is the difference between “possible to come to terms in one evening in one room” and “impossible without a serious organizational structure that itself becomes publicly visible long before the moment of agreement.” Twenty-six people you can still seat at one long table. Two hundred twenty-six — you can’t. Any attempt to assemble such a number of coordinating participants becomes noticeable simply by logistics.

There’s another way of looking at the same gap. Imagine a conspiracy — correspondence, a Telegram chat, a closed meeting. The more participants, the higher the probability that one of them will turn out to be disloyal, accidentally let something slip, or leak the correspondence. For a group of three this probability is small; for a group of twenty it’s already noticeable; for a group of two hundred and twenty-six it’s practically inevitable. The sociology of conspiracies is well studied; historians know that any conspiracy with more than a few dozen participants comes to light within a few weeks or months. This is a property of human nature, not of Qubic; but the construction of Qubic uses this property. It turns an attack that in Bitcoin requires coordinating four players into an attack that in Qubic requires coordinating roughly a hundred times more players. The requirements for organizational complexity grow accordingly, as does the probability of a leak, as does the inability to stay below the radar.

A qualification is in order. This comparison is not “Qubic beat Bitcoin.” Bitcoin wasn’t built to have a high decentralization coefficient in 2026; it was built to launch, in 2009, in complete isolation, without investors, without a team, without an exchange, without legitimacy, the first network of electronic money in history that couldn’t be shut down by a single administrative decision. It met that task. The structural detail by which hashrate consolidates over time is the price paid for an architecture in which anyone can join or leave at any moment. That price was invisible in 2009 because no one was there yet. By 2026 it had become noticeable.

Qubic was built from a different starting point. By 2022 the Bitcoin lesson was in plain view for everyone. Qubic’s developers had the option of laying in a structural anticonsolidation mechanism from the very beginning, at the cost of the network not being, in principle, a “anyone can become a computor at any moment” network — you have to pass through epoch selection and take a seat within the 225 available. This is a tradeoff: openness to arbitrary connection in exchange for guaranteed distributedness. Whether to throw this tradeoff one way or the other is a question that’s not only technical but historical. In 2009, one option was chosen; in 2022, with the experience of 2009–2022 in hand, the other was chosen.

In chapter three I formulated this as a structural requirement. For cooperation in the network to be sustainable, a win inside the network must not be convertible into the right to change its rules. Bitcoin doesn’t provide this isolation: accumulated hashrate is converted into a share of voice in choosing a block, and through support for this or that client, this or that developer, this or that direction of development — into a share of voice in choosing the future trajectory of the protocol, too. Qubic restores this isolation: one participant — one vote, no accumulation increases his weight in the votes of the current epoch, and the ability to become a participant in the next epoch depends not on accumulated capital but on work performed in the previous one.

At this point it’s worth saying separately that “useful work performed” in Qubic is not the same kind of work as in Bitcoin. In Bitcoin, work is the solution of a meaningless cryptographic puzzle whose only function is to prove that you’ve spent electricity. In Qubic, work is something different. It’s that very “Murdoch’s gas pipe” I promised in earlier chapters. But how it’s built is the topic of the chapters that follow, not this one. Here it’s only important to fix one thing: selection into an epoch happens by a metric tied to a contribution useful to the network, not to an abstract expenditure of resources. A computor that has spent a great deal of electricity on meaningless hashes wins nothing by it in Qubic. It has to perform work the network needs. Exactly which work — we’ll see in chapter eight.

And one more remark before closing this chapter. The whole 676 mechanism we’ve described here is one side of Qubic. The second, no less important — is what counts as “useful work” and how its result reaches the hands of users. 676 computors without useful work are just a distributed counter. Useful work without 676 computors is distributed computation without a guarantee that someone hasn’t substituted the result. Together, they’re what Qubic was conceived for, and it’s their union that makes the network something more than the sum of its parts. But first the frame holding the whole construction had to be described.
What’s Next
To sum up.

The Qubic network rests on a fixed pool of 676 computers simultaneously playing the roles of observers, verifiers, and voters. Any decision requires the support of at least 451 participants — that’s two-thirds, the mathematically calibrated boundary beyond which the network is resilient to the collusion or failure of a third of its members. Within a single vote, each of the 676 participants is equal to every other; accumulation of resources doesn’t convert into voting power. The unit of time is the tick; in each tick one proposal is considered from one of the 676, rotated deterministically. The unit for refreshing membership is the epoch; once a week part of the membership is replaced, but no more than 225 at a time, which guarantees that any coordinated invasion will take at least four epoch transitions, and the whole of that time the network will be controlled by the prior supermajority.

This construction is the foundation. Everything else rests on it that the remaining chapters of part three will be about: how useful work turns into a defensive structure for the network, and how the token is issued and burned, and how the last remaining point of human governance works — the figure of the Arbitrator, who, by plan, is to disappear on April 13, 2027.
But before talking about what gets built on this foundation, it’s worth closing one question that was left open in this chapter.

We said that once a week part of the computor composition is replaced. That the “bad” yield their seats to the “good,” that no more than 225 out of 676 are replaced at a time. But the transition itself — the very moment when one epoch ends and another begins — has so far been described from the outside, from the standpoint of statistics. Who, exactly, ends up among those leaving, and by what rule? How does the selection happen among the candidates for the open seats? At what point in time does this happen — what if during the transition someone sent a transaction, does it go to the old epoch or the new one? What happens to the unfinished obligations of a departing computor? How does the network manage not to stop in the moment when a quarter of its voting members is changing?

These are questions about time in Qubic. About how the network exists not in a continuous present but is divided into discrete weekly cycles, each of them a small life of its own, with its own birth, development, and end. About the mycelium that regenerates not once a year but every Wednesday evening, and meanwhile keeps living as a whole.
The next chapter is about weeks of epochs.

If chapter six described the network’s anatomy — what it’s made of — this one describes its physiology: how it breathes, how it metabolizes, how it regenerates. Recall the metaphor I carefully introduced in chapter six and promised to return to. Mycelium — a distributed network of fine threads stretching underground without a center and without an owner. Its individual sections continuously die off and are replaced by new ones; the whole, meanwhile, lives longer than any of its fragments. Chapter six ended with the promise that the weekly turnover of computors is — not metaphorically, but mechanically — the same thing. That promise will be kept here. Qubic is the frame on which a structure rests that has yet to be described; the gas pipe gets assembled in the chapters that follow. This one, the seventh, is still about the frame — but about its temporal dimension. Coalbrookdale of the digital age, day two: the floor laid down the night before is set onto supports that have to bear not only weight but also what flows through them.
What an Epoch Is Made Of
Take an arbitrarily chosen week in the life of the Qubic network — say, this one, from Wednesday evening to next Wednesday evening. What happens in it?

The composition of the six hundred and seventy-six computors is fixed. These specific six hundred and seventy-six — no fewer, no more — make up, for all seven days, the parliament we talked about in chapter six. Not one of them can be added in the middle of the week. Not one of them can be officially expelled. Regardless of whether the computor is working or has broken down, voting honestly or trying to sabotage, getting rich or going broke — for all seven days it holds its place in the composition. Within the week, time is sliced into ticks — that very basic round of voting we’ve already discussed. Ticks are many: in the current configuration, one tick takes around half a second to a second, which means there are roughly a million of them in a week. Each tick is a full round: one computor-leader proposes, the remaining six hundred seventy-five verify and vote, a quorum of four hundred fifty-one makes the new state canonical. A million such rounds in a row — and one epoch has been lived through. It’s important to understand what, exactly, the epoch accumulates. This isn’t just a journal of what happened; it’s the network’s structured memory. Each of the six hundred and seventy-six computors, at the close of the week, is assigned a numerical evaluation — sometimes called its “score.” That score measures how much useful work the computor performed over the week. What “useful work” is in Qubic is the topic of the next chapter, I promised, and the promise will be kept; for now it’s enough to know that this work has an objective metric, equally computable for all participants. At the end of the epoch the network has a ranking: six hundred and seventy-six names, each with a number.

In parallel, there’s another list. These are candidates — computers that aren’t part of the current six hundred and seventy-six but, over the course of the week, have also been performing valid work and accumulating their own score. They don’t vote, don’t take part in consensus, but the network sees them and counts them. At the end of the epoch the network has their ranking too — a separate one.

That is, an epoch isn’t just a week during which the network operates. It’s a week during which the network simultaneously operates and observes itself. All six hundred and seventy-six “inside” are constantly under measurement. All the candidates “outside” too. When the week ends, the network has at its disposal not only the blockchain of transactions but also a complete ranked list of who worked how.

Within an epoch none of these rankings goes into effect. For all seven days, the rules of the game are the same for everyone. No computor, no matter how high a score it has accumulated by midweek, gets any additional vote because of it, nor any additional transactional priority, nor even an informational advantage. Within an epoch the network is symmetrical with respect to all six hundred and seventy-six. I want to underline this separately, because this is where one of the subtlest things in the whole architecture of Qubic happens.

What does “the epoch as one round of an iterated game” mean? Axelrod’s tournament, which I worked through in chapter two, was made up of games: each pair of programs played against one another not once but two hundred rounds in a row. Only that structure allowed a cooperative strategy to win — because the opponent remembered past behavior and responded to it. A cooperative strategy doesn’t win in one round; in a thousand rounds, it wins.

An epoch in Qubic is one such round, only with six hundred and seventy-six players at the same time. Each of their weeks of behavior becomes one cell in the overall results table. In the next week, conditions may change — the composition will be different, rules may be refined — but the changes aren’t random; they follow deterministically from what happened in the previous epoch. The ones replaced will be precisely those who showed the worst result; the ones admitted will be precisely those who showed the best. No one appoints “the bad ones”; the process itself determines them. This is sharply different from how Bitcoin lives. Bitcoin has no discrete epochs. The network operates in continuous time: block after block, a new one every ten minutes. Changes to the protocol happen through forks — through public, sometimes painful processes in which part of the community accepts the new version and part doesn’t, and sometimes the network splits. Bitcoin is a long, long sequence without seams, in which any structural change requires opening it up. Qubic lives differently. It has seams, and they fall every Wednesday.
What Happens on Wednesday

What exactly happens at the moment of an epoch transition I’ll now describe step by step. But first — one warning. I’ll be describing the process as a deterministic algorithm; that’s true, but it isn’t the whole truth. In the real history of Qubic, in the four-plus years since the first epoch in April 2022, this algorithm hasn’t always run smoothly. Why, will become clear later in the section; for now, let’s assume the algorithm works. So, the sequence.

A few ticks before the epoch boundary — call it moment T — the network locks in the final scores of all six hundred and seventy-six active computors. It ranks them from bottom to top. The list is known: these names worked best, these worked worst. In parallel, the network already has a ranked list of candidates. These are the very computers that were performing valid work all week but didn’t belong to the six hundred and seventy-six. Their score is an objective parameter, equally computable, based on the same metric as for the active ones. The two are competing on a single ruler, not on different ones.

At moment T — more precisely, at a stipulated moment on Wednesday UTC — the network compares. If the best external candidate has a score higher than the worst active computor, they swap places. The worst is dropped, the best is admitted. The process repeats: now the next-worst of the remaining six hundred and seventy-six is compared with the next-best of the externals. And so on.

But not infinitely. At the two hundred and twenty-fifth replacement, the process stops, even if the next external candidate is still formally better than the next active one. Two hundred twenty-five is a rigid ceiling, we worked through this in detail in chapter six; it’s structural protection of the network against too rapid an invasion. So: if it has turned out that one hundred and twenty computors really did work badly, all one hundred and twenty of them are dropped. If three hundred such ones turned up, only the two hundred and twenty-five worst out of the three hundred are dropped; the rest stay another week, under the promise of doing better. And if there were only fifty such, all fifty are dropped, and no one fills slots up to two hundred and twenty-five; openings for new entrants don’t appear in such numbers.

A new epoch begins. The composition of the six hundred and seventy-six is refreshed. Last week’s score is recorded in the blockchain as historical fact; the network remembers it, but in the new epoch it confers no privileges. The new week is a clean slate by accumulated work. Everyone starts again.

The selection mechanic isn’t manual. Nobody from the Qubic team sits on Wednesday morning with a spreadsheet deciding whom to swap. The process is deterministic, executed simultaneously by all six hundred and seventy-six nodes independently. Each computor, knowing the full list of ticks of the past epoch, can compute the score of each participant on its own — both internal and external. If all six hundred and seventysix computed the same thing — and they should, because the input data are the same for everyone — the new epoch begins automatically. No central decision. In CfB’s descriptions, the mechanism by which an active computor officially loses its status sounds like this: a computor behaving incorrectly or failing to keep up with its load, at some moment, starts emitting cryptographically invalid ticks. These invalid ticks become their own proof of its problem — they get included in the blockchain as evidence the whole network sees. At the epoch boundary, such a computor automatically loses its place. Its replacement isn’t carried out by people, or even by the Arbitrator — it’s carried out by the computors themselves through the protocol, processing the proof.

Separately, on transitions. An epoch change isn’t an atomic operation. It doesn’t happen in one microsecond. The actual procedure, as far as is known from the team’s descriptions, is stretched out over hours. In the early epochs, in 2022, when gradual transitions were being tested, a change could take six hours — from 9:00 UTC to 15:00 UTC; mining would stop for the entire interval, and the network would “reassemble” itself. By the end of 2024, gradual transitions had been replaced with so-called seamless transitions — transitions without a full halt. The network keeps ticking, but at some moment the internal computor list at each node updates — and the next tick goes through with the new composition. How exactly the synchronization happens, I’ll work through a paragraph from now.

Transactions crossing the epoch boundary aren’t lost. If a user sent a transaction a minute before Wednesday and it didn’t make it into a block of the old epoch, it goes into the first possible tick of the new one. From the user’s standpoint there’s no difference at all between a transaction “Wednesday before noon” and “Wednesday after noon.” For the user, the network is one and the same. Only inside, under the hood, has it slightly changed the composition of its voters at the moment of the transaction. Why Wednesday, specifically. The answer is simple and pragmatic. Wednesday is the middle of the working week in most time zones of the world where Qubic has operators. It’s a day when the maximum share of computors is most likely to be online and monitoring what’s happening. Monday and Friday are tied to start- and end-of-week effects — when operators haven’t yet fully settled into work mode or are already partially distracted by the weekend. Saturday and Sunday — fewer people at the consoles. Wednesday is a reasonable compromise, nothing mystical.

Why a week, specifically. Here the answer is a bit more interesting. Too short an epoch — say, a day — would make the score evaluation statistically noisy: random fluctuations in performance would produce equally random ejections, and the composition would jitter without substantive cause. Too long — say, a month — would mean a slow reaction to bad participants: a malicious or simply broken computor could damage or impede the network for months before being replaced. A week is an empirically found compromise. It isn’t an “optimum” proven mathematically; it’s a reasonable value at its design point.

Here, by the way, it’s worth remembering that Qubic isn’t unique in the idea of dividing time into epochs. Other networks with discrete time exist — Cardano uses five-day epochs, Solana’s epochs are significantly shorter. The originality of Qubic isn’t in the concept itself, but in the parameters and in what, exactly, gets fixed at the epoch boundary. In most other networks, an epoch is the time between recalibrations of some single parameter. In Qubic, an epoch is the full life cycle of the voter composition. And one more observation worth lingering on. The epoch is the unit in which one round of an iterated game takes place. Here a promise left unclosed earlier begins to turn into an engineering fact: the fourth condition of cooperation — a win in the game must not give the player the ability to change the rules of the game itself. This condition now has two implementations: a static one — no accumulated wealth increases the weight of a vote; and a dynamic one — a computor that earned a great deal over an epoch gets the right to remain in the next epoch, but not the right to change its rules. Two different kinds of prize, and the division between them is wired into the epoch boundary.
How to Switch Without Stopping

The epoch transition in Qubic is not a simple engineering task. Imagine you have to swap out a quarter of a soccer team’s roster mid-match in such a way that the match doesn’t stop. The incoming players have to already know the tactics, know where the ball is, who passes to whom, what combinations are being run. The outgoing have to clear the field but not take with them anything the team will need going forward. And all of this — in the moment, without a whistle.

In the programmer’s world the task sounds like this: at moment T we have up to two hundred and twenty-five nodes leaving consensus and the same number entering. The new ones have to know the network’s full current state — the most recently accepted blocks, all open obligations, all states of smart contracts. The outgoing have to correctly hand them this state without halting the flow of new transactions. And the network at this moment must neither lose validation, nor allow conflicts, nor get stuck trying to come to an agreement.

The Qubic protocol solves this through what can be called phase-in and phase-out. An incoming candidate knows that it can become a computor on the upcoming Wednesday in advance — by its own accumulated score. This isn’t a last-minute surprise; it can prepare. For several days already it’s been pulling down the current state of the network, getting it not in one big chunk at moment T but gradually, in the background. By moment T it already has everything it needs for the very first tick of the new epoch. It doesn’t vote — because it isn’t yet part of the six hundred and seventy-six — but it’s already ready.

At the boundary T the switch happens in one step. Each of the six hundred and seventy-six independently computes the new composition. Each updates its internal participant list inside itself. From the very first tick of the new epoch the new ones are voting. The old ones, just departed, can still remain in contact for some time as observers — their votes are no longer accepted, but they see the network, can finish their technical business, can try to come back as candidates the following week. No abrupt breaks.

Where this description starts to seem too smooth, I have to stop and add an honest caveat. CfB’s own commentary directly says: “Not all epoch transitions are smooth.” That’s true. The history of Qubic knows two different kinds of transitions. One is “seamless”: no new features get rolled out, rules don’t change, only the computor composition refreshes. Such a transition has, since 2024, indeed proceeded without a network halt. The other is “breaking”: along with the change of composition, a new version of the protocol, new logic, new capabilities are deployed. In this case all computors must update their code, and the transition can be accompanied by downtime — sometimes several hours, and in the very early days even more.

And here’s an important detail: the Qubic team does breaking transitions regularly. Every Wednesday, if there are new features for rollout that week — the transition is breaking. If there aren’t any — seamless. When over the holidays, in December 2024, the team decided to do a series of seamless transitions in a row, CfB himself explained it simply: “no breaking updates which means no progress with monero.” That is, seamless is stability at the cost of an absence of development; breaking is development at the cost of possible downtime. Qubic in practice constantly balances between these two modes, and from week to week the choice can shift.

This may seem strange to a reader accustomed to the crypto discourse around Bitcoin, where any hard fork is an event that triggers months of discussion and sometimes splits the community. In Qubic a hard fork is a routine midweek event. The reason is that consensus in Qubic is built differently. In Bitcoin, a change of rules requires the voluntary agreement of miners, each of whom can keep working under the old protocol indefinitely — and if enough hashrate stays on the old version, you get a parallel chain. In Qubic, hashrate and voice are separated: hashrate is needed only to land in the six hundred and seventy-six and to fight for a place among them; within an epoch the rules apply identically to all the voters, and if six hundred and seventy-six have agreed to a new version — the new version becomes canonical. A faction left on the old one simply won’t enter the next composition. No fork happens.

Now a brief historical aside that explains a great deal. Seamless transitions are not what existed in Qubic from the beginning. This was a major multi-year engineering task. The first records of work on it date to December 2022; back then CfB wrote to the team: “This epoch we should develop and test seamless epoch transition, expect daily updates.” In 2023 — a series of preparation changes. In 2024, in January, seamless mode was finally deployed to mainnet. That is, the network for two years — 2022 and 2023 — lived with transitions that sometimes took hours and stopped mining. Only afterward did what most users today see as “the invisible Wednesday change” appear. This is important to remember for two reasons. The first is honesty: to claim that Qubic was born with a ready seamless architecture would be untrue. The second is a demonstration of method. Developing critical infrastructure in an open network with real users and real money flowing through it is work that doesn’t get done in a month. Four years ago, on the day of Qubic’s first epoch on April 13, 2022, most of what now runs automatically didn’t yet exist even on paper. The network was learning to live — and while it learned, it lived, little by little.

Four years isn’t a random number. The mainnet launch date — April 13, 2022. The planned date of the Arbitrator’s departure — April 13, 2027. Five years between them, and the coincidence of numbers is definitely not accidental. It’s too early here to discuss this date in detail; its full treatment is in chapter fourteen. It’s enough to note that the weekly cycle of epochs we’ve just described becomes the unit of count for these five years. Not calendar, but network.
Under the Hood: Symmetries and Arithmetic

Chapter six showed how the number six hundred seventy-six gives rise to the quorum of four hundred fifty-one and the replacement limit of two hundred twenty-five through one and the same BFT mathematics. It’s worth pausing on the arithmetical symmetry between these two defenses — and seeing that it isn’t decorative but functional.

The quorum of four hundred fifty-one protects the network within an epoch — at the moment of voting. It’s protection against a minority, even a large one, pushing through a false decision. The two hundred and twenty-five, by contrast, is protection between epochs, at the boundary of a transition. It’s protection against an attacker rotating the composition in his favor too quickly. The first works on the scale of milliseconds; the second on the scale of weeks.

What’s remarkable is that both defenses are mathematically the same. Six hundred and seventy-six minus four hundred and fifty-one equals two hundred and twenty-five. If the maximum number of those simultaneously replaceable equals the difference between the full composition and the quorum, then you get the following property: even under an epoch change ideal for the attacker, when his people occupy all two hundred and twenty-five seats, the remaining four hundred and fifty-one old computors make up exactly a quorum. The new ones can’t pass a single decision on their own — there are only two hundred and twenty-five of them, and at least four hundred and fifty-one votes are needed. To push through any decision, they need votes from the old. This means that whether one likes it or not, any attempt to capture the network from within is doomed to be a drawn-out process. Chapter six already showed it arithmetically: a minimum of four epochs, that is, four weeks, with ideal competitive performance — and during all of that time control belongs to the previous composition. What’s also important is that the previous composition is not obliged to sit passively over those four weeks. It sees what’s happening, sees the ranked list of candidates, understands the structure of incoming force, and can — at the protocol level, with nothing illegal — take measures. For example, vote on a change of rules complicating mass simultaneous entry. Or change the score itself, making it more resistant to a specific type of attack. Voting on a rules change isn’t permitted within an epoch, but at the epoch boundary — as we’ve seen — it is.

There’s another nuance worth noting. The selection mechanic is built so that a rationally minded attacker won’t try to capture all six hundred and seventy-six seats in a single week. Why would he? His own mining is bounded — he can produce, say, this much score per epoch. If he scatters that score across all six hundred and seventy-six positions, he won’t take a single one: for each individual position his strength turns out to be weaker. It’s more rational to concentrate all his strength on the two hundred and twenty-five best candidates — that is, on the maximum allowed simultaneous rotation. That gives him three times the efficiency per position. But it also slows him down threefold: instead of one step toward capture he has to take three.

Put differently, the structure of the protocol doesn’t merely defend against rapid attack — it actively steers the rational attacker toward a slow one. And a slow attack is an attack visible for months. This is a fundamental difference from situations like GHash.IO in 2014, where concentration from thirty percent to fifty-five could happen in a few weeks and where there was no mechanical brake to slow the process. In Qubic the brake is built in as a constant.

A computor’s earnings don’t convert into the weight of its vote, nor into the speed of its entry into or exit from the composition. The maximum that earnings give is an objective chance to remain or to land in the composition, and that chance is bounded by the same threshold of two hundred and twenty-five, which doesn’t depend on how much, exactly, the computor earned. The winner’s prize inside the game is to stay in the game. No more.
What’s Next

To sum up. The Qubic network lives not in continuous time but in discrete cycles of one week each. Within an epoch the composition of six hundred and seventy-six computors is fixed, all vote with equal weight, every tick is a full round of consensus. At the end of the week the network has at its disposal a ranked list of all the active computors and all the candidates — by an objective metric of work performed. At the epoch boundary, automatic replacement happens: the worst yield their seats to the best, up to two hundred and twenty-five replacements at a time, under a rigid arithmetical limit that preserves four hundred and fifty-one old computors in the new composition. Transactions go through without interruption, the network doesn’t stop if the week has no breaking updates; and if it does — a brief downtime is possible, and the team consciously chooses what matters more to it on each particular week: stability or progress. At the level of the human metaphor, the mycelium regenerates every seven days: some threads die off, some appear, the whole goes on living. At the level of game theory, every epoch is one round of a large iterated game with six hundred and seventy-six participants, and it’s precisely this, as Axelrod showed in 1980, that turns cooperation from an unstable exception into a stable equilibrium.

Two engineering anchors — the quorum of four hundred and fifty-one and the replacement limit of two hundred and twenty-five — are arithmetically symmetrical, and together they make capturing the network a task requiring not hours and not days but weeks, in plain sight of the entire community.

We’ve now described the network’s space — six hundred and seventy-six voices occupying seats — and its time — weekly cycles during which those seats refresh. But not once have we answered the question this whole book started over. What, exactly, are these six hundred and seventy-six participants doing during the seven days of their epoch? What work earns them their place in the next week — and why is it “useful,” rather than, as in Bitcoin, arbitrary? What is the force that turns this mycelium? Not the meaningless hashes we discussed in chapter one. Not arithmetic for arithmetic’s sake. Something else — what Qubic was conceived for. What in chapter one we called “Murdoch’s gas,” collected into a pipe.

The next chapter is the key one in this book. It’s about useful work of computation that simultaneously defends the network and produces something that did not previously exist in the world. It’s called “Murdoch’s Gas in Action — UPoW.”
The Gas No One Collected into a Pipe
What, exactly, do six hundred and seventy-six computors do for the entire week? What work earns them their place in the next epoch — and why is it “useful” rather than, as in Bitcoin, arbitrary?

This chapter is the answer to that question. And it’s also a return to the very metaphor I carefully introduced in chapter one and promised one day to bring to bear. Let’s go back to Coalbrookdale of 1792.

William Murdoch is standing by a furnace in which coal is being charred for the production of coke. The process by then has been in use for eighty years already: since 1709, since the time of Abraham Darby, the iron-foundry industry of England has rested on this very transformation of coal into coke. From the furnaces, every day, dense black smoke pours out — a byproduct of the charring, inconvenient, sometimes dangerous, always released into the atmosphere as waste. That’s how it had been done all this time: coal yields coke, smoke flies into the sky, rain washes the soot off facades, and no one complains, because coke means cast iron and cast iron means the empire. Murdoch looks at the smoke differently. He runs a pipe from the furnace to a lamp in his own workshop, purifies the gas, lights it. It burns. It burns evenly and for a long time. It works.

Over the next fifteen years this idea will grow into the lighting of London with gas. By the 1820s an entire gas industry will have grown up — a new economy founded on the byproduct of an old one. Charring coal now produces two valuable outputs simultaneously. The first is heavy, tangible — coke. The second is invisible and powerful — gas.

In chapter one I wrote one phrase which has hung over the book ever since as a promise. I called Bitcoin mining the Murdoch’s gas of 2009 that no one has yet collected into a pipe. The process is running: computer cycles are being burned by the billions, power stations are operating, chips are heating up. For the sake of what? Of one thing — finding a digest whose first N bits are zeros. Found — the block is credited, the reward issued. All the rest of the computational byproduct gets thrown into the atmosphere. Goes off as heat. Into nothing.

In 2013 one engineer looked at this picture and saw exactly what Murdoch saw in 1792. Not “how to make a more efficient Bitcoin.” But “what if we collect the byproduct.” In 2022, on the basis of this idea, the Qubic network started up. By 2024 the UPoW mechanic, which this chapter is about, had stabilized.

Three questions to be answered. First: what exactly do Qubic miners solve every tick? Second: why does the result of this work simultaneously serve consensus and something else — and what, exactly, is that “else”? Third: does it work today as designed — or only halfway?
Let’s start with the mechanics.
One Task, Several Outputs

A Bitcoin miner solves one task. He varies the value of the nonce field in the block header, computes sha256 of the header, looks at the resulting digest, checks: are the first N bits zeros? If not — change the nonce, compute again. If yes — the block is found, transmitted to the network, the reward taken. That’s it. The whole Bitcoin-mining industry, tens of billions of dollars in hardware, hundreds of terawatt-hours per year — is brute-force search for a coincidence: a digest with the required number of leading zeros.

What’s happening inside? Each sha256 computation passes through sixty-four rounds of internal transformations, and at each intermediate step some state results — bits, register states. By construction of the function, these intermediate states mean nothing outside sha256. They aren’t data, they aren’t a signal, they don’t contain any recoverable structure. They are computational byproduct that exists for exactly as long as it takes to produce the next one. The chip computes them, the chip forgets them. At the output — a digest. One output, one value, one purpose.

And this, it’s important to say, is not a bug. It is the right design of the function for its purpose. A hash function whose task is to be a cryptographically strong transformation must not leave useful traces in its intermediate states. If sha256 produced something useful in the course of computation, that would make it vulnerable: predictability of byproducts contradicts the requirement of indistinguishability from a random function. Bitcoin isn’t “badly made.” Bitcoin is made correctly — for what it does. But for what Qubic does, a function of a different design is needed.
Here is how the task is described by Come-from-Beyond — the creator of the system, with whom the reader has already met in chapter four. The quote is public, from his post of July 23, 2024:

“Qubic miner task is similar to Bitcoin hashing and can be reduced to finding such digest that first N bits are zeros, we set the difficulty manually (dev team chooses it every epoch) by deciding the value of N. Each computor simulates the ANN (which we have represented as a hash function during the reduction above) and generates the 'digest’ which is verified to have first N bits set to zeros.”

Read the phrase slowly. Qubic miner task is similar to Bitcoin hashing — the Qubic miner’s task is similar to Bitcoin hashing. And can be reduced to finding such digest that first N bits are zeros — and reduces to searching for a digest whose first N bits are zeros. The same task. Not similar, not analogous — formally reducible to the same one. But further: Each computor simulates the ANN (which we have represented as a hash function during the reduction above). Each computor simulates an artificial neural network — which through a formal reduction is represented as a hash function. This is the structural difference. The digest whose first N bits are zeros is generated not by sha256 but by running data through a neural net. At the input — some parameters, inside — a forward pass through layers of the ANN (matrix multiplications, nonlinear activations, aggregations), at the output — a sequence of bits which is checked for leading zeros.

I’ll underline: this is not an analogy and not a metaphor. The quote says explicitly: “which we have represented as a hash function during the reduction above” — represented as a hash function through a formal reduction. That is, it is mathematically established that the run through the ANN behaves, in the relevant properties, as a hash function, and therefore the task “find an input for which the first N output bits are zeros” has the same meaning as in Bitcoin. The difference is that the very process producing the digest now leaves traces.

The intermediate states of the ANN simulation — neuron activations, weight distributions on trained layers, the structure of how the data passed through the network — these are not empty bits inside sha256. These are data which, in the most honest sense, are neural-network data. They can be used for training. For evolutionary selection of architectures. For everything that makes up modern machine learning.

One bit of work by a Qubic miner produces three outputs simultaneously. The first output is consensus proof. A digest found with the first N zeros is a confirmation that the computor performed a valid simulation. This is the equivalent of “found a block” in Bitcoin: a proof of work which the network can verify and credit. On this output the certification of ticks is built. This is what makes UPoW a proof-of-work in the strict sense — there is work, there is its proof, the work cannot be faked more cheaply than performed.

The second output is AI training data. The intermediate states of the ANN simulation. The concrete values on which the work was done. This data is a valuable byproduct, reserved in the project for a consumer named Aigarth — a separate component of the system that uses the obtained results for evolutionary selection of neural-network architectures. I’ll talk about Aigarth in detail only in chapter eleven; here one thing matters: UPoW produces the data, Aigarth consumes it. As Come-from-Beyond himself put it on May 13, 2024: “Miners do useful PoW, not Aigarth”. Producer and consumer are two different nodes, and the separation between them needs to be kept in mind.

The third output is score. Score is the structured memory of the network which, by the results of the epoch, determines who stays, who leaves, who arrives. The content of the score can now be unfolded.

Score is the aggregated number of valid digests found by a computor over an epoch. Each digest is one successfully performed ANN simulation, each simulation is one unit of useful work. The epoch’s score is the sum of these units over the week. The network doesn’t just count votes or ticks; the network counts work of a specific type. The more valid simulations a computor has done, the higher its score. The higher the score, the more confidently it stays among the 676 for the next week, not falling into the 225 rotation slots.

What in chapter seven was called “the network’s memory” has now received content. The memory is a tally of how many times in a week you’ve produced precisely the kind of work the network considers grounds for keeping you in your place. Not money paid, not proof of stake, not social reputation — but a count of valid neural-network simulations. Architecturally this too is a rarely encountered solution: “the one who stays in the game is the one who has done more work by its rules.”

Now we can come back to the parallel that hung over chapter one. Bitcoin is the Darby phase. Coal burns, coke is given, smoke goes off. Compute is burned, consensus is given, everything else gets thrown out. The scheme is complete and working; it has no hole — it just has one output. Qubic is the Murdoch phase. The same process rebuilt so that the same input produces several outputs at once. Not “an improved Bitcoin PoW” — a different industrial regime of the same computational combustion. Just as coking in 1792 was not “better burning of coal” but a phase from which the chemistry of byproducts began in England.

In 1792 no one in Coalbrookdale thought “ugh, what bad coking, before we were doing it wrong.” Coking was being done correctly even before that — for the sake of coke, which is needed for cast iron, which is needed for the empire. Murdoch simply saw that the process had a potential second output that until then had been ignored. Bitcoin PoW is analogous: it does precisely what it is required to do; its function by construction has no useful byproducts, and that is the right design for its task. UPoW isn’t better. UPoW is about something else.

And here I have to pause. Before unfolding what “the system has three outputs, but one of them is so far not used at full strength” means, strict order needs to be brought to one place where the community regularly gets confused. Three different things that get called by similar words but do different jobs need to be separated. This is a short section, but without it the next, central section of the chapter won’t work as intended. Three Layers of Work: What Makes Qubic Qubic A reader familiar with crypto may quite reasonably think: “useful PoW is no news. Flux rents out compute for scientific computations. Gridcoin paid for BOINC tasks back in 2013. Old hat. What’s the sensation?”
The answer is that none of that is UPoW. That’s PoUW. A one-letter difference, but a structural one.

PoUW — Proof of Useful Work. In existing implementations (Flux, early Gridcoin, a number of academic projects) useful work exists on top of the consensus mechanism. Inside the network classical PoW or PoS is running — for security; in parallel with it the network provides infrastructure through which external clients rent compute for scientific calculations or rendering. Two independent layers, joined by one token. Network nodes can simultaneously secure the chain and perform useful tasks — but “securing the chain” and “useful tasks” are two separate jobs, each with its own purpose. UPoW — Useful Proof-of-Work. In Qubic, useful work is itself the consensus mechanism. Not “in addition to” and not “on top of.” The very same ANN simulation that Aigarth needs is what produces the digest that certifies the computor as an active participant in the network. One process, simultaneously doing both jobs. There aren’t two layers that need to be combined.

Come-from-Beyond on April 3, 2024, formulated this in a short phrase: “UPoW is not equal to PoUW”. Not the same thing. I’m putting this into a separate section deliberately, because substitution of one for the other is the most frequent mistake in discussions of Qubic. It’s easy to get confused, because the letter order is almost identical, and the functional difference — fundamental.
Now the second separation that needs to be made here. UPoW is one thing. External mining, in which Qubic also engages, is another.

In parallel with UPoW, two more streams of computational activity run on the network. The first is external mining. First, from May 2025 to April 2026, the network mined Monero. From February 2026, a DOGE add-on was launched.

It’s important to understand what external mining is structurally. It is not part of UPoW. It is performed by the same computors but with a different task, on different infrastructure, with a different result. DOGE mining gives the network revenue (an inflow of coins which are then converted into QU through the buyback mechanism and burned — these are details for chapter nine). UPoW gives the network consensus. These are two different jobs which a computor can perform in parallel, but which are architecturally not the same thing.

Come-from-Beyond formulated this on July 15, 2025, directly: “Too much misconception about #Qubic #UPoW on X. Mining of $XMR isn’t a part of it, mining for #Aigarth is. Finding blocks for #Monero looks useful but it doesn’t influence certification of validators directly.” And separately, in the same thread: “Monero mining isn’t UPoW”.

Here it’s important to go slowly. External mining “looks useful” — looks useful indeed. Very much so. It brings revenue to the network, it provides hashrate, in 2025 it even temporarily made Qubic the largest participant in the Monero network. All of that is real outcomes. But it does not directly influence the certification of validators. A computor doesn’t get a place in the next epoch for having mined a Monero block. A computor gets its place for having produced enough valid digests — for UPoW. There’s empirical proof of this, and it’s strong. In Discord posts of April 17, 2026, Come-from-Beyond described the observed picture: out of 676 computors, around 20 do only UPoW, without XMR and without DOGE. They receive at the same time about 80% of the maximum revenue of the epoch. That means the bonus from external mining makes up around 20% of full income. This isn’t an after-the-fact estimate; it’s a direct measurement on a live network.

From this follows a statement worth saying aloud. Roughly 80% of the network’s value is produced by UPoW. Roughly 20% by external mining. And — the critical test: switch off DOGE — the network keeps working. Switch off UPoW — the network is dead. UPoW is the foundation. External mining is an annex.

Here chapter three closes. There I wrote: the mining process must itself produce decentralization. Bitcoin doesn’t do that — mining produces concentration through ASIC economies of scale, and two pools today control most of the hashrate. Qubic does it differently. UPoW produces score. Score determines who stays among the 676 in the next epoch. The process of producing digests and the process of producing the network’s composition are literally one and the same process. Not “we mine, and in parallel update the composition through some other procedure,” but “we mine — and by that very fact update the composition.” The cycle is closed on itself: work generates the right to keep working; the right to keep working is determined by how much work you have done.

This also structurally closes another promise. In chapter three I formulated Axelrod’s fourth condition: a win in the game cannot be converted into the right to change the game itself. In the architecture of UPoW this condition is fulfilled like this: a high score gives you the right to stay among the 676 for the next round of the game. It doesn’t give you increased weight of vote, doesn’t give you an enlarged share of consensus, doesn’t give you influence on parameters. Only — the right to keep playing. Won more — you stay. The rules of the game — you don’t change. A clean implementation of what Axelrod, describing the tournament, formulated as a necessary condition for the resilience of cooperation.

And a brief historical remark that fits here. On September 23, 2021, seven months before the launch of mainnet, Come-from-Beyond named in a public tweet three architectural properties of the future network: “Useful PoW, unlike #Bitcoin / 100% certainty of transaction outcome / Feeless transfers like in #IOTA”. Useful PoW — unlike Bitcoin. One hundred percent certainty of transaction outcome. Feeless transfers, as in IOTA. UPoW was named by name even before the network existed. Not post-hoc rationalization (“we built something, and now we’re explaining what it was”); a declaration stated before the start, verifiable afterward.

A separate clarification for the attentive reader. Qubic as an engineering project has a long prehistory. In chapter five I mentioned Jinn — a research effort from the early 2010s, where the concept of useful work was first thought through as a possibility. UPoW is its realization a decade later, in another context and on a different basis. From idea to working network — a decade passed. That’s a normal pace for a nontrivial infrastructural idea.

Now, with the separation of three layers in hand, I can speak directly about what I warned of in the first section of the chapter. About that gap between built and running at full strength which the system’s creator named publicly himself.
Honest Disclosure: “Useless PoW” and Why It’s Here

By this point the reader may suspect that UPoW is too beautiful to work. He’s half right. The idea works. The implementation isn’t yet at full strength. The system’s author said this himself, twice, publicly — and the second time, in July 2025, used a word that is hard to forget.

The first quote, verbatim. On July 17, 2025, Come-from-Beyond wrote on Discord: “On serious note, current mining params are useless, currently UPoW means Useless Proof-of-Work”. And in the same thread, in a separate phrase: “just like our current UPoW”. It wasn’t critics who wrote this — the system’s creator wrote it himself, in front of witnesses, on a public platform, in a channel where the engineers and the token holders are gathered.

The word “Useless” isn’t accidental. The usual marketing register allows “not yet at full strength,” “remains to be polished,” “in the process of optimization.” Come-fromBeyond chose none of those soft formulations. He chose a word which on any reading sounds like a statement of fact: at the moment — useless. And with a second move he reinforced it: just like our current UPoW.

And this isn’t the first such statement. On December 7, 2023, a year and a half earlier, the same thought had already been voiced — a bit more softly, but with the same structure. “Right now our Useful PoW is Half-useful, because Aigarth cannot process all the provided solutions”. Right now our Useful PoW is Half-useful, because Aigarth cannot process all the provided solutions. The problem has been recorded not since last year. It has been known to the system’s creator since at least the end of 2023. What, exactly, do these two quotes mean? I’ll work through it slowly, because this is the structural center of the chapter, and on the precision of the wording depends whether the reader will understand it correctly.

The infrastructure of UPoW works fully on all of its design goals for consensus. Computors simulate the ANN. Digests are validated. Score is assigned. Rotation of 225 places happens every Wednesday. The network is decentralized, secured, functioning. If you look at Qubic today as a blockchain — everything is in order, the consensus layer does exactly what it promised to do, and that first of UPoW’s three outputs (proof for consensus) is produced in full.

The problem is not in the first output. The problem is in the second. AI training data is produced every tick — but not all of it is consumed. Aigarth, designed as the consumer of this data, cannot yet process the full volume of solutions the network supplies it. The network generates more than Aigarth eats. The difference is precisely what Come-from-Beyond calls half-useful and useless.

The reasons, in his own words, are two. The first is the throughput limit of Aigarth. The consumer is so far smaller than the producer; this is an engineering scaling task on which work is in progress. The second is the parameters of the task itself. The ANN that the computors simulate is chosen and tuned so as to provide validity for consensus. For Aigarth’s needs it isn’t optimized — it may be of the wrong architecture, the wrong sizes, with the wrong properties to be maximally useful for evolutionary selection of useful neural networks. This is an architectural design problem solved only by changing parameters and — ultimately — by the deploy of Aigarth in its production form. The parallel back to coal here suggests itself. Murdoch ran the first pipe in 1792. But gas lighting for the first few years worked only in his own workshop in Redruth. London began to be lit by gas — really, with street lighting of the streets — in 1807. The gasworks industry, in earnest, as an industry, took shape by the early 1820s. Between “we can collect the gas” and “gas lights London” — fifteen years passed. Between “gas lights London” and “gas powers industry” — another ten. That’s a normal pace for an infrastructural shift.

In the case of UPoW: mainnet started up on April 13, 2022. UPoW as a mechanic stabilized in 2024. The planned deploy of Aigarth — April 13, 2027. Between “the mechanic works” and “the mechanic is used at full strength” the project has reserved approximately five years. That’s a working pace.
Now an important question: why is this said publicly rather than swept under the rug?

Come-from-Beyond could have stayed silent. He could have waited until Aigarth caught up, and spoken about UPoW only in the past tense: “built,” “works.” The press materials accompanying any technological project would easily allow that. None of Qubic’s critics had brought “Useless PoW” to the public in the system creator’s own formulation — because the formulation itself was created by him. He could have kept it to himself.

He didn’t. And this is no random habit. In chapter four I described a principle Comefrom-Beyond has been following for a second decade: don’t sell what isn’t there yet. Hiding “Useless PoW” would have meant violating that rule in the very place where it gets tested most palpably — in the central mechanic of the central chapter of the entire project. To say it aloud is to assert the rule more strongly than any pr message could formulate it. In a world where ninety percent of token projects hide engineering problems behind marketing until the moment of collapse, putting one’s own main weakness out in public is not weakness and not an admission of defeat. It is discipline. What is Phase 3 and what does DOGE have to do with it?

First: the XMR-mining code is removed from the core. Not switched off by a flag that could be flipped back in a minute — removed completely, so that for a return a new release with restoration of the code would be required. This is a surgical architectural commitment. The Monero chapter is closed.

Second: Phase 3 of compute distribution is activated. The new proportion is roughly 80% to Aigarth training, 20% to DOGE mining. In previous phases a substantial part of compute went to XMR mining; that part is now freed and given to Aigarth. For the first time since the launch of mainnet, Aigarth has access to 100% of the compute reserved for AI work.

Phase 3 isn’t “the moment when UPoW became fully useful.” It’s the moment when the gap between built and used began to close through scaling of the consumer. How quickly it will close, and whether it will close by the planned date, is a question for Part Five of the book. There I will be returning to questions of Aigarth’s architecture and to its deploy.
From Phase 3 to the planned deploy of Aigarth — 356 days. Fifty-one weeks. Fiftyone epochs. In the terms of time introduced earlier — fifty-one rounds of the iterated game.
I’ll close this section with an honest frame.

UPoW in April 2026 is infrastructure that one engineer began to think through in 2013, spent a decade implementing, and launched on mainnet in 2022. It works against all its design goals except one: the AI component so far uses part of what is produced. This is a crack between built and utilized. It exists. It has been recorded by the creator publicly, twice, with an interval of a year and a half.

This is the honest state of UPoW as of April 2026. Neither less, nor more. Under the Hood: Numbers, Revenue, and One Architectural Bonus Now to the gears. The mechanics of UPoW are expressed not only in words; behind every formulation of the previous sections stand specific constants which the team sets in code and which can be looked up in the Qubic repository. This section is for the reader who wants to know exactly what the working architecture is assembled from. I’ll start with the parameter N from the quote of July 23, 2024. In the code of the Qubic core this parameter is called ADDITION_SOLUTION_THRESHOLD_DEFAULT, and it determines how many leading zeros there have to be in a digest for the solution to count as valid.

I’ll underline an important nuance. In Bitcoin, difficulty is self-regulated by the algorithm: every 2016 blocks the network looks at how quickly solutions are being found and adjusts difficulty so that the average interval stays around ten minutes. In Qubic, difficulty is set explicitly by the development team every epoch. This is an engineering decision that makes sense. The hardware base of Qubic is the computors, and their composition for the next week is known in advance; there is no need to imitate blind self-regulation when one can calibrate the parameter for the current hardware directly. It’s the same straightforwardness we encountered in chapter seven in epoch transitions: not “it’ll work itself out,” but “the team made a decision.”

The reference implementation of the miner from Qubic is open-source and is called Qiner. The technical reader can go to the repository and look at exactly how the ANN simulation is built at the level of code — not from words but from sources. It isn’t a black box; it’s a public engineering implementation of what was discussed in sections 2– 3 as a structural reduction. I won’t be retelling the code here — that’s material for a separate breakdown — but the very fact of its openness matters: the claims about the mechanics are independently verifiable.

Now to the money. How exactly does the network pay for a computor’s work? The revenue formula, recorded in PR #844 of the Qubic core and active in Phase 3: revenue = IPC × M × (S² + B·E) / DIVISOR I’ll work through what each symbol means.

IPC — Issuance Per Computor, the issuance to one computor per epoch. The constant equals 1,479,289,940 QU; this is the unit of a trillion new QU issued in an epoch, divided by 676. The upper ceiling a computor can reach for an ideal week. S — a scaling constant, equals 1024. All factors are normalized to the range [0, S]. B — the weight of the bonus for external mining, equals 256.

M — the mandatory component, takes values from zero to S. Assembled from two parts: tx factor (weight 85%) — how actively the computor leads ticks, and oracle factor (weight 15%) — to what extent it participates in the commit/reveal cycle of oracles. This is work the network considers obligatory. The component multiplies the rest of the formula. Didn’t perform the mandatory work — everything else gets multiplied by a smaller number, down to zero.
E — mining factor, also in the range [0, S]. In Phase 3 this is only DOGE shares. This is work the network considers optional. The component is added in via the term B·E, doesn’t multiply the base.

I’ll run through the ranges. With full mandatory work (M = S) and zero external mining (E = 0) the formula gives revenue making up about 80% of IPC. With full mandatory work and full mining (E = S) — exactly IPC, 100%. If a computor fails the mandatory work — the mandatory component collapses, and regardless of how much DOGE it has mined, it gets little.

The construction directly corresponds to what I described in the third section in words. Work on which consensus depends — TX relay, oracles, UPoW — is rigidly built into the multiplicative layer of the formula. Work on which only the network’s revenue depends — DOGE mining — is built in as a weak, additive bonus. Switch off DOGE — you’ll lose around 20%. Switch off the mandatory part — you’ll lose everything. And here let’s note one thing about UPoW’s second output, which in the fourth section was discussed as a bottleneck. AI training data isn’t paid for directly by the formula. A computor doesn’t receive revenue for producing intermediate ANN states useful to Aigarth; it receives revenue for having found a valid digest — the first output — and for having performed the mandatory network work. The second output is currently pure byproduct, written into the atmosphere awaiting a consumer. Or, to flip it, the economy pays for two outputs out of three: consensus and the rotational score (through the mandatory part and through the fact of finding digests). The third, the AI component, is paid for on the credit of expectation.

There’s one more property of UPoW I’ll mention separately, because it isn’t earned by design but by structure. Bitcoin PoW through the sha256 function is theoretically vulnerable to quantum acceleration: Grover’s algorithm gives a quadratic speedup for the preimage-search problem, and at the appearance of sufficiently large quantum computers, Bitcoin mining will find itself in a new reality — not broken, but rebuilt. UPoW is built differently. The task “find an input to an ANN for which the first N output bits are zeros” doesn’t reduce to any of the problems for which quantum algorithms with speedup are known. There is no quantum algorithm performing a forward pass through an arbitrary neural network faster than the classical one.
Come-from-Beyond on November 10, 2025, formulated this in a single phrase: “Unlike PoW, our UPoW isn’t vulnerable to QC”. Unlike PoW, our UPoW isn’t vulnerable to quantum computers.

Here the tone with which I say this matters. This is not a primary design goal. Quantum resistance was not on the list of tasks for the sake of which Qubic was conceived in 2013. It’s a side property of the architecture. But such is the nature of many elegant engineering solutions: when a thing is made correctly for one reason, it turns out to be correct also for reasons its creators didn’t have in mind. Murdoch collected the gas for the sake of lighting his workshop, not for the sake of having chemical works run on the same gas a hundred years later. As it happened, the collected gas turned out to be useful both there and here.

The last thing I’ll say in this section is a short quote I’ll be coming back to in Part Five of the book. On November 20, 2023, Come-from-Beyond described Qubic’s functional map in a single sentence: “Aigarth uses Qubic’s UPoW, also Qubic has everything that an AI would need: Smart contracts as brain, Oracles as sensors to outer world, Outsourced computations as Manipulators to change that outer world.”

Smart contracts as brain, oracles as sensors, outsourced computations as manipulators — and UPoW as the source of energy for everything. On this map UPoW isn’t “a feature of consensus” but the energy subsystem of an AGI substrate. Like the heart in a body: it pumps, it doesn’t think, but without it the rest doesn’t work. Unfolding this map is the job of Part Five; here it’s needed only as a reminder of what, in the end, all this machinery is for.
Parsons, the Turbine, and the Twice-Collected Gas

There is one more figure worth calling into this chapter to close it. Not Murdoch — with Murdoch we’ve already worked, and we’ll be working again in the finale. Charles Algernon Parsons, England, 1884.

Before Parsons, the steam turbine worked in a single stage: high-pressure steam struck a large bladed wheel, transferred to it part of its energy, and exited the other side — still with an enormous reserve of energy, which simply went off into the surrounding space. The efficiency of the first turbines was around 20%. Four-fifths of the steam’s energy — out the chimney, literally.

Parsons built a multi-stage turbine. Steam passed not through one wheel but through a series — gradually, giving up at each stage part of its energy and moving on to the next. The first stage took what it was strong enough to take. The second — what passed by the first. The third — what passed by the two. And so on, in a cascade, until the steam exiting the last stage carried with it only residual pressure. Efficiency, thanks to this construction, rose from 20% to 50–60% and higher.

The principle Parsons applied to steam is formulated abstractly like this: don’t collect everything in one operation, but build a cascade of operations, each of which collects what the previous didn’t. Multi-stage extraction. Extraction in several stages. The idea is applicable to anything that constitutes a process with surplus energy at the output.
UPoW is multi-stage extraction applied to compute.

Bitcoin PoW is built as a single-stage turbine: compute goes in, a digest comes out, all the rest of the computational energy is lost as heat. One stage, one output. UPoW rebuilds the same process into a cascade:

The first stage — compute goes into the form of an ANN simulation and at the output yields a digest with N zeros. Consensus proof. This is the output Bitcoin also has. The second stage — the intermediate states of the simulation, which in Bitcoin were thrown out by construction, here remain as data. AI training data. An output Bitcoin doesn’t have.
The third stage — the aggregate of valid digests over an epoch is folded into a score, which determines the rotation of the network’s composition. Score. An output Bitcoin doesn’t have.
One input — three outputs. The engineering form of what Murdoch did with coal, applied to computational work 217 years later.

I’ll underline one thing so the parallel doesn’t read as metaphor. Parsons and Murdoch worked on one type of task. Not on one substance — they worked with steam and with coal respectively — but on one form of question: how to rebuild an existing process so that it produces several outputs instead of one. Neither one of them invented a new process. They rebuilt an existing one. UPoW is one more point in this series. Not “the invention of a new PoW” but the application of an old principle (multi-stage extraction) to a new substance (compute instead of steam or coal).

This chapter is called “Murdoch’s Gas in Action” — not “UPoW Explained.” The title is chosen this way precisely because, 217 years after Murdoch ran the first pipe from furnace to lamp, the same engineering idea is being applied to the digital analog of that very gas.
The Gas Is Collected. The Pipe Is Laid.
Three sections of compressed mechanics behind us. Now a brief return to the overall view.

Qubic miners solve the same task as Bitcoin miners: find a digest whose first N bits are zeros. But their digest is generated by simulation of a neural network, represented as a hash function through a formal reduction. One job at the input — three outputs at the output: proof for consensus, data for potential AI training, score for rotation of the network’s composition. The infrastructure works against all design goals. The second output — the AI component — is so far not used at full strength; the system’s creator himself spoke this aloud twice publicly, first in December 2023, then in July 2025. Phase 3 was activated: the XMR-mining code is removed, Aigarth for the first time gained access to 100% of the compute reserved for it. To the planned deploy of Aigarth — 356 days.

Chapter six described the space of this network — 676 voices. Chapter seven described its time — weeks of epochs. This one described its energy — UPoW and what it produces. And economics always begins with energy.

From Murdoch in 1792 to Parsons in 1884, 92 years passed. From Bitcoin in 2009 to Qubic in 2022 — 13 years. Industrial cycles have compressed from centuries to years, but their internal logic hasn’t changed: first the process, then the gathering of the byproduct, then the multi-stage optimization. We, the readers of this chapter in 2026, stand at a point which by analogy with coal corresponds to somewhere around 1805– 1810: the gas is collected, the first lamps are burning, but the great gas industry — is still ahead.

The KEY chapter of the first half of the book doesn’t end on a triumphant note precisely because triumph isn’t yet earned — in 2027 a test lies ahead, and now — work. Just as in 1792 Murdoch lit a lamp, but the streets of London didn’t yet know they would soon be lit by gas.

The next chapter is about the economics that keeps this machine running. We’ve described what computors do. We haven’t discussed how the network pays for this work — what exactly happens with the QU token every Wednesday, why issuance and burning go in parallel, why Qubic didn’t choose the Bitcoin model of fixed supply. The breathing token: every epoch a trillion new QU come into being, a substantial part is burned through the buyback mechanism, and supply pulses in time with the weeks of epochs.
Murdoch’s gas is collected. The pipe is laid. Now let’s figure out who is paying for its operation — and what the price of gas is in a world where gas makes not light but intelligence.
Inhale, exhale, week

Let’s start with a simple reminder. A Qubic epoch is one week. Every Wednesday, around twelve o’clock UTC, the network restarts, 225 of the 676 computor seats can change hands, the counters reset, and a new round begins. We covered this mechanic in Chapter 7; here it’s needed as the backdrop for one specific thing: with that same restart, every week, one trillion fresh QU enters the network.

Not “about a trillion.” Exactly a trillion. This is the network’s inhale. Then, over the seven days until the next Wednesday, the exhale happens. QU are burned—through several independent paths, each with its own purpose, each with its own logic. Some are hardwired into the protocol, some depend on decisions by the computors, some depend on outside economics the network has no direct control over. By the end of the epoch, the balance of inhale and exhale gives the net change in circulating supply. In 2025–2026, this balance regularly came out negative: the network burned more than it issued.

Hence the working name of this chapter. The token that breathes. Not “deflationary,” not “inflationary”—breathing. Every week one inhale; over the course of the week, a series of exhales of varying depth. Supply pulses in time with the epochs. In Chapter 7 I used the word “pulse” for the rhythm of the network. In this chapter the related physiological metaphor returns—breathing. That’s a deliberate choice. In Chapter 8 the register was industrial—gas, pipe, turbine, multi-stage extraction; the chapter was about energy.
