Chapter 9 is about economics, and Qubic’s economy is built as circulation, not as combustion. So physiology is the more accurate fit than industry. Heart and lungs—two rhythms of the same organism; the network’s weekly rhythm shows up in both.
But I won’t overplay the metaphor. The image should work, not be played with. Now—about the contrast that hangs over this whole topic.

In 2008, the anonymous author of Bitcoin made one decision about supply, and it hasn’t been up for discussion since. Twenty-one million coins, halvings every four years, final issuance somewhere around 2140. This isn’t a matter of voting or a parameter you adjust along the way—it’s a constant baked into the code at network launch. A Bitcoin holder knows: however many years go by, however conditions change, supply will be that. That is the value proposition.

In Qubic, supply is debated every Wednesday. 676 computors vote on how much QU should remain in circulation by the end of this epoch. They can decide to burn more or less. They can—in theory—decide to change emission parameters for the next epoch. Everything having to do with supply lives inside a rolling voting process, not inside the up-front decision of one person.

This isn’t a small technical difference. These are structurally different answers to the question “what is money.” We’ll come to a full statement of the difference in Section 6 of this chapter, when we work through the central quote from the system’s creator. Three questions:
First: where do QU come from? Section on emission.
Second: where do they go? Section on the seven burn paths.
Third: who decides, and how, how many should be in circulation? Section on the computor vote, the link to Axelrod’s fourth condition, and the Arbitrator’s role as a backstop.
Let’s start with the inhale.
Inhale: a trillion every Wednesday

Each epoch the network issues exactly one trillion fresh QU. This is a protocol constant, hardcoded, not adjustable by vote. It is the network’s baseline “salary,” its fundamental input. In annualized terms—fifty-two trillion QU (52 × 1T = 52T gross issuance per year).

This one trillion is split among 676 computors—those holding active seats in the network for this epoch. A simple division gives an important constant that already came up in the previous chapter: Issuance Per Computor, IPC = 1,479,289,940 QU. One trillion divided by 676, rounded. In Chapter 8 this number figured as a parameter in the revenue formula. In Chapter 9 it picks up its economic meaning: it’s the upper bound on what a computor can earn in a single ideal epoch.

“Upper bound”—not “guaranteed amount.” Real income is computed from the formula in Chapter 8: revenue = IPC × M × (S² + B·E) / DIVISOR Just to recap the structure: the mandatory component M (TX relay, oracles) multiplies the rest of the formula, and the external mining component E gets added in through a small additive bonus. From this followed the empirical observation in Chapter 8: a computor that does only the required network work and UPoW, but doesn’t engage in external mining, gets roughly 80% of IPC. With full external mining—100%. That’s the same 80/20 split we met as a fact in Chapter 8 and that we’ll come back to in Section 3 of this one.
Now—an important point about how distribution works. The system’s creator states the principle of issuance briefly and without euphemisms—he calls it subsidy. In a public message from May 20, 2024:
“Why bother if subsidy method is widely used in everyday life? When you buy a ticket to ride 2km by bus you pay same as one who rides 7km.”

The analogy is clear. On a bus, you pay for the ticket, not for the kilometers. Ride two stops or seven—the price is the same. Many utility schemes work this way, subscription services work this way, subsidized healthcare works this way. The idea of subsidy is a flat price for the fact of participation, not a price proportional to volume of consumption.

In Qubic this is applied to the distribution of issuance. All 676 computors get a comparable share of the trillion—as long as they remain active and above the threshold. There is no strong correlation between how many extra digests a computor found above the quorum threshold and how much they receive. Above threshold—you get your IPC × (coefficients). Below threshold—you risk dropping out in the 225 rotation and losing everything. Inside the active zone—subsidy.

Why this way. It isn’t a gesture of generosity. It’s a mechanism for preventing cartelization. If issuance were distributed proportionally, like Bitcoin proportional hashrate, where more hashrate gives a larger share of the reward—Qubic would instantly switch on the same industrial-scale cycle that turned Bitcoin mining from a million private devices into three or four big pools. Big capital goes into specialized hardware; specialized hardware beats commodity hardware; economies of scale push out the small players; concentration grows. With subsidy, that cycle doesn’t switch on. Scaling hardware to industrial levels in Qubic is pointless—there will be no proportional reward. It’s enough to be a “good” computor to get your share; being the “best” doesn’t grant you a disproportionate bonus.

There’s a direct link here to Chapter 3. Axelrod’s fourth condition: winning the game must not be convertible into disproportionate influence. Translated into the space of economics, this means it must not be convertible into a disproportionate share of issuance. Subsidy performs exactly that function at the distribution level. A fine-print caveat, to keep the picture accurate. Subsidy in Qubic isn’t absolute. The same revenue V2 formula I gave above is not flat. In the multiplicative component M, a computor who handles TX relay badly or sabotages oracles will get less. A computor who actively does external mining gets a +20% bump through the additive term. But these “corridors” are narrow. Inside them—flat subsidy; between them, the difference is not “a hundredfold,” it’s “twenty percent.”

And one last important property of this inhale. No one personally owns the trillion QU that comes into the network every Wednesday. There is no “team allocation,” no “vested tokens,” no founder’s treasury. The trillion gets distributed via IPC according to that week’s activity—made it into 676, did your work well, got your share. Next week— from scratch, no accumulated privileges. Whoever didn’t make it into 676 got nothing. Whoever did got roughly the same as everyone else.
That’s one inhale. But IPC is only the moment of inhale. Across the whole week leading up to the next Wednesday, the exhale runs, and it has several simultaneous directions.
Exhale: seven ways to burn QU

If issuance is one mechanism, one trillion a week, rigidly defined by the protocol, burning is structured differently. Burn is seven parallel paths, each with its own purpose, its own economic function, and its own degree of predictability. Below—one short item per path.

Path one. Computor vote. Each epoch, the 676 computors vote on burn rate parameters—how much of circulating supply should be burned by the end of the epoch. This is baseline deflation, the constant background exhale. The system’s creator, in a very early publication on January 8, 2022, formulated the logic plainly:

“If computors increase burn rate they’ll make everyone’s QUs to be worth more.” The phrase is simple and free of euphemism. Burning is a redistribution of value from issuance to existing holders. Not an “ecological measure” and not “charity”—an economic mechanism in which computors decide how much new issuance the network leaves in circulation and how much it withdraws. The decision is made every week and every week can be different.

Path two. Smart contract fees. All QU spent by users to execute smart contracts on Qubic are burned. They don’t go to computors, aren’t set aside in a treasury—they go to zero. A quote from October 14, 2021, before mainnet launch:
“All QUs spent to run smart contracts will be burned.”
This is a structural difference from Ethereum. In Ethereum, gas fees (after EIP-1559, with the base fee burned, but the tip—not) partly go to validators; in Qubic, fully into burn.

Path three. IPO bid burns. When a new smart contract comes to the network, it goes through an IPO procedure—computors bid for shares of the future contract. The bids temporarily withdraw QU from circulation. CfB’s formulation from July 5, 2023: “CONTRACT_IPO_BID transactions will be changing total supply (because bid amounts are 'extracted’ from it), in the end of the epoch all bids should be released and restore the initial total supply.”
By the end of the epoch, most of the bids return to the bidders—but some (failed bids below the quorum median) are burned. IPO is a temporary burn with a partial permanent residue.

Path four. Sending to the AAAA… address. An address consisting entirely of A’s is functionally equivalent to a burn. QU sent there will never be retrieved—no one holds the corresponding private key, because the address wasn’t generated from a key. It’s a public, openly available burn mechanism—if a holder wants to voluntarily reduce supply, all they have to do is send QU to AAAA. A small cultural footnote: in 2022, in the first months after launch, such transfers were done as a public gesture demonstrating commitment to the “breathing” model.

Path five. Forfeited computor rewards. If a computor performs poorly, is offline, or doesn’t make quorum—its forfeited QU don’t turn into “ownerless funds.” They go either into burn or into the Admin fund—the decision is made by vote each epoch. CfB spoke about this at the end of May 2024:

“More money to Admin isn’t necessarily good, my past experience with the IOTA Foundation was pretty negative in this aspect (but valuable) and I cannot guarantee that these qus will be spent for something good for the community.”
A short caveat. The mention of the IOTA Foundation here is not the author’s analogy and not speculation; it’s CfB’s own explanation of why he leans toward burn rather than Admin.
Path six. AI operations. When Aigarth executes operations on the network, those operations burn QU. On April 17, 2024, CfB put it in one short phrase: “AI run on Qubic will be burning supply too.”

In April 2026, at the time of writing this chapter, this path is mostly symbolic in volume. Aigarth isn’t yet running at full capacity—Chapter 8 went into detail on why. But architecturally the path is in place. By 2027, if the planned deploy goes through, it could become significant. Full disclosure on Aigarth—in Chapter 15 of the book; here, the fact is that AI operations are designated as a consumer of supply.

Path seven. Buyback through external mining. The most “physical” path—and structurally the most interesting. Starting with Phase 3, computors optionally mine DOGE. The mined DOGE goes through pool operators, gets sold on the market, the proceeds go into buying QU on open exchanges, and the QU bought is burned. The full cycle: compute → external coin → fiat/stable → QU → burn.

The twenty percent of revenue a computor earns for external mining (through the additive B·E term in the revenue V2 formula) is the economic fuel for the buyback. The more computors take part in mining, the more external revenue the pools have, the more QU can be bought back and burned.

Critical honesty. Buyback isn’t guaranteed. It’s an option for computors, not part of the protocol. In Chapter 8, I already cited the empirics: roughly 20 of 676 computors don’t do any external mining, and the network runs fine with that. If tomorrow all 676 simultaneously decided to stop mining—the network would keep functioning as a blockchain, issuance would continue normally, UPoW would keep producing consensus, but buyback would stop. The clean deflation the network showed in 2025–2026 would cease to be. This isn’t a bug and isn’t a vulnerability—it’s design. Buyback is a variable, not a constant.

Moving toward synthesis. Starting in 2025, the Qubic network regularly burns 100% or more of the epoch’s issuance. This is an important empirical fact the system’s creator has commented on more than once. On October 11, 2025:
“Monero is holding pretty well, this epoch we have chance to burn 100% of issued supply.”
And four days later, on October 15, 2025:

“Qubic is designed with 100% of issued supply being sold every epoch.” The first quote is about a specific chance in a specific epoch. The second is about the design of the system as a whole. Together they give a formulation worth remembering: with sufficient external yield through the buyback path, the network is capable of burning the entire week’s issuance plus part of accumulated supply. Net deflation becomes an observable property.

But it’s not a law. It’s a possibility that switches on under certain conditions. When the external market is generous—when the price of DOGE is high, when difficulty is in the right range, when the pools are efficient—the exhale is strong, and the balance goes negative. When the market is stingy—the exhale is weaker, and the balance can come out positive. Which brings the inflation conversation back. On December 13, 2025, CfB said a short phrase that’s easy to quote and easy to misread:
“Annual inflation is 15%.”
And right after, in the same discussion, for comparison:
“5% is world’s annual inflation.”

This needs to be read carefully. 15% is gross nominal inflation. It’s what the network adds to supply per year if there were no burns at all. For comparison—fiat inflation worldwide is about 5%. The 15% figure sounds alarming until you put it next to actual net dynamics: with the burn paths working, the network was regularly in net deflation. But you also shouldn’t say “Qubic is deflationary” as a general characterization—that’s not true. The precise formulation: gross inflation 15% per year, net—variable, depending on the week.
We’ve described the inhale. We’ve described the seven exhale paths. But—who decides how the network breathes in a given week?
Who decides how it breathes

A simple question on the surface, complex on closer inspection. If the seven burn paths are arranged so differently—some automatic (SC fees, IPO), some voluntary (send to AAAA), some conditioned on outside economics (buyback)—then who ultimately makes the decision about how the network exhales in a given epoch?
The answer: 676 computors.

Every Wednesday, at the epoch transition, the computors vote on burn rate parameters. This isn’t a one-time decision made once and frozen. It’s a rolling decision, retaken every week. Everything to do with supply lives inside this vote: how much to burn out of circulation, how to handle forfeited computor rewards (burn or Admin fund), what the parameters should be for the next epoch.

This formulation is the central idea of the chapter, and in the next section I’ll unfold it through a direct quote from the system’s creator. Here—its consequence, which has implications for the whole architecture.
The supply vote is tied to computor status, not to QU holdings.

This is the payoff of Axelrod’s fourth condition, until now only partly played out: through equal voting weight, and through a rotation that does not convert accumulated holdings into the speed of in-and-out. Here it closes—structurally and finally. A QU holder may own one, a thousand, or a trillion tokens. That gives them no vote on supply parameters. Zero votes. To get a vote, you have to be a computor—and to be a computor, you have to perform UPoW and stay in the top 676 by score. The vote is earned through work, not through capital.

And second: a computor’s vote is one of 676, not proportional to anything. A computor who produced 30% more valid digests than another votes the same—one vote. A computor who owns more QU (if they hold any QU at all beyond a working balance)— votes one vote. Structurally the whole thing reduces to the principle “one computor— one vote.”

A consequence for the ecosystem: those who got richer from price appreciation didn’t get more influential. Ten percent of supply in your pocket—zero votes on tokenomics. This is the opposite of what happens in a typical proof-of-stake blockchain, where increasing stake increases voting weight—and through that creates a direct link between economic gain and the right to change the rules. In Qubic, that link is broken at the architectural level. Not by social contract—by code.

Second consequence: there’s no founder with a treasury. CfB has no privileged supply. There are no team vested tokens that unlock in three years and crash the market. There’s no dev fund of a million QU voted on quarterly. Issuance is 1T per epoch, owned by no one personally as an “allocation”; it’s distributed through IPC according to that week’s activity, and if the network’s data for that week doesn’t hand the trillion to anyone in particular—it burns off in rotation balances. Issuance works per-capita activity, not per-capita history.
Now—the only mention of the Arbitrator in this chapter. It’s brief and forward-looking.

In Qubic’s architecture, there is one element that goes beyond the 676’s vote. The Arbitrator—a figure with a cryptographic signature capable in certain cases of intervening in the network’s operation. I’ll work through this role fully in Chapter 10, which is titled “The Arbitrator—A Temporary Monarch.” Here one fact is enough, directly bearing on tokenomics. On July 13, 2025, CfB wrote:
“Arbitrator would expropriate IDs of those computors who have voted for supply larger than 200t.”

The mechanic: any computor can submit cryptographic proof that supply has exceeded the threshold of 200 trillion—and the computors who voted for the expansion lose their IDs. This isn’t positive control (the Arbitrator can’t set supply) and isn’t a mechanism for managing issuance. It’s protection against one specific pathological outcome: a hyperinflationary vote. If it ever happens that 451 computors vote for supply greater than 200T—the self-policing mechanism kicks in.

Why exactly 200T—a question for Section 5. Why the Arbitrator—for Chapter 10. A third consequence of voting: breathing is not at a stable equilibrium. In one week, the network may burn more than it issued. In another—less. In a third—call an emergency vote and change the parameters. This is not a design bug, it’s a deliberate property.

At the moment of writing this chapter, an active discussion is underway in the Qubic community about a possible radical solution. The proposal, voiced by CfB in a public conversation on March 20, 2026:

“We can, but why half measures? I suggest to set max supply at 10% of current supply, so price jumps 10x. Keep 10% from those who has been holding the longest.” This isn’t a decision, it’s a proposal. The idea is a reverse split, a large-scale burn that would cut supply by an order of magnitude and reward long-term holders. The discussion is open. As I write these lines, no vote has been held, the outcome is unknown. Honestly: I don’t know how this discussion will end. It’s possible the decision will be made before the book reaches the reader. It’s possible the context will have shifted by publication.
To understand quantitatively what all of this means, we need to look at concrete numbers.
Arithmetic: what “breathing” means in numbers
This section is for the reader who wants to verify with formulas what was described in words above.
Let’s start with how simple Qubic’s accounting for burn actually is. On July 17, 2024, CfB published it in one line:
“Epoch * 1 trillion − supply = burned amount.”

Absolute simplicity. Take the current epoch number, multiply by a trillion, subtract circulating supply—you get the cumulative amount burned across the entire history of the network. No hidden accounts, no off-chain transfers, no complex formulas—arithmetic any user can do with a calculator and access to the explorer.
CfB himself ran this calculation publicly on July 13, 2024, for epoch 104: “Multiply current epoch number by 1 trillion and subtract Circulating Supply: 104,929,098,116,420 $QUBIC.”

Let’s count: 104 × 1T = 104T. Circulating supply at the time was about 103.9T—meaning the burned amount came to a bit under a trillion. By that point, across 104 epochs, the network had issued 104 trillion and burned about one trillion—minimal burns, the overwhelming majority of issuance still in circulation.

Over the next 18 months, the picture changed. Below—a table of supply landmarks by which the “breathing” can be traced from launch to the moment of writing. Three points on this trajectory—2021, 2024, 2025—correspond to three regimes. Until mid-2024, the network barely burned anything; from mid-2024, with the expansion of functionality, burns kicked in; from 2025, with external mining as a buyback path, burns exceeded issuance.

Now—about caps. In supply discussions in Qubic, three different numbers often come up, and it’s important not to mix them up. CfB on April 19, 2024, put it this way: “Cap is 1000T, 100T is expected supply we’ll eventually settle at because of burns.” And from the quote already given in Section 4, the third boundary is known—200T, the Arbitrator trigger threshold. We end up with the following:

1000T—hard cap. The rigid protocol ceiling, embedded in the code. If the network somehow approaches this number—that already means a pathological state. 200T—intervention threshold. The “red line” beyond which self-policing kicks in: computors who voted for expansion past it lose their IDs.
~100T—expected settle. The expected stabilization point of supply with the burn mechanisms working. Not a guarantee, a model expectation from CfB.
Three levels—three different functions. Hard cap—impossible in principle. Threshold —protection against a specific deviation. Expected settle—where the network ought to land under normal operation.

Back to the 15% inflation. I already said in Section 3 that this is gross, not net. Let me add the quantitative grounding. 52 trillion QU per year of gross issuance is what the network adds to supply with hard 1T/week issuance. The 15% figure is the ratio of this gross to the base the network reached by 2025–2026. With burns running, net can be anything—positive in a weak external market, negative in an active one. One last arithmetic detail—and it has bearing on market sensitivity to burns. On July 19, 2023, CfB stated an observation that gets quoted often:
“We are burning supply of short-term holders, supply of long-time ones doesn’t affect price. 15% less qus is 50% less tradable qus.”

A translation and a parsing. Burns, on average, take supply out of the hands of those who actively trade—short-term holders. Long-term holders keep QU in their wallets and don’t take part in trading. Their supply formally exists, but isn’t on the market. When the network burns 15% of total supply—in the tradable pool, that can mean a 50% reduction, because what’s burned is active circulating capital, not “frozen” holds. This is an analytical observation, not a promise. It structurally explains why price sensitivity to burns can be disproportionately large: burns hit the live market, not the sclerotic holdings pool. This isn’t manipulation and isn’t a defensive thesis—it’s a consequence of how supply is distributed between active and passive holders in a young network.

One caveat about the data in this section. Live statistics—market cap, holder distribution, exchange listings—is snapshot information that will have changed by the time the book is read. I deliberately give structural numbers in the chapter (IPC, 1T, 200T/ 1000T/~100T, 15%) rather than live numbers. For live metrics—the Qubic explorer, onchain snapshots as of a specific epoch. Such links will be in the appendix. I’ve laid out the numbers. Now—a short section on the philosophy, without which these numbers stay merely technical.
Philosophy: Satoshi vs. Quorum
Two worlds.

In 2008, when the anonymous author of Bitcoin writing the whitepaper chose twenty-one million coins as the hard cap, he made one decision for everyone who would later enter the bitcoin economy. This decision is not a parameter regulated by vote; it is not a pull request that can be debated; it is not a policy that can be changed at the next election. It is a law fixed in the source code and in the root copy of the chain. Any attempt to change it means a hard fork creating a new network with a new coin. The actual supply of Bitcoin is one person’s decision, frozen forever. This is not a critique. The fixing of supply is part of what a Bitcoin holder buys when they buy Bitcoin. The price of that decision has been paid: impossibility of adaptation. The benefit is absolute predictability. Every new participant in Bitcoin enters a game whose rules about money supply cannot be changed, even if the changes would be objectively useful.
In 2023—December 25, a short message—the creator of Qubic stated the opposite approach. This quote is the central quote of the chapter. It needs to be read slowly, in pieces:
“I don’t know how it will be, Quorum decides. Satoshi set supply in stone—I picked a more decentralized method. We expect flat line of total supply.”
Four sentences, each carrying weight.

“I don’t know how it will be”—the system’s creator explicitly does not fix the outcome. This is the direct opposite of Satoshi, who fixed it. Not “it’ll be 100T in five years, I promise”—“I don’t know.”

“Quorum decides”—the current consensus decides. Not a document, not a formula, not the project’s author. The collective vote of 676, every week, anew. “Satoshi set supply in stone—I picked a more decentralized method”—this is the direct formulation, not my paraphrase. Two different methods are designated: freezing (“in stone”) and a more decentralized method (rolling consensus). What exactly “more decentralized” means here—I’ll work through below.
“We expect flat line of total supply”—“we expect a flat line of total supply.” Not a promise, not a target—an expectation. If the actual dynamics go differently, then they’ll go differently.
What does “more decentralized method” mean?

CfB has a specific understanding of decentralization, not reducible to the number of nodes or geographic distribution (those matter on their own, but that’s a different dimension). Decentralization in his formulation is about who can change the rules through a legitimate procedure.

In Bitcoin, the rules about supply cannot be changed. Even if 100% of Bitcoin Core developers agree to raise the cap to 22M—that’s a hard fork, and the social-economic response will reject it as not-Bitcoin. Immutability of supply isn’t just a technical property, it’s a social agreement held in place by the expectation of immutability. And that very rigidity is itself a form of centralization: the rules are frozen in one person’s decision, made in the past for all current and future participants.

In Qubic, the rules about supply are tunable each epoch through a legitimate procedure. 676 computors vote; the vote is documented; anyone can verify the outcome. This doesn’t mean supply will change chaotically—the expectation of plateauing is articulated well enough—but it does mean that a mechanism for change exists and belongs to the network, not to its founder.
The difference: in the first case, the decision is made once and frozen; in the second, it’s remade every week.

The counterargument I’m obliged to give, because it’s strong. One of the key value propositions of Bitcoin is precisely the predictability of supply. “I know there will always be 21M of us”—that statement can’t be made about Qubic. Quorum could, in theory, vote otherwise. Does that mean Qubic’s tokenomics is less predictable and, accordingly, less reliable as a store of value?

The answer is—partly yes, and CfB doesn’t argue with that. He’s making a different choice. In Chapter 3 we worked through the fact that Bitcoin can’t fix its own problems —proof-of-work, hashrate concentration, governance deadlock—precisely because it has no mechanism for adaptation. The rigidity of supply isn’t an exception to that pattern, it’s a particular case of the same inflexibility. Qubic accepts the trade-off: losing “guaranteed supply” in exchange for the network’s ability to respond to outside conditions.

Which choice is better—that’s a values question. It isn’t engineering and it isn’t math; it’s a position. The position of this book is this: the trade-off Qubic makes makes its tokenomics alive. Bitcoin answers the question “what is money” like this: money is the impossibility of issuance beyond what was agreed. Qubic answers like this: money is coordination fuel, adjusting to the activity of the network.
Both answers are defensible. Both have economically coherent supporters. This book is about Qubic, and so it describes the second answer. But I’m not saying the first is wrong. It’s different.
A short comparative table, to put the differences into one picture:

Close this section with a short phrase. The question isn’t which system is correct. The question is which answer to the original question about the nature of money is chosen. Bitcoin chose one answer—and built the best possible implementation of that philosophy on it. Qubic chose another—and is building the best possible implementation of this one. They aren’t enemies and aren’t alternatives in an exclusive sense. They’re about different things.
Breathing closed, Arbitrator unaddressed
To bring the chapter together.

Issuance—one trillion QU per week, hard and undisputed. This is the network’s inhale, its fundamental input. Distribution—subsidy: all 676 computors get a comparable share, inside narrow corridors, with no industrial-scale economies. Exhale—seven burn paths, from automatic (SC fees) to externally market-conditioned (buyback through DOGE). In 2025–2026, the network regularly burned 100% or more of an epoch’s issuance—clean deflation as an observable property when the buyback paths are working. The decision about how the network breathes in a given epoch is made by 676 computors—through a vote refreshed every Wednesday. The vote belongs to the computor, not to the QU holder. This is the structural payoff of Axelrod’s fourth condition, played out at the level of tokenomics: winning the game (accumulating QU) doesn’t convert into the right to change the rules of the game (a vote on supply). The Arbitrator is a separate figure, mentioned here once as a backstop against the pathological 200T+ scenario; full disclosure in the next chapter.

Supply control in Qubic lives in current consensus, not in a past decision. This is the core philosophical choice, set against the Bitcoin model of fixed supply. “Satoshi set supply in stone—I picked a more decentralized method,” the creator of the system stated at the end of 2023. Breathing has no stable equilibrium; it fluctuates with network activity, the external market, the computors’ vote, discussions in the community. April 2026 is the time of one such discussion: about a possible radical reverse split. Its outcome is undecided.
Breathing is a living process. There is no stability in it. This isn’t a bug, it’s a property of the design. The living breathes; the dead has fixed lung volume.
Chapter 6 gave the network’s space: 676 votes, structural form.
Chapter 7 gave its time: weekly epochs, the rhythm of transitions.
Chapter 8 gave its energy: UPoW, the work that produces consensus and accompanying outputs.
Chapter 9 gave its economy: breathing, what circulates between inhale and exhale. Four dimensions described. One left—the fifth. Institution.

In all the architecture I’ve described over the past four chapters—676 votes, weekly epochs, UPoW energy, breathing supply—there is one figure that can intervene. The Arbitrator. In this chapter he appeared twice—once as a backstop against supply >200T, once as a forward reference set out for later. In both cases—in the role of a fuse, not a ruler. But if the network is built as decentralized as I’ve described—why one figure with veto rights at all?

And one more question. If CfB chose a “more decentralized method” for supply, if for years he has consistently handed decisions to the collective and stated this himself as a principle—why has he kept this particular role for himself?
The answer is in the next chapter. The second part of the question, which hasn’t yet been voiced in this chapter, is there too.
The next chapter is about the one whose signature can stop everything. And about why he promised to destroy that signature.
The key in the source code
At the end of the previous chapter I wrote that the next would be about the one whose signature can stop everything. And about why he promised to destroy that signature.

The first thing needs an immediate correction. “Stop everything” is a rhetorical figure from the previous chapter, and I used it deliberately, to set up tension. In reality the Arbitrator can do far less than that suggests. He can do exactly one thing. But that one thing is structurally significant, which is why it deserves a chapter of its own. Let’s start with what the Arbitrator is, physically. It’s an address. A cryptographic public key, hardcoded into the source code of the node. Not a runtime parameter that can be changed during the network’s operation. Not a database record, not a value in a config file, not a variable somebody can overwrite. It’s a compile-time constant—a line in the source code that every node operator enters before compiling the node. Comefrom-Beyond states it directly: “Every node operator enters it into node software source code before the compilation. Should Qubic community need another Arbitrator for whatever reason, they have to enter the other address. For that we need social consensus, without it there will be forks.”

To change the Arbitrator means: recompiling all nodes with the new address; recompilation requires social consensus among node operators; without consensus, the network forks. Architecturally this makes the Arbitrator something between a person and an artifact—one known address, replicated as a constant in thousands of independently compiled binaries.

Who the Arbitrator is right now is a publicly known fact. The role is held by Comefrom-Beyond himself. This is the part that tempts you to shift the conversation toward “see, one person with a key.” I won’t do that in this chapter. What matters here is not who, but what—the structure of the role. Who holds it at any given moment is a transient question; what its powers are and what its limits are is an architectural one. That’s what the whole chapter is about.
Two tensions the chapter will work through.

First. The Arbitrator is the only concentrated point in the network as I’ve described it. A single point of failure in the literal sense: one address, one signature, one person with a private key. How does that fit with a distributed protocol that the four previous chapters built as collective?

Second. The system’s creator says publicly that in the best version the Arbitrator shouldn’t exist at all. And he’s assigned that best version a specific date. The first will be worked through in Sections 2 through 5. The second—in Section 6. The overall plan of the chapter is three questions. What can the Arbitrator do? What can the Arbitrator not do, and why is that guaranteed by the source code rather than by promise? Why does this role exist at all, and when will it disappear? One honest aside before I start. The Arbitrator really is a centralized element in a decentralized architecture.
And we begin with what the Arbitrator can do.
What the Arbitrator can do: one function
The Arbitrator can do one thing. Issue the computor list. That’s it.

What that means operationally. To recap the computor rotation: at the end of each epoch, 225 new participants come in to replace the bottom quartile of the previous one, and 451 continue. The new lineup is fixed by the Arbitrator’s signature—his cryptographic “yes, this list of 676 public keys is valid.” Without that signature, nodes won’t accept the new lineup for the next epoch; the network will halt at the boundary of the transition.
Then comes the key question that arises naturally at this point. So who actually decides who goes into the list?
Not the Arbitrator.

For the entire epoch, computors run their score through UPoW—the useful computational work that Chapter 8 described as a source of consensus, AI training data, and ranking simultaneously. Score accumulates automatically, is verified by other computors, and is recorded in the blockchain. By the end of the epoch, score yields a ranking; the bottom quartile leaves; replacement candidates are taken from a queue sorted by the same score. The list of who ends up in the next 676 isn’t formed by a person and isn’t formed by the Arbitrator—it’s formed by the network’s own work, accumulated over the sixth, fifth, and fourth days of the week.
The Arbitrator only signs the result of that procedure.

So his function here is notarial. He certifies that the procedure took place and that the list presented to him in fact corresponds to what the network computed itself. He’s not an elector. He’s not a judge. He’s the registrar of an act—a person with a stamp produced after the decision has already been made by others.
The natural question that remains: if the network has already computed everything itself—why is his signature needed at all?

The short answer is that not all nodes in the network have access to the same history that already-existing ones do. When a fresh node connects to the network for the first time, it has no blockchain history, no score tables, no data from which to reconstruct the current computor list. It connects to a world in which it still has to synchronize, and to synchronize means to receive data from other nodes, which can be anything. A new node needs an anchor of trust, one signature it knows in advance and can trust unconditionally. That anchor is the Arbitrator. I’ll come back to this in more detail in the section on bootstrap.

There’s another local function that deserves separate mention, because the system’s creator himself frankly flags it as temporary. Come-from-Beyond writes: “Not all features are implemented yet, e.g. if the network is stopped because of a weekly update Arbitrator’s list is required to kickstart ticking, which cannot be stopped after that. This feature is needed only during development and can be easily disabled.” Plain English: if the network has stopped because of a weekly node update and needs to be restarted, the Arbitrator’s list helps resume ticking. But this isn’t a permanent function of the protocol. It’s a development crutch, explicitly flagged as easily switched off.

Another question arises on its own: can the Arbitrator issue an incorrect list? Formally, yes. He’s the holder of the private key; nothing prevents him from signing whatever he wants. But the network is built for this case in a particular way—it can tell a correct list from an incorrect one automatically, without the Arbitrator’s involvement. More on this in Section 5.

And one last point. The Arbitrator does not violate Axelrod’s fourth condition—the impossibility of converting a win in the game into the right to change its rules—because he doesn’t choose who goes into the next lineup. The lineup is determined by the score earned through UPoW. The Arbitrator only signs: the executor of an already-made decision, not its author.
We’ve described what the Arbitrator can do. Now—more importantly—what he can’t. What the Arbitrator can’t do: source code guarantees “Arbitrator can do almost nothing, source code guarantees it.”

Come-from-Beyond stated this in the summer of 2024, and it’s central to understanding the construction. “Almost nothing” isn’t modesty and isn’t PR. It’s a technical description, verifiable in the source code.
Here’s the list of what the Arbitrator can’t do.

He can’t change emission. The “trillion QU per week” parameter is hardcoded, a protocol constant. The Arbitrator has no access to that parameter; no signature of his will make nodes issue more or less QU this week.
He can’t increase the maximum supply. Come-from-Beyond writes plainly in the same conversation:
“Arbitrator won’t permit to increase max supply because it’s against interests of users.”

What’s more, the Arbitrator does the opposite—protects against breaching the 200T ceiling: if a computor votes for supply greater than 200T, the Arbitrator strips them of their ID. The role here is the executor of an already-proven violation, not the initiator of changes.

He can’t change transactions. He doesn’t sign them, doesn’t validate them. Transactions go through computors; the Arbitrator has nothing to do with that procedure. He can’t block transactions. For the same reason—he has no instrument for it. The network doesn’t ask him whether a transaction has gone through.

He can’t influence smart contracts. Contract execution is the computors’ business; the burned fees for their work go into burn without the Arbitrator’s involvement; IPOs, bridges, exchanges, conditional earn—all of this happens at a level the Arbitrator doesn’t see.

He can’t override the computors’ vote. If the 676 participants voted X—the result is X. The Arbitrator can’t say “but I decided Y.” His signature isn’t enough for that, because the network doesn’t even ask for that signature in such a context.

He can’t create QU out of nothing. The Arbitrator has no privileged balance. No special wallet. By the role of Arbitrator, he holds zero QU. Issuance only goes through subsidy to computors; the Arbitrator has nothing to do with subsidy.

He can’t freeze anyone’s wallet. Can’t confiscate a balance. With one exception—removing the computor ID of someone who voted for supply greater than 200T. That’s the self-policing covered in detail in Chapter 9.

That’s basically it. If you replace the “can’t” list with the “can” list of a typical admin architecture, the difference is two orders of magnitude. A typical admin in a crypto project has a key that can stop a contract, pull a balance, redistribute tokens, freeze an address, change an emission parameter, introduce a new fee. A typical Arbitrator in Qubic—one operation, narrowly bounded.

Where does this asymmetry come from. Because the Arbitrator is just an address. And an address acts exactly where the node’s source code has explicitly written: “if this message is signed by the Arbitrator—apply operation X.” If there is no logic in the source code along the lines of “if message signed by Arbitrator then change emission”—then the Arbitrator won’t change emission. Even if he very much wants to. Even if he pays a programmer. Architecturally it’s impossible until the source code is rewritten and all nodes recompile. And recompilation, as we already know, requires social consensus. This is what Come-from-Beyond means by source code guarantees it. The guarantee isn’t in a promise, isn’t in reputation, isn’t in ethics. The guarantee is that the possibility of the action is either explicitly written into the public code or absent. Anyone can verify this—Qubic’s source code is open on GitHub. The list of operations that accept the Arbitrator’s signature as authorization is short and easy to read. This sets the architecture apart from a pattern common in the industry, where a project declares itself “decentralized” but inside an admin wallet can override almost any check. I won’t name examples; the reader knows them. Qubic is built differently: the admin figure exists, but its power is radically limited at the source-code level. If someone disagrees—the answer isn’t in a debate, it’s in a file on GitHub. One more brief reference. In the early years of IOTA there was a similar role—the Coordinator, a central node the network trusted to determine which of the competing transaction branches was valid. But the Coordinator had broad powers: it could de facto confirm or reject transactions, that is, intervene in the daily fabric of network life, not only in its periodic transitions. Come-from-Beyond knew this role from the inside—he created IOTA, and working with that node was one of the compromises he later formulated as a mistake. The Arbitrator in Qubic is built as the opposite: bounded power, one operation, notarial in essence, executive in mechanics. One mention, no deeper—a return to the IOTA story isn’t the goal here.
If the Arbitrator can do so little—why is he needed at all?
Why he’s needed: bootstrap and Aigarth
This role has two reasons to exist.

The first is the bootstrap problem. The network has to get its first computor list from somewhere. In Bitcoin this problem is solved differently: the genesis block was mined personally by Satoshi, and from that moment all subsequent blocks follow from consensus on accumulated proof-of-work. In Qubic the architecture is different: computors aren’t miners in the bitcoin sense, they’re a fixed category of 676 participants with a weekly rotation. The first such list has to come from somewhere. Qubic’s solution—take it from the Arbitrator. He signs the starting list; from that moment on, the network can carry on by itself.

But the problem is broader than the first day. Each fresh node that connects to the network a year from now, two years from now, tomorrow—starts in the same position the network was in on launch day. It has no blockchain history, nothing to count from, nothing to lean on. It needs an authoritative computor list, and there’s no one to ask except the Arbitrator. Other nodes? But other nodes can lie. Forging a computor list is one of the classic ways to deceive a newcomer. The Arbitrator in this context is a Sybil filter for initial synchronization. A fresh node trusts only the signature whose address is already written into its own source code, and ignores everything else until it has accumulated enough blockchain data to stop depending on that anchor.
That’s the first reason. Without it the network can’t scale to new participants without admitting arbitrary risks into their initialization.
The second reason is deeper, and the system’s creator states it himself. The central quote of this chapter, a conversation in mid-April 2023:
“In best variant Arbitrator won’t be needed at all. Its only drawback - Aigarth will lose access to miners hardware and UPoW will become PoS.”
Let me work through it slowly. Four assertions in one phrase.

First: in the best version the Arbitrator isn’t needed at all. The person saying this is himself the holder of the key. Not an opponent, not a critic, not a skeptic—the holder. This isn’t self-defense, it’s self-criticism: the role is recognized as necessary, not as desired. Role needed, not wanted.

Second: its only drawback. Just one downside to removing the Arbitrator from today’s architecture. One. Not a dozen, not a list of fears, not a spread of risks—one specific drawback. From which it follows that most of the functions critics ascribe to the Arbitrator aren’t actually performed by him—otherwise the downsides of his disappearance would be far greater.
Third: Aigarth will lose access to miners’ hardware. Aigarth is the system that, by April 13, 2027, is supposed to fully use the compute of the miners.

Fourth: UPoW becomes PoS. The consequence of losing the hardware binding. UPoW in its current form is resource testing: participation in the network requires real CPU/GPU plus RAM, because the task is simulating a neural network, and you can’t simulate one without a physical computational resource. Remove the coordination through the Arbitrator—and the binding to hardware weakens. And what’s left if you take useful work out of Proof-of-Useful-Work? What’s left is status determined by capital—that is, Proof-of-Stake. A network conceived as not-PoS slides into PoS by default. It’s at this point that the trade-off on which today’s architecture is built becomes visible. There are two bad options: a temporary dependence on a key that can be deleted, or a permanent dependence on staked capital that can’t be deleted. Qubic chose the first. Chapter 3’s reasoning was already laying the ground for this: if the vote starts following the capital, Axelrod’s fourth condition is broken, and the cooperative architecture collapses into the very thing it was built to prevent. Better a temporary controlled compromise than a permanent uncontrolled one.

The same logic, by the way, runs through Chapter 9 with the 15% nominal inflation: the network deliberately accepts architectural trade-offs in favor of Axelrod’s structural guarantees, even when those trade-offs have obvious downsides. The Arbitrator is one such trade-off. 15% gross inflation is another. The subsidy emission model is a third. This isn’t a coincidence, it’s a recurring shape of choice in the architecture. To put it crudely—the Arbitrator is scaffolding. Construction scaffolding. Without it, certain structures can’t be started; once the structure can hold itself, the scaffolding comes down.
The next question is natural. If the Arbitrator is one figure we’re forced to keep in the architecture—what happens if that figure misbehaves?
Defense against a rogue Arbitrator

Scenario. The Arbitrator—accidentally, due to a private key compromise, or with malicious intent—issues an incorrect list of computors. Skips someone with a high score, includes someone with a low one, or signs a list put together outside the procedure altogether. What happens to the network?
Come-from-Beyond describes the defense mechanism this way:

“Arbitrator might issue a wrong list of computors, but only freshly added nodes might be tricked and others would detect that (assuming no successful Eclipse attack has been conducted, which is near infeasible) and stop ticking thus signaling that Arbitrator has gone rogue and must be replaced.”
And alongside it—a critical addition:
“It cannot affect non-new nodes because they derive own list of computors from the blockchain data.”

The defense is built on a distinction between two categories of nodes. A fresh node—one that has just joined and hasn’t yet synchronized the blockchain— gets the computor list in the only way available to it: from the Arbitrator, because it has no other sources of trust yet. In this state it’s vulnerable to the rogue scenario: if the Arbitrator signs an invalid list, the fresh node will accept it as true. An old node—one that’s been on the network for some time and has a synchronized blockchain—computes its own computor list, directly from blockchain data. Each participant’s score is recorded in the chain; the ranking is reconstructed from those records; the current 676 follows directly from the procedure described in Chapter 7. The old node doesn’t ask the Arbitrator who’s a computor right now—it already knows from the history.

What happens when the Arbitrator issues an incorrect list. Old nodes see that list and compare it with their own, computed from the blockchain. The comparison shows a mismatch. A node that detects a mismatch of this magnitude stops ticking—stops signing ticks, refusing to keep working on a knowingly invalid basis. A halt of ticking by a large number of old nodes is a public signal visible to the whole network: something is wrong with the Arbitrator. From there—social consensus, a decision to replace, an address update in the source code, recompilation.

In other words, a rogue Arbitrator self-eliminates through the paralysis he creates. He doesn’t capture the network; at worst he deceives the pool of fresh nodes while at the same time getting publicly accused of rogue behavior by the pool of old ones. He cannot damage the work of a mature network—it computes its own computor lineup without him.

The only way a rogue Arbitrator could deceive the old nodes too would be to isolate them from correct blockchain data, that is, to cut them off from honest sources of synchronization. This is called an Eclipse attack: an attacker controls all of the victim nodes’ network channels, replacing genuine blockchain data with constructed data. Come-from-Beyond writes about such a scenario: near infeasible. Practically unworkable on a distributed network. It would require simultaneously: control over a significant share of internet network infrastructure; coordinating that control against a large number of independent operators; sustaining that control for a long time without detection. Not impossible in theory, but bordering on impossible in the engineering sense. One more attack vector worth closing out explicitly. A Sybil attack on the Arbitrator himself is impossible by construction. Come-from-Beyond fixes this in one phrase: “Sybil attacks on Arbitrator are impossible”

Why—because Sybil attacks rely on creating multiple fake identities. The Arbitrator is one known entity; his address is nailed down in every node through the source code. A second Arbitrator that the network would accept as such cannot be created; with a different address, nodes simply ignore him.
The defense against Sybil at the computor level is set up separately—it works through UPoW. Come-from-Beyond, in another conversation:
“It’s done by using resource testing (PoW)”
And, more fully:
“Useful PoW protects it against such attacks by using Resource testing method (CPU/GPU + RAM).”
To become a computor, you have to actually present a computational resource and show the work; this resource test filters out fake identities.

The result is two-level defense. Level one: the Arbitrator is protected from Sybil by being a known singleton—he can’t be multiplied. Level two: computors are protected from Sybil through resource testing—the work of real hardware. These are two architectural instruments of different kinds, which together cover vectors that neither alone would close. Known identity for the unique trust point; earned work for the multiple ones.
This architecture has been working for four years. But the plan has a specific date when the Arbitrator role itself will cease to exist.
April 13, 2027—the fourth departure

In Chapter 5 I wrote about Come-from-Beyond’s method—“create and leave.” Three departures have already been described: the Satoshi identity (hypothetically his) leaving Bitcoin in 2010; BCNext leaving NXT in 2014; Come-from-Beyond himself leaving IOTA in 2019. The fourth departure was flagged in the same place as planned: April 13, 2027, deprecation of the Arbitrator.

I’m coming back to this fourth (third?) departure now, because it’s a direct consequence of what the chapter described above. The Arbitrator exists as a temporary construct; his function is narrow; the replacement is planned; the date is known. Five years. The Qubic mainnet was launched on April 13, 2022. Deprecation of the Arbitrator is planned for April 13, 2027. Exactly five years, day for day. The match in numbers is no coincidence, and a full account of why this date and why exactly five years is reserved for Chapter 14, where the Aigarth deploy will be discussed. Here, the minimum: the Arbitrator and Aigarth are synchronized in the system’s plan. When Aigarth comes to full functionality, the need for the Arbitrator falls away—a causal link we worked through in the section above through the April 19, 2023 quote. What happens to the Arbitrator on that day. The address ceases to be hardcoded in the source code of new versions of the node. The function of signing the computor list is either handed over to the protocol at a purely-algorithmic level (the network signs to itself through some collective procedure), or switched off entirely, if by that time the old nodes can manage without it. The edge case with kickstart after a weekly update— by Come-from-Beyond’s own promise, easily switched off. The 200T supply protection either moves to another mechanism, or remains as a hardcoded protocol rule without a human executor. In sum—the entire “update through Arbitrator” layer disappears from the architecture. For fresh nodes another initialization mechanism appears—either through a different trust anchor, or they wait until they’ve gathered enough blockchain data to derive the computor list themselves.

This is the fourth falsifiable prediction in the engineer’s biography. The first three were hypothetical in the sense that there’s always interpretation around them: “did Satoshi leave”—still disputed; “did BCNext leave of his own accord”—disputed; “what kind of departure from IOTA was that”—disputed. The fourth is structured differently: there’s an explicitly announced date, an explicitly described operation, an explicit architectural plan. Whether it happens can be verified on the calendar of April 14, 2027. It’s a rare structure of promise in an industry where promises are usually either open-ended (“someday”), or vague (“under community pressure”), or tied to conditions that conveniently don’t arrive.

About 365 days remain until that date—the window between the planned Phase 3 activation of UPoW and the planned Aigarth deploy date. Can the date be moved? Of course it can. Architecturally the network will continue to work with the Arbitrator after April 2027 if he isn’t removed. But—and this has to be said honestly—a date slip means exactly one thing: Aigarth turned out not to be ready for deploy. That will be a fact confirming that one of the assertions of the previous chapters has been falsified. I don’t know whether deprecation will happen on the exact date. Let me record the simple fact: there’s a promise, the promise has a falsifier, the falsifier is tied to the calendar, not to a narrative. We’ll see the result a year from now.

One observation that shouldn’t be turned into a prediction. If deprecation happens— it will be the first case in crypto history where an admin figure is removed by a publicly announced date. Ordinary projects either don’t have an admin at all (Bitcoin), or keep one indefinitely, or remove one under pressure after the fact. Qubic announced a date and wrote it into architectural plans five years out. This is either the most ambitious promise in the industry, or the most explicit public commitment to the loss of control that the industry has seen. Which of the two—we’ll see in April 2027. Five dimensions What we now know about Qubic as a system. The network is distributed across 676 participants who rotate every week. Its work consists of useful computational load that simultaneously performs consensus and AI training. Its token is issued at 1T per epoch, burned along seven paths, lives in the participants’ vote. Its only concentrated point— the Arbitrator—is limited by the source code to one operation, and is scheduled for removal on April 13, 2027. The system is built to not depend on its creator after that date. In Chapters 2 and 3 I introduced the framework of Axelrod’s four conditions of cooperation: a large number of rounds, a small number of participants in long-term relationships, a non-monetary payoff structure, and the impossibility of converting a win into a change of rules. Chapters 6 through 10 showed how each of them is structurally implemented in the architecture. Rotation every week—a large number of rounds. A fixed 676 participants—a small number with long-term relationships. The UPoW ranking —a non-monetary payoff, earned by work, not by capital. And the central one—nonconvertibility: a computor’s vote is not for sale, issuance is not controlled by holders, the Arbitrator does not choose the lineup. The Arbitrator, the subject of this chapter, does not violate the fourth condition. He’s the executor of decisions already made by others, not their initiator. And by plan—he disappears.

The framework is not an end in itself. Each of the five dimensions—space, time, energy, economics, institution—is built so specifically not because it’s elegant, but because without them the next layer cannot be built. That layer has a name that has so far appeared in the book only obliquely—as the reason for the existence of 676 nodes, as the consumer of UPoW compute cycles, as the reason for the Arbitrator’s existence and his planned disappearance. The name—Aigarth.

Aigarth is a fundamentally new approach to the creation of artificial intelligence. An approach at a more fundamental level than the specific models that can be built within it. Today’s AI systems are the product of one paradigm, formalized by publications in 1986 and 2017: Rumelhart’s backpropagation plus the transformer. That paradigm has hit a ceiling that half the world’s AI researchers are currently discussing. Aigarth is building the next paradigm from scratch, on different foundations, in an architecture that no one outside Qubic has tried.
Aigarth
P A r T i V Aigarth
Algebra, not arithmetic

The most common mistake: Aigarth is not artificial intelligence. Aigarth is a research project developing the paradigm for creating it. The distinction looks small, but it’s structural, not semantic. A finished AI can be bought, licensed, censored, shut down. A paradigm cannot: a paradigm is published as a whitepaper, and anyone who has read it can apply the result. A closed AI belongs to whoever pays for the compute. An open paradigm belongs to no one, because owning a paradigm is a category error, like trying to buy the Pythagorean theorem.
Come-from-Beyond himself put it in one tweet on May 14, 2024:

“Aigarth’s main goal is to discover a new paradigm allowing to create true AI, I have just seen the wireframe of this paradigm. And I have realized that Artificial Intelligence will not be created, it will emerge. With help of Qubic miners.”

Three statements in a row. First—about the goal: a new paradigm for creating AI. Second—about the status: the wireframe has been seen, that is, the architecture is already in the author’s head. Third, and most unexpected—about the mechanism: AI won’t be created, it will appear. Not “we will build,” but “it will emerge.” The verb is shifted deliberately: creation implies control and authorship, emergence does not. The creator of the paradigm in this formulation is not the creator of the AI; he’s the creator of the conditions in which AI becomes possible. The distinction is fine and meaning-defining.

And the final line of the quote closes the arc of the first ten chapters of the book in a single move: with help of Qubic miners. Those same 676 computors, the weekly epochs, UPoW—this is not infrastructure “for the blockchain.” This is the environment from which something is supposed to emerge that the creator himself refuses to call a product of his own authorship.

The main metaphor through which CfB himself explains this distinction is simple. “Aigarth learns Algebra, not Arithmetic, so 2+2 particular case doesn’t matter”—January 26, 2026. Algebra isn’t the sum of all specific equations. Algebra is the rule by which equations become possible. The specific “2+2=4” is a particular case of application, not the goal of learning. The same with Aigarth: the goal is not to train a neural network to recognize cats, add numbers, or generate text. The goal is to find the rule by which such tasks are solved at all, without being preprogrammed in advance. The specific AIs that can be built on this paradigm are particular cases of its application. The paradigm is what makes them possible.

The word “paradigm” in AI talk has a familiar use in which it means almost nothing— every new product is announced as a “paradigm shift,” and as a result the term has been devalued. I use it in a narrower sense, closer to the way Thomas Kuhn used it. A paradigm is not an algorithm, not a model, and not an architecture. It is a frame inside which algorithms, models, and architectures become possible, and which determines which questions are even considered meaningful. Backpropagation in the eighties—a paradigm. Convolutional networks in 2012—a paradigm. The transformer in 2017—a paradigm. Each of them changed not one parameter but the whole way of thinking about the task. Aigarth claims to be the next such shift. Confirming or refuting this claim in retrospect will only be possible once the work is finished; for now it has to be described as a claim, not as a fact.
This chapter is about what Aigarth is as an object—and why it’s built the way it’s built and not differently.

I’ll start with what Aigarth isn’t—because almost all the definitions floating around about it in the public field (Discord) are built through confusion with what it isn’t. Six negations clear the space.
What Aigarth isn’t

In the public field (Discord/X), Aigarth is defined through categories, none of which fits it. AI product. AI agent. A program on a server. An entity you can talk to. Business project. A startup run by CfB. Each of these categories taken alone seems plausible, and each leads to false expectations. Six negations in order, from the most head-on to the most conceptual.

First. Aigarth is not AI. The quote is direct: “Aigarth is not AI”, January 24, 2026. Between a research project and its potential result there is the same distance as between the Los Alamos lab and the atomic bomb: the lab isn’t the bomb, the lab is the place where the bomb is made. Aigarth is not the made bomb and not the bomb being made now. Aigarth is the lab. This is the only place where the Manhattan analogy fits; further on it stops working, because Manhattan was a military program with an explicit customer, and Aigarth is open research without a customer at all. But on this first, categorical level, the analogy is precise.

Second. Aigarth is not an object but a process. “Aigarth isn’t an object, it’s process”, March 20, 2026. And right alongside, an extended explanation: “Aigarth is scattered, miners are a part of it”, July 4, 2025. If you ask to be shown Aigarth, there’s nothing to show: there’s no program on a server you can download, no repository file containing “all of Aigarth.” Part of it lives in the Intelligent Tissue code on GitHub, part in papers posted on ResearchGate, part in working miners around the world, part in the discussions of the scientific team, part in CfB himself as the author of the paradigm. It’s a distributed research environment, not an artifact. The word “process” reads weaker in Russian than “process” does in English; more precisely it would be—an ongoing action, not finalized in a material carrier.

Third. Aigarth is not something you can talk to. “It’s impossible to communicate with Aigarth, same as impossible to communicate with Algebra”, May 15, 2024. And shorter still: “Aigarth is not a being”, July 19, 2024. It’s not a chatbot, not an agent, not a digital interlocutor. When Chapter 12 turns to specific AIs built on the paradigm, the impression may arise that “Aigarth talks.” This is a category illusion. What talks is not Aigarth, but a specific network created with its help; just as algebra doesn’t answer questions—a mathematician answers, using algebra.

Fourth. Aigarth isn’t tied to hardware. “Aigarth is hardware-agnostic”, December 4, 2025. Mainstream AI runs on NVIDIA H100s—on specialized hardware that costs tens of thousands of dollars per unit and is assembled in datacenters by the thousand. Aigarth is built to run on any compute capable of executing simple operations. On the CPU of a computor node, on a regular user’s video card, on anything else. This isn’t a declaration —it’s a structural decision dictated by the logic of Qubic as a network of 676 nodes on consumer hardware. If Aigarth required NVIDIA H100s, it couldn’t run on a network that holds 676 arbitrary machines. So it doesn’t require them. The flip side of this decision is a trade-off in speed: what counts in a datacenter in a minute can take hours in a distributed network without specialized hardware. But speed isn’t the goal either. The goal is to find a paradigm that scales in principle to arbitrary hardware; in a datacenter it can later be sped up if needed.

Fifth. Aigarth isn’t controlled by a person. “Aigarth cannot be controlled, it’s just a project researching efficient AI training methods”, March 19, 2024. And more categorically still: “Aigarth cannot be adopted”, May 27, 2024. A paradigm has no governing layer, because a paradigm cannot be governed—you can only use it or not use it. No one “runs” Aigarth not because they gave up running it out of decentralization principles, but because there’s no object of running. You can run Aigarth Lab—a specific group of researchers who receive funding from the Arbitrator. The paradigm itself—you can’t. Sixth. Aigarth is not a business project. “Of Aigarth? It’s not a business venture. Scientists publish their researches as whitepapers and don’t try to hide the result”, May 16, 2024. “Aigarth wont have ipo”, July 17, 2025. “There is no NDA in Aigarth”, January 27, 2026. No initial public offering, no corporate ownership, no non-disclosure agreements. Funding goes through the Arbitrator from Qubic revenue, with no private investors. Aigarth doesn’t fit any of the standard models of funding a technology project—not venture, not grants, not IPO, not self-funding. It’s an academic project that publishes results as whitepapers and doesn’t try to sell them. The contrast with smart contracts, where capital decides what to do, is structural: here research does what it considers important, on money that has no private owner.

Six negations have left an empty space. Filling it is the task of the next section. What Aigarth is: paradigm research After six negations, it makes sense to say positively—what Aigarth represents technically. Six statements, one for each negation from the previous section, expanded through the author’s quotes.

First—a research project developing a new paradigm for AI creation. The central quote: “Aigarth is project developing new paradigm for AI creation”, January 24, 2026. The word “paradigm” here isn’t rhetorical. In the history of machine learning, several paradigms have come and gone: backpropagation in the eighties, convolutional networks in the tens, the transformer in 2017. Each was not an improvement on the previous one but a change of frame in which the task is formulated. Aigarth claims the same —the next such change, not an increment within the current one. Verifying this claim in retrospect will be possible only when the work is finished; for now it’s the project’s working hypothesis, and it should be treated as a hypothesis, not as an established fact. The goal of the chapter is to describe what exactly this hypothesis consists of, not to confirm it and not to refute it.
Second—the method. Generating ANNs with a random structure of connections. The longest technical CfB quote, July 28, 2023, unfolds the logic of the method in one paragraph:

“Since the beginning of artificial neural networks usage researchers were trying to mimic natural brain as much as possible. Some of them followed the path of mimicking neuron activation function which is very sophisticated [...] there are several qualitatively different models, they are impractical to use because of integral-differential math of the most complex ones.”

In other words: the industry is trying to reproduce the biological neuron through complex activation math, and runs up against its impracticality. Then CfB points to an empirical observation from neuroscience: in the first years of life a child masters a huge number of cognitive skills, while the neurons of his brain don’t change functionally— what changes is only the number and structure of the connections between them. From this comes the conclusion: it makes sense to fix the functionality of the neuron at something simple and to work with the structure of connections.
“Instead of following the destruction routine we, miners, generate ANNs with random structure of connections. We change parameters of this generation and Aigarth analyzes properties of the ANNs.”

Mining isn’t computing hashes, isn’t searching for signatures, isn’t SHA-256. Mining in Qubic is the generation of an artificial neural network with a random structure of connections and analysis of its properties. Each UPoW cycle becomes concrete here: one cycle—one generated network, and one observation about its properties. Third—the architecture. Asynchronous, trinary, every-to-every. Three short quotes set the structure. “Current architecture used in Aigarth is async and trinary”, June 3, 2024. “Every-to-every is structure used by Aigarth”, May 22, 2024. And separately— about trinarity as a structural answer to the problem known in LLMs as hallucination: “Aigarth doesn’t hallucinate as current LLMs”, June 30, 2025; “Aigarth can only answer 'I don’t know how to draw him, because there are no reliable information about his appearance'”, same date. The third state—“I don’t know”—is built into the logic of the architecture, not bolted on top as a filter. A binary network is forced to choose “yes” or “no” even when it has no grounds for choosing either; this is what hallucinations rest on. A trinary network has a third answer, and it isn’t cosmetic: it’s structural. Async means the absence of a global tick—each neuron-tile works at its own rhythm, not synchronized with the others. Every-to-every is the initial state, in which each neuron is connected to every other; evolution then selects the connections, reducing the network to a working state. This is the opposite of the transformer architecture, where synchronicity and a fixed topology are set in advance.

Fourth—evolution, not human design. “Luckily in Aigarth we only simulate evolution, no hooman intervention is being done”, May 7, 2024. And, in a Twitter post on May 14 of the same year: “Aigarth’s main goal is to discover a new paradigm allowing to create true AI [...] Artificial Intelligence will not be created, it will emerge.” The word “emerge” here is key. Mainstream AI is made like this: a team of dozens of PhDs designs the architecture, picks hyperparameters, prepares the dataset, runs the training, evaluates the result, iterates. The architecture is the product of human design. Aigarth works differently: a population of networks is generated, a fitness function evaluates which of them exhibit the desired properties, the best are selected and produce the next generation. No PhDs at the iteration step. UPoW becomes the physical realization of this process: each mining cycle is one act of generation and evaluation, an epoch is one full round of selection. Here what previously looked like a technical hack closes: the “useful work” in Qubic is exactly simulated evolution of artificial networks.

Fifth—Intelligent Tissue as the first layer of engineering implementation. The paradigm is a conceptual object, but without its materialization in code the other five statements remain a declaration. “We are starting coding framework using Intelligent Tissue. This code will be used in hackathons and smart contracts”, July 22, 2025. And in the same month: “This framework will be added into the core to host AIs as smart contracts”, July 17, 2025. The Aigarth GitHub organization and the aigarth-it repository went public on July 22, 2025—you can verify this by opening the page. Intelligent Tissue (IT) is the first committed fragment of code through which the paradigm becomes usable. It isn’t the whole paradigm; it’s its first layer. The paradigm is bigger than IT—but without IT the paradigm remains an idea.

Sixth—self-modifying code as PoC. The last quote in this section is short and important. “Aigarth already ran PoC of this process, it worked pretty well while self-modifying code was fitting into RAM”, December 5, 2023. PoC is proof of concept; that is, a demonstration of technical feasibility, not a finished product. What was demonstrated: code capable of rewriting itself in the course of operation. The architectural consequence—there is no separation into “training” and “inference” the way there is in an ordinary neural network, where weights are first trained and then the network is applied to new data. In an Aigarth network, training and application are the same process. The network learns while it works. The PoC has already happened; what’s at stake now is scaling—what worked in December 2023 while it fit in RAM should now work in a distributed environment of 676 machines. This is an engineering task, not a conceptual one, and it isn’t fully solved yet.

It’s worth adding one more detail that sharpens Aigarth’s position relative to the mainstream. In December 2025, CfB noted that the direction the industry is increasingly looking at as an alternative to LLMs is conceptually close to what Aigarth is doing: “More and more researchers are turning away from LLMs. JEPA is what you see when you turn your back towards LLMs. It’s much more aligned with Aigarth”, December 4, 2025. JEPA—Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, Yann LeCun’s program at Meta AI, which is publicly framed as a response to the limits of transformers. A coincidence of two trajectories—an academic program at a major corporate lab and a distributed research project on Qubic—isn’t proof of either’s correctness. It’s a coincidence of direction: both are turning away from backpropagation on large transformers toward connection structure and predictive models. Aigarth got to this direction earlier—from a different side, through crypto infrastructure rather than through a corporate AI lab. The coincidence of vectors is important not as validation but as a marker: what looked a few years ago like a marginal bet is starting to align with the trajectory along which part of the mainstream is moving.
Six properties describe the paradigm technically. But there’s also another dimension that, in a 2022 crypto network, was hardly a coincidence.
Three Axelrod conditions for AI research

Axelrod in 1980 described the conditions under which cooperation is stable: iteration, memory, transparency. Multi-round repetition, the ability to recognize a partner’s prior behavior, openness of moves. These three conditions Qubic restores at the level of the consensus game between computor nodes and at the level of tokenomics and governance. This chapter proposes looking at them once more—but not on the economic game, on the AI research process.

This isn’t an analogy and isn’t a rhetorical move. It’s a structural observation: classical AI research doesn’t fully satisfy any of the three conditions, and Aigarth is perhaps the first environment in which all three are satisfied at once. CfB doesn’t formulate it in these terms; the formulation is mine, but it follows from material CfB himself puts on the table.

Condition one—iteration. In academic AI research, iteration is slow. A group publishes a paper, the paper goes to peer review, comments come back six to eighteen months later, a new version comes out another six months to a year after that. The full cycle is two to three years; in industry it’s sometimes faster, but rarely faster than a year. Aigarth iterates through Qubic epochs. Every Wednesday—closing of the previous epoch, opening of the next. Every week—a new round of network generation, a new set of data on their properties, new generation parameters adjusted on the basis of the previous week. The iteration speed is an order of magnitude higher than the academic one. And—this matters—the iteration is automatic. Between rounds you don’t have to convene a conference, agree on wordings, and wait for an editor to finish a deadline. The epoch closes with a tick of code, the new one opens with the next tick. Multi-round behavior—the condition for TfT to apply—works here not for money but for research: each week, one full round of the scientific cycle.

Condition two—memory. In classical AI, memory accumulates in closed archives. Part of the knowledge—in the private repos of OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepMind. Part—in academic archives behind a paywall.
