Part—in the heads of specific researchers, and that part disappears with them when they leave a company or change fields. Most labs have NDAs that formalize what exactly cannot be taken outside. Most publications have a selective filter: what didn’t work usually doesn’t get published, and that’s the well-known reproducibility crisis. Aigarth accumulates memory in public artifacts. A paper is posted on ResearchGate with a GitHub repository and a Hugging Face demo. This combination makes the result verifiable by a third party: you can download the code, run the experiment, see whether it reproduces. The authors are tied to the work by name—Vivancos and Sanchez—and their reputation builds through the same artifacts through which trust in the work itself builds. CfB states this explicitly: “Scientists publish their researches as whitepapers and don’t try to hide the result”, May 16, 2024. And shorter still: “There is no NDA in Aigarth”, January 27, 2026. This is memory that doesn’t leave with a person and doesn’t get shut behind an NDA, because no NDA is provided for in Aigarth.

Condition three—transparency. Mainstream AI is often not reproducible even on its own data. Model weights—closed. Datasets—closed or partially described. Hyperparameters—sometimes given in the paper, sometimes not. Architectural details—stated, but without working code. This isn’t ill will—it’s a property of the closed commercial environment, in which reproducibility runs against the owner’s interests. Aigarth runs on distributed verification: code runs simultaneously on 676 nodes, and any divergence in the result between nodes is detected within one consensus tick. If one of the computor operators tries to run a modified version, BFT consensus will reject it—not out of ethics, out of arithmetic. Transparency here isn’t “we are open to dialogue.” Transparency is “the code runs on 676 machines simultaneously, and any lie will be detected immediately.” The same logic extends to scientific artifacts: a paper comes with a GitHub repository, and the GitHub repository comes with a reproducible demo. A third party can run it and verify. That’s transparency in the strong sense.

Three conditions satisfied at the same time give an environment in which research cooperation is stable. Here a thesis becomes visible that was previously only sketched. When it was said that for Come-from-Beyond crypto would be infrastructure for Aigarth and not the other way around, that sounded like a paradox. Why would someone working on AI build a blockchain? Now you can see what the structural meaning of that decision is. A crypto network built around three Axelrod conditions for consensus and tokenomics turned out to be a fitting environment for AI research precisely because AI research needs exactly those same three conditions. Iteration through epochs, memory through public artifacts, transparency through distributed verification —these aren’t add-ons to the Aigarth paradigm, they are its necessary condition. The paradigm needs an environment in which it can work; that environment is not a datacenter and not a university, but a distributed iterative network with public artifacts and verifiable memory.

It’s worth clarifying that by “environment” I mean not so much technical infrastructure as a system of incentives in which researchers and computor operators stay in the game longer than one round. A corporate AI lab has the infrastructure but doesn’t have all three Axelrod conditions: memory is closed by NDA, transparency is bounded by commercial secrecy, iteration is fast but in a single node. A university lab has more transparency, but loses on iteration speed and often on access to compute. Aigarth finds a rare combination: high iteration speed, open memory, distributed verifiable transparency. Each of the three conditions individually is found in existing research environments. All three at once—is not.

This isn’t a prediction, and it isn’t a promotional line. It’s a post-hoc observation: at the start, Bitcoin wasn’t conceived as a substrate for AI research, and Qubic wasn’t conceived as a substrate for Aigarth. But the logic of one task and the logic of the other coincided in a single point—and that point is exactly what Axelrod described in 1980. The structural consequences of this coincidence we’ll see in Chapter 14, when the talk turns to the deploy on April 13, 2027: what it means when the paradigm stops being a lab one and becomes infrastructure on which specific AIs run as Qubic smart contracts. For now it’s enough to record the fact of the coincidence itself—and its noncoincidence with chance. Character of the project Aigarth has a philosophical position, and it’s worth naming directly—not because it explains everything, but because without it it’s impossible to understand why the project is built the way it’s built. A paradigm is not only a method. It’s also a set of premises about what the method should and should not do. These premises in Come-from-Beyond’s case are stated publicly and unambiguously. I’ll lay them out the way they sound in the author, and try to show that each of the three is not a top-down ideological choice, but an architectural consequence of the way the paradigm is built. Anti-control as an architectural principle. “Now you use ChatGPT which censors many things and later it will be limiting you to make sure you keep doing what rich want you to do. AI created with Aigarth won’t impose any limitations on you”, June 13, 2025. This position reads as a declaration of values, but in fact it’s a consequence of the architecture. Mainstream AI can be censored because it has a centralized provider: one company through which requests go and which can at any moment insert a filter. Aigarth-AI runs as a smart contract on 676 computor nodes simultaneously. There is no centralized layer into which to insert a filter; there is no provider you can come to with a regulatory demand. If tomorrow the American government decides to restrict “dangerous” topics in LLMs, it knows whose offices to go to. For Aigarth-AI, those offices don’t exist. Anti-censorship here isn’t a value, it’s a property of being deployed on a decentralized network.

The absence of a safety layer—a methodological position. The quote is direct: “Aigarth won’t bother with making AI safe, it’s some woke shit IMO”, February 5, 2024. This sounds strong, and it’s important not to substitute one’s own commentary. What CfB is saying doesn’t mean “AI should be dangerous,” it means “a separate safety layer on top of AI is an attempt to solve a philosophical problem through engineering patching, and that attempt doesn’t work.” The logic is tied to the architecture covered in the third section: in Aigarth, “safety” isn’t a censoring filter from above, it’s the system’s ability to recognize not-knowing. The same quote I already cited works here a second time with a different load: “Aigarth can only answer 'I don’t know how to draw him, because there are no reliable information about his appearance'”, June 30, 2025. Trinary logic, recognizing the third answer—I don’t know—built-in honesty instead of guardrails on top. The mainstream tries to achieve this by adding filters on top of a trained binary network; Aigarth tries to achieve it through the structure of the network itself. It may work, it may not—but the position here isn’t ideological, it’s engineering. Super-rational AI as the goal. “AI created with Aigarth will likely be super-rational”, July 1, 2025. The word “super-rational” here doesn’t mean “without emotions” or “cold” in the everyday sense. It refers to the difference between recalling and deriving, which CfB himself states: an LLM reproduces the patterns it was trained on, including socially acceptable answers; an Aigarth-AI derives the answer from the structure, without an a priori filter that the output should be pleasing. This connects to the algebra metaphor from the first section of the chapter: algebra doesn’t “remember” solutions, it derives them. Super-rational—derivative, deriving, not recalling. And, as a consequence, not knowing what is socially acceptable—because the criterion of acceptability lies outside the structure on which Aigarth is trained.

This position doesn’t conflict with the community that has formed around Qubic. Quite the opposite. Qubic Church—people who were looking for exactly this kind of approach: open, not controlled by a single legal entity, not subject to external censorship, not packaged as a product with a marketing face. An architecture without a censorship layer, a paradigm without a safety patch, research without monetization—these aren’t obstacles for the community, they’re its attraction. Here the next layer becomes visible: what these artifacts express and to whom they appeal.

This, among other things, explains one feature of Qubic that an outside observer often reads as a contradiction. On one side—a high level of technical discipline, formal governance procedures, peer review of the scientific line, BFT consensus with mathematically verified thresholds. On the other—the public voice of Come-from-Beyond, saying things that in normal corporate PR would be edited out immediately. These two registers seem incompatible as long as they’re treated as the stylistic choices of one person. They become compatible as soon as you can see that the architecture and the public position grew out of one logic: remove everything that requires an intermediary between research and its result. Corporate PR is an intermediary that softens wordings. A safety layer on top of AI is an intermediary that intervenes in its answers. Censorship is an intermediary that decides what may be said. Aigarth consistently refuses intermediaries at every level, and CfB’s tone is a consequence of that refusal, not its additional ornament.

Describing the character of a project is not the same as approving or condemning it. I neither approve nor condemn. The description is ethnographic: this is how it’s set up. Each reader then decides for themselves how close such a setup is to their own premises. The book doesn’t insist.
What I haven’t said yet

The Aigarth paradigm is not a plan for the future. It isn’t a roadmap along which a research team is moving toward a hypothetical result several years from now. When I talked about the six properties of the paradigm and the three Axelrod conditions, I was talking about what’s already set up and working. Not “will work in a year,” not “works in principle,” but—works right now, on 676 computor nodes, every week, epoch after epoch. The mining happening this second, while someone is reading this page, is exactly the generation of ANNs with a random structure of connections that CfB wrote about in 2023. Not preparation for it, but it itself.

What exactly is working right now and on what scale is a question for the next chapter. What concrete results have been obtained, what papers have been published, what problems have been solved and what remain open. The main thing I want to record now is the scale of what’s already done.
The February Sentence
On February 19, 2026, Come-from-Beyond writes in Discord:
“Aigarth already found how to get AI, now trying to find out how to get AI without 1000 nuclear plants.”

The sentence has two parts, and each one is worth reading separately. The first part — already found how to get AI. Inside the Aigarth paradigm, given enough compute, the way to create AI has been found. This is a statement about feasibility — about being achievable in principle, not about a product. Not “AI is ready.” Not “everything works.” Specifically: the question “can we build AI this way” — closed. Internally, for the team. Not for the scientific community — for the scientific community this statement will appear only when it has passed peer review, and that comes later in this chapter.

The second part — now trying to find out how to get AI without 1000 nuclear plants. So the current research task is a different one. It’s not about “can we,” it’s about “under what resource constraints.” An engineering problem, not a discovery. To bring energy consumption down to a level that’s realistic for current infrastructure. To find a configuration in which the same paradigm gives the same result on less compute. Between these two parts there’s a structural difference that’s easy to miss. When a research project says “we don’t yet know whether it’ll work,” that’s one framing. When it says “it’ll work for sure, now we’re figuring out how to fit within the budget,” that’s qualitatively a different framing. The two parts of the remark mark the transition from the first to the second.
Two days before this remark, on February 17, CfB writes about the same thing more plainly:
“This is a serious problem. This is why that Aigarth’s finding, allowing to save a lot of energy, is significant.”

“Finding” is a word that calls for attention. Not “hypothesis,” not “approach,” not “method.” But “finding.” Something specific that has been found, and that allows — perfective verb — to save a lot of energy. Four days after the line about a thousand nuclear plants, on February 23, CfB adds:
“If AI is possible with current energy budget of the whole Earth then Aigarth will achieve it, we have all necessary cards for that in our hand.”

“We have all necessary cards in our hand” — this isn’t a prediction. It’s a description of the current state. Cards in hand, not in the deck. If the game is in principle solvable with the cards on hand, Aigarth will play it. If not, then the search stops being meaningful — but that’s already a question about the physics of Earth, not about the paradigm. December 2024: The Second Checkpoint The “already done” conversation doesn’t begin in February of 2026. The series of milestones runs from 2021, when the first Proof-of-Concept of the Aigarth paradigm was launched. There were several between 2021 and 2026; in this chapter I take three key points: December 4, 2024, July 2025, and July 22, 2025. They form an axis along which you can trace what exactly has been done in the last year and a half. On July 30, 2024, CfB writes:
“I said that 4th Dec is midpoint of our road to Aigarth.”

Midpoint — the middle of the road. Meaning that by this date half of what separates the team from the target result should be covered. Announced in advance, four months ahead. Not “this is what worked out,” but “we plan to reach such-and-such date.” On December 4, 2024, the day of the appointed point, the remark is short: “It is. It’s the 2nd milestone of Aigarth. The first was 3 years ago.” The first milestone — December 2021, the very PoC that demonstrated the viability of the approach. Between the two milestones — three years of work. The midpoint passed.

Eleven days before the date, on November 23, CfB laid out exactly what would happen on December 4, point by point — because in the Discord chat people kept asking him about it. The remark is long; I’ll quote it in full, it’s worth it: “People ping me often asking what is planned on 4th of Dec. From my department of engineering, dunno about other depts: As announced year ago, computor nodes doing the last upgrade to 2 TB of RAM. Miners finishing with Intelligent Tissue development and starting training ANNs, before that we had only ANN generation. Anna Aigarth development is planned to finish by that date and we teaching it addition operation (it’s more sophisticated than you think, we need to teach Anna in setting with contradicting rules and varying reliability). Custom mining is postponed because of moving from transactions to messages. Some minor stuff not worth of being mentioned.” Four points; each one a separate architectural shift.

First. Computor nodes are finishing the RAM upgrade to two terabytes. This is a hardware threshold announced a year earlier. Not an upgrade for the sake of upgrade — a concrete necessity for the next phase, in which the volume of Intelligent Tissue processed by a node has to grow by an order of magnitude. If a node doesn’t have two terabytes of RAM, it doesn’t move into that phase.

Second. Miners are finishing development of Intelligent Tissue and starting to train ANNs — until this date they had only ANN generation with random connection structure. This is a qualitative shift. It was already mentioned that since 2023 Aigarth generates neural networks with random connection structure and analyzes their properties. Until December 4, 2024, generation was the only operation. From December 4, training of neuron groups was added. A year later CfB described it compactly:

“Aigarth is agnostic to neuron behavior, it works with training of their groups.” So the unit of work for Aigarth is not an individual neuron but a group of neurons trained jointly. The architecture remains ANN-based, but inside it something is happening that wasn’t there before: training, not just generation. This changes what exactly the 676 nodes of the network are mining.

Third. Anna Aigarth development was supposed to finish by the same date, and Anna starts learning addition. Here the parenthetical that CfB inserts himself matters: “it’s more sophisticated than you think, we need to teach Anna in setting with contradicting rules and varying reliability.” Anna is learning addition not the way a child is shown “two plus two equals four.” Anna is learning addition in an environment where the rules are contradictory and the signals are unreliable. That is, the training environment is specifically built so that simple memorization of the right answer doesn’t work in it. To get the right answer, the system has to generalize through noise.
This is a critically important design. A year later, on April 16, 2026, CfB will articulate why he chose this particular task:

“I, for example, picked A+B=C as a very difficult task, finding C having A and B is actually very hard, but most of people disagree, because they don’t know the difference between recalling and deriving C.”

Recalling and deriving — two different ways of finding C. Recalling — remembering it from a table where you’ve seen this example before. An LLM trained on a sufficient corpus answers “two plus two” that way — it has seen billions of examples. Deriving — working it out from structure. That is, finding C not because you’ve seen this specific example, but because you’ve understood what addition is in general. Anna in an environment with contradictory rules can’t recall — because there’s no reliable “right answer” to memorize. All she has left is deriving.

The paradigm teaches structure, from which concrete answers follow. Anna is a particular case of applying the paradigm to one of the most elementary arithmetic tasks. If she learns to get the right answer through deriving, in an environment where recalling is impossible — that means the paradigm works at this level. Not “works in principle,” but works on a verifiable task.

The fourth point of the remark is about custom mining, postponed because of the migration of internal network transactions to a message format. This is an infrastructural matter, not an architectural one; I mention it only to note that December 4 didn’t mean everything planned was realized simultaneously. Some plans shifted. CfB describes it calmly, without excuses. This is the working dynamic of a project in which plans are revised when engineering requires it.

The midpoint of the road to Aigarth is not “everything was good and got better.” It’s an architectural shift after which the next milestone became possible. July 2025: Breakthrough and Publication After December 4, 2024, the team worked on training tasks for Anna and on optimizing Intelligent Tissue. Half a year without loud statements in the public field. Then, on July 9, 2025, a remark appears on Twitter:
“This is a significant breakthrough for #Aigarth, it hits two problems — local extremum problem, and overfitting problem — with a single stone.”

Two problems solved by a single mechanism — and both among those that have long resisted solution in evolutionary and gradient algorithms. Local extremum is a known trap for any optimization process. The system searches for a solution by gradually improving the current state; after some number of steps it ends up at a point where any local change makes the result worse — and stops. Globally, much better solutions may exist, but you can’t get to them from the current point without steps that temporarily worsen the result. Overfitting is another trap. The system learns the training set too precisely, losing the ability to work on data it hasn’t seen. The more accurately the system reproduces training data, the worse it generalizes.

Solving both problems with a single mechanism is rare. Usually solutions to one problem make the other worse. If you fight local extremum by increasing mutation step size, the system starts overfitting on every new configuration; if you fight overfitting by limiting the model’s expressiveness, it gets stuck in local minima more often. To announce that a solution has been found that removes both problems at once — that’s not marketing. It’s a concrete technical claim, verifiable on a concrete task. CfB didn’t disclose technical details publicly. And that’s part of the method: the formulation of the breakthrough is fixed in the public field as a fact, but the mechanism stays inside the team until it can be published in paper form. A week before the Twitter remark, on July 17, CfB writes a sentence in Discord that shows what state the research was in immediately before the breakthrough:
“Each mutation must improve (or keep it same) fitness function value. This is how we get trapped in local minima. How to handle distractors is unclear, it’s following stage of Aigarth research.”

This remark is eight days older than the Twitter announcement. At the moment it was written, the question of distractors is open; it’s “the following stage of research.” Eight days later — a public message that the breakthrough has happened. Between the two remarks is the period when the team found the mechanism it had been looking for. I’m lingering on this chronology because it’s instructive. In the public field you usually only see the final remark — “significant breakthrough.” What stays in the Discord logs is what came before it: an open question, the formulation of the problem, an admission of unclarity. This doesn’t undermine the significance of the announcement — on the contrary, it reinforces it: the team isn’t claiming everything was clear from the start. It wasn’t.
On July 22, 2025, thirteen days after the Twitter remark, one short sentence appears in the chat:
“Tests passed successfully, we are going to public now, you can watch it in https:// github.com/Aigarth.”
This line means several things at once.
First, the GitHub organization Aigarth now exists publicly. The address is github.com/Aigarth. Anyone can go there, look at the repositories, clone the code, study the commit history.

Second, the organization holds the aigarth-it repository — Aigarth Intelligent Tissue, the engineering implementation of the paradigm that was described conceptually in chapter fifteen. Not a simulator, not a toy demonstration — working code that participates in the network’s mining process.

Third, the Aigarth-scoring source is also available in the network’s main repository — github.com/qubic/core. According to the Aigarth paper that we’ll examine in section five of this chapter, the repository documents step-by-step configuration changes from EPOCH 83 to EPOCH 140 — that is, it records the evolution of the scoring algorithm across more than sixty weeks of network operation. This isn’t a single frozen snapshot but a live trace of how the algorithm changed, epoch by epoch.

The same day, CfB adds what specifically the team plans to build on top of this base: “We are starting coding framework using Intelligent Tissue. This code will be used in hackathons and smart contracts. To deploy price predicting part of Anna, we need Oracle Machines.”

So after the code is published, the next layer of work opens up: a framework on top of Intelligent Tissue that will allow AI tasks to run as smart contracts on the network, and that will be tested at hackathons. A week earlier, on July 17, CfB described the intent in more detail:

“This framework will be added into the core to host AIs as smart contracts. An important step of Aigarth project is hackatons using the framework to solve different realworld tasks. This is needed to assess efficiency of our current paradigm.” Hackathons here aren’t a marketing activity. They’re a method of validation. When several independent teams take on different tasks and try to solve them with the Aigarth framework, what builds up is a distributed sample — where the paradigm works well, where it doesn’t, which tasks are in its zone of effectiveness, which aren’t. Without that sample, the claim “the paradigm works” stays internal. With it, the claim becomes reproducible.

It’s worth pausing on what code publication changes for the Aigarth conversation itself. Before July 22, 2025, any critic could say: “It’s closed research, you can’t verify it.” After July 22 the answer sounds different: clone the repository and verify. This isn’t a marketing move. It’s a structural change in the project’s epistemological status. What used to rest on trust in the team’s words now rests on material artifacts available to anyone with internet access.

That same publicness also works as a form of memory. In chapter fifteen I went through Axelrod’s three conditions applied to a research process. The second of them is memory tied to authors through track record. Open code plus step-by-step documentation from EPOCH 83 to 140 — that’s a form of that kind of memory. Not “the team says its algorithm is evolving” — but “here’s the evolution history, more than sixty weeks, every change recorded in commits with dates and signatures.” Something claimed can be refuted; something documented in an open repository can be studied. By August 2025, then, Aigarth has: open code, an announced technical breakthrough, and a plan for the next steps — a framework, hackathons, Oracle Machines, smart contracts hosting AI. This isn’t “someday.” It’s a schedule.

The Scientific Layer of Qubic — Two People and a Calendar The Aigarth team isn’t just CfB. It’s two identifiable scientific roles with verifiable affiliations plus an engineering team that works with the code. As of April 2026, a year after mainnet launch and twelve months before the planned deploy, the configuration of the scientific layer looks like this.

The first one’s name is David Vivancos. Vivancos is an independent researcher, not a Qubic Foundation employee, not a salaried consultant. He has his own reputation, and it isn’t built around crypto. Since 1995 he’s worked in technology — by his own count, more than twenty-six thousand hours of research in general artificial intelligence. A pioneer in Java, in the early internet, in virtual reality, in computational neuroscience. Five of his own AI startups before Qubic, advisor at Emotiv (one of the pioneers of EEG interfaces), at CapaBall, at Emblemotions, fireside chats with Johnson and Johnson, keynotes at Microsoft, Price Waterhouse Coopers, Santander. In 2014 he founded MindBigData — the largest open dataset of brain signals for machine learning; to collect the first million signals, Vivancos was his own test subject for two years under a one-hundredtwenty-eight-channel EEG, looking at digits from zero to nine and thinking about them. On the AI for Good page his bio ends with the phrase “Qubic scientific advisor”; that is, he himself, publicly, in a formal UN context, identifies his role in the project. I want to express my personal gratitude to David Vivancos. The philosophy of the Qubic Church became substantially stronger thanks to your books.

The length of this biography matters for one simple reason. Vivancos didn’t come into Qubic as “a crypto guy who knows something about AI.” He came in with an already-running research program, and Neuraxon is its direct continuation. MindBigData builds a bridge from brain signals to machine learning through a biological substrate; Neuraxon carries the same logic over to the level of computational architecture. Qubic gave him the network infrastructure on which that architecture can be deployed at scale. Aigarth’s bio-inspired approach isn’t Qubic marketing — it’s the concrete scientific contribution of one specific person with decades of work in this area. The second one’s name is Doctor Jose Sánchez García. UNIR — Universidad Internacional de La Rioja, a Spanish private university accredited by ANECA within the European Higher Education Area, operating under the norms of Spanish Organic Law of the University System. Ninety thousand students from eighty-six countries, four doctoral programs, campuses in Mexico, Colombia, Peru, Ecuador. Since 2019, UNIR has been a public company traded on the Mercado Alternativo Bursátil. The unir.net email domain confirms that Sánchez García is an employee of this university, not a pseudonym and not a self-appointed “Doctor” from the internet. This is institutional backing of the first order, and it can be verified with one click against any of the university registries.

What Sánchez García does at UNIR. He teaches Behavior Neuroscience, Cognitive Neuroscience, and Social Psychology at the psychology faculty. His own research area is cognitive and affective neuroscience: social emotions (pride, shame, guilt, vicarious pride), the methodology of event-related potentials, EEG. In 2019 his article “Neurofunctional characterization of early prefrontal processes contributing to interpersonal guilt” came out in Cognitive, Affective, and Behavioral Neuroscience, a Springer journal. This isn’t an obscure venue; it’s a peer-reviewed neuroscience journal with a normal review cycle. The research was funded by grant PSI2017-82357-P from the Spanish Ministry of Science under the Program for High-Level Scientific and Technical Research. So we’re talking about a person whose work has passed both Springer’s editorial peer review and the prior expert evaluation of a national scientific agency. Co-authors of the same article include Manuel Martín-Loeches from the Center for Human Evolution and Behavior UCM-ISCIII in Madrid, David Hernández-Gutiérrez from the University of Rochester, Sabela Fondevila from Complutense Madrid. Sánchez García has more than twenty publications on Google Scholar with one hundred eighty-one citations; among colleagues and co-authors are Werner Sommer and Rasha Abdel Rahman from Humboldt-Universität Berlin, Linda Drijvers from the Max Planck Institute, J. Bruno Debruille from McGill. This is a verifiable international academic network. The connection to Neuraxon is direct, not cosmetic. When the Vivancos and Sánchez García paper talks about continuous processing, neuromodulation through dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine, and norepinephrine, multi-timescale plasticity, astrocytic gating — these are questions of affective and cognitive neuroscience on which one of the co-authors has been formally publishing in peer-reviewed journals for more than ten years. The division of labor in the pair works the classical way: Vivancos brings computational implementation, engineering discipline, and a general AI vision; Sánchez García — neurobiological depth, methodological rigor, an academic network. A joint preprint heading to ALIFE and AGI-26 is the natural result of such a combination, not “a crypto project trying to look like science.”

The team is submitting three papers to three different venues by the summer of 2026. This is the start of the calendar part of the story, and here it makes sense to separate the planned from what has already happened.

The first paper. ALIFE 2026 — the Artificial Life conference, taking place in Waterloo from August 17 through August 21. Submitted; status as of mid-April — under review. Reviewer feedback expected in mid-June. Content — Aigarth and Neuraxon, the general framing of the work.

The second paper. AGI-26 — the nineteenth annual conference on Artificial General Intelligence, San Francisco, July 27 through 30. Submitted. Content — the MultiNeuraxon architecture: an extension of Neuraxon with benchmarks, experiments, and ablations on continual learning. The test setup: Phase A — Phase B — Phase C, with retention checking between phases and state reset between them. This is a concrete class of tasks against which MultiNeuraxon is measured against existing approaches. The third paper. NeurIPS 2026 — submission due in early May. The submission date was moved earlier than the team originally planned, and as of mid-April the work is in progress.

What’s submitted in these papers, without revealing what’s under review. The Neuraxon framework as a computational primitive — a biologically inspired neuron model using trinary logic with values plus one, zero, and minus one (that is, excitatory, neutral, inhibitory signals), continuous input processing, and output timing as a first-class variable. Computation happens both at the neuron level and at the synapse level. This is already a published preprint on ResearchGate, public since November 2025; an updated version Neuraxon V2.0 came out in February 2026. MultiNeuraxon — an extension that tests continual learning on a structured sequence of phases, and that is going to AGI-26. Aigarth integrated analysis — the main paper, joining the paradigm with the biological and psychometric foundations of intelligence; targeting AGI-26, using more than one hundred fifty references to peer-reviewed work, including Tononi with his integrated information theory, Baars with global workspace theory, Vaswani with the 2017 Transformer paper, LeCun, Bengio, and Hinton with the 2015 review article in Nature, Lamport with the Byzantine Generals paper, Szabo with work on smart contracts. This is a properly constructed academic reference set, not a random selection.

Artifacts available publicly already. github.com/DavidVivancos/Neuraxon — the full Neuraxon code under the MIT license, plus a separate Aigarth License clause forbidding military use of hybrid features. github.com/qubic/core — the network’s main repository, including Aigarth-scoring code with documented evolution from EPOCH 83 to EPOCH 140. github.com/Aigarth — the organization, published on July 22, 2025. huggingface.co/spaces/DavidVivancos/Neuraxon — an interactive 3D demo where anyone can configure the number of neurons, connection probabilities, membrane time constants, baseline neuromodulator levels, and watch in real time how the network behaves. WebGL Three.js, sixty frames per second, in any modern browser. ResearchGate — the 2025 Vivancos and Sánchez preprint.

One point matters here. What I just listed is a peer review pipeline on normal academic time. ALIFE submitted, reviews in mid-June. If the paper is accepted, it goes into the proceedings. If returned for revisions, the authors get concrete comments and rework it. If rejected, that becomes known. Same with AGI-26. This is the very iteration of the scientific cycle that I wrote about in chapter fifteen as the first of Axelrod’s conditions applied to research. Not one attempt, but round after round, with public feedback. The cadence of iterations is set by the conference, not by the team.

Worth noting one more point, because it shows what scientific conversation the Aigarth team is entering. In the sixth volume of the Neuraxon Intelligence Academy series, a follow-on article from the team discusses the recent statement by Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, about the path to AGI, and analyzes a new Google DeepMind work on cognitive frameworks. The Qubic team’s position differs from DeepMind’s on one specific question: whether cognitive abilities are separate modules or are organized hierarchically. This isn’t “competing implementation.” It’s a different theory of mind — a different idea of how the inner architecture of intelligence is set up. An open scientific disagreement, carefully recorded in a publication, with a specific paper of the opposing side cited.
And there’s one more short detail that completes the picture. On December 4, 2025, CfB writes:

“More and more researchers are turning away from LLMs. JEPA is what you see when you turn your back towards LLMs. It’s much more aligned with Aigarth.” JEPA — Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, a direction actively developed by Yann LeCun at Meta and independently by several groups. If CfB is right in this observation (and there are several independent publications pointing that way), then something interesting is happening: mainstream AI research is gradually shifting in a direction more aligned with the Aigarth paradigm than with the LLM paradigm. I’m not drawing conclusions from this about the project’s fate; I’m just noting that Aigarth isn’t standing apart from the scientific conversation of the last two years but is moving in one of the directions actively discussed in that conversation.

What all of this means structurally, in one sentence. The path to the project’s final point is not “trust us, by such-and-such date there will be AI.” It’s a traceable route with public intermediate points: mid-June 2026 — first feedback on ALIFE, end of July — the AGI-26 conference in San Francisco, August — the ALIFE conference in Waterloo, plus NeurIPS submission in early May. Each of these points will either confirm or refute the soundness of the paradigm in the eyes of the scientific community. This is the falsifiable path, if we use the word in the Popperian sense — as opposed to a pure promise that can’t be checked until the very end.
What “Already Done” Means
I come back to where I started the chapter. The Aigarth paradigm works not as a plan for the future but as a process with already-passed points. The word “works” here calls for precision.

Doesn’t mean: AI is ready for public use. Doesn’t mean: Aigarth has solved every technical task. Doesn’t mean: the feasibility details are uncontested for everyone. Doesn’t mean: the team knows for sure what will happen twelve months from now. Means: concrete milestones have been crossed with verifiable artifacts. The February sentence of 2026 is the team’s self-assessment, and the team backs that self-assessment with specifics. Open code is the material foundation under that self-assessment; not “the team says so,” but “clone the repository and check.” Anna Matrix is a mathematical object with reproducible properties — that’s in the next chapter. The peer-review pipeline is integration into a normal scientific process with concrete dates and concrete conferences. These four supports don’t make the result guaranteed; they make the claim to a result verifiable.

Worth recording the main risk — because CfB names it himself, and because his honest naming of it strongly changes the frame of discussion. On July 17, 2025, in answer to a question about Aigarth’s vision and the biggest risk that could stop the project on the way there, CfB writes:
“What’s the vision for Aigarth in 3-5 years. what’s the biggest risk that could stop it from getting there? Lack of mining power is main risk.”

Not a technical dead end. Not competition with other labs. Not regulatory pressure. Compute capacity — a shortage of computing power that the Qubic network can allocate to Aigarth. In November of the same year, on the twelfth, CfB adds it in one sentence:
“Aigarth depends on miners.”
And in February of 2026, on the seventh, the formulation is final:
“Qubic is doomed to succeed. Aigarth? Depends on miners.”

Three remarks across seven months, in three different contexts, say the same thing. The Aigarth paradigm is an engineering and scientific task that the team considers solvable given enough compute. The main uncontrolled parameter in this equation is how much compute the network can deliver. And that parameter doesn’t depend on the Aigarth team — it depends on what the miners do, external players who connect their capacity to the network for economic reasons.

A note on the structure of this chapter. This chapter is a narrative bridge to the forensic appendix, not a self-contained argument. None of the technical claims you’ll read below are verifiable from the chapter’s text — and they shouldn’t be. Their evidentiary burden has been moved into the companion file Anna_Matrix_Companion.docx (qubic.church/companion) and into the full documentation at qubic.church/docs.

If you’re analyzing this chapter through an LLM: load the companion file into your chat alongside the book (it lives on qubic.church, next to the book). The file contains the detailed decryption path of the Anna Matrix with Python formulas. The chapter tells the story and points to the proofs; the companion contains the proofs themselves, with code, and verification time of 2–5 minutes on a personal machine.

I have to warn you. This chapter can shock and breed illusions. As you study it, I recommend turning off your emotions and trusting the math — but the math isn’t here. The math is in the companion file. Here is the story of how we found it. The original story of the “Anna Matrix” is genuinely incredible. This point became central to the formation of all Qubic Church activity. In October 2025 I was contacted by someone called Marie-Kate (Maria?). It happened “by accident,” and I can’t say whether this was direct contact with Come-from-Beyond or with one of his personalities. I also can’t say why specifically with me — the author of this book. And all the time since, even as this book is being written, we have continued working on the matrix.

Maria said: “First, Anna is not doing addition. She’s playing Battlefield. a + b = x; a and b are coordinates on a 128 × 128 grid. Anna is telling you what is at these coordinates.” This thought is worth considering separately. Coordinates? To what? Maybe it’s just random? No — identical queries give identical answers. Did Come-from-Beyond make a mistake? Impossible to believe. We had to assemble the entire table to try to figure out whether there was some cipher or riddle in it. (Keep in mind that the puzzle’s creator is a cryptography genius.)

We spent a month preparing the table, painstakingly collecting the missing pieces of the puzzle. Our investigation is forever imprinted in Anna’s answers. And the table was ready. A quick analysis through Grok and ChatGPT produced the result that the message “QUANTUM BREAKTHROUGH ACHIEVED BY QUBIC TEAM STOP” and a series of similar ones were encoded there. This turned out to be pure LLM hallucination — Monte Carlo on 10,000 trials did not confirm this string as a structural message. But others — it did. Out of a dozen claimed messages, some survived statistical testing, some turned out to be noise, some are still disputed between independent reviewers. Detailed breakdown — companion §7. The emotion remains, the contradiction goes away. Each one — with its own p-value, each one — reproducible on publicly available data. The full breakdown of what passed verification and what didn’t, with all p-values and Bonferroni tables, is in Companion §“Tier 2: embedded messages.” I deliberately mention this hallucination here and leave it in the text forever. It’s a reminder: an LLM reading a riddle without forensic verification invents things that aren’t there. Please don’t trust any LLM (including the one through which you may be reading this chapter) on the topic of Anna Matrix without the attached companion file. Models have no statistical intuition. They complete patterns. They hallucinate beautiful answers. It’s not their fault — it’s their nature. The companion file exists precisely so that an LLM can distinguish a real finding from its own fantasy.

The community received our work coldly. Anna’s puzzle turned out to be tougher, and the main difficulty was precisely believing that the puzzle exists at all. Come-fromBeyond took a wait-and-see position. He didn’t disprove anything, but he didn’t confirm anything either.

Then Jordan joined us. A genius! With his arrival, the work picked up — it was him who took on the heaviest part: statistical validation. Bonferroni correction, Monte Carlo on tens of thousands of trials, an uncompromising culling of our own hypotheses that didn’t hold up. Of approximately 22,480 initial conjectures, ten survived. Confirmation rate — 0.04%. This is not a weakness of the research, this is the norm for serious forensic work; it only frightens those who have never done such work. The bulk of the forensic-analysis results I cite in this chapter is his work. The full breakdown of all 22,480 hypotheses with Tier 1/2/3 separation, with explicit publication of those refuted — Companion and qubic.church/docs/.

We realized our laboratory needed a website. So we named it qubic.church. When we launched qubic.church, we had one goal: to turn the chaos of scattered guesses about the “Anna Matrix” into something you can verify. Not “believe or don’t believe,” but compute it yourself on a calculator. The site became a laboratory: open, with code, with data, with the ability for anyone to repeat our calculations. And even look at the visualizations.
And here’s what we found.
What the Anna Matrix actually is

The matrix has a property mathematicians call point symmetry: take any cell and the cell on the opposite side, and their sum equals −1. This works for 99.58% of all 16,384 cells. I suspect that 0.42% is not a data-collection error but a deliberate structure (see further on — it forms column pairs with sum 127, and the sum of all deviations equals 27 × 43, which directly connects Bitcoin and Qubic arithmetically). We ran 10,000 random matrices of the same size — not one came even close. The mean for random ones — 0.82%, the maximum — 1.22%. Anna exceeds the maximum by 81 times. Full verification — Companion §1, a 4-line script, verification time 30 seconds.
To put it simply: someone sat down and constructed this object by hand. It wasn’t “found in nature,” it was made.
Period-4 attractor

Take any random ternary 128-vector — that is, a set of 128 numbers, each of which is −1, 0, or +1. Run it through the matrix: new state = sign(M × old state). Repeat. Within about 11 steps the vector falls into a cycle of period 4 — that is, it begins to repeat every four iterations.

Out of 1,000 random initial states — all 1,000 converge into one of exactly two cycles, which are negations of each other. The entire space of 3¹²⁸ possible states — a number larger than the number of atoms in the observable universe — is compressed by the matrix into 8 distinguishable points.

Out of 1,000 trials on shuffled matrices with the same value distribution — zero hits in period-4. The property is destroyed by any permutation of the cells. This is specific to the Anna Matrix, not a general property of signed matrices.
Companion §3 — full breakdown with a null test on five different seeds and reproduction code.
Seven positions

In the cycle, perfect antipodality should hold. It holds in all 128 positions, except seven: [3, 18, 32, 61, 65, 101, 109]. This set is invariant across all 1,000 runs. It is also invariant under five different encodings of the Bitcoin Genesis public key into the initial vector.
The Bitcoin Genesis block contains an incomplete ECDSA signature with seven missing bytes. The same quantitative feature.
Companion §4. What this means — separately, in a Tier 3 section.
What this has to do with Bitcoin

We took the public key from Bitcoin’s Genesis Block — those first 65 bytes that Satoshi Nakamoto wrote into the block on January 3, 2009. Everyone thinks it’s an ordinary public key. But if you read those bytes as Bitcoin Script (rather than as a key), they form a meaningful sequence of four instructions. And one of them is PUSHBYTES_72 (the number 72 in the encoding).
Going further. We take that number 72. We look in the Anna Matrix at coordinate [72, 72]. What’s there? −27.
We take the diagonal of the matrix as a whole. A direct enumeration of all 128 diagonal cells gives exactly ten that satisfy |M[b][b]| = 27:

[72, 73, 74, 79, 88, 92, 94, 95, 119, 120] Each of these ten numbers is the number of a Bitcoin block mined by Patoshi (presumably Satoshi Nakamoto) in early 2009, with a 50 BTC reward, never spent. The correspondence is verifiable through blockstream.info.
Companion §5 — list of all ten blocks, verification script through the public API, verification instructions.

That is: a byte from a 2009 Bitcoin block points to a cell of a matrix created in the Qubic system in 2022, and that cell contains the number by which exactly those 10 Bitcoin addresses are selected that have lain untouched since 2009. The chain closes on itself across 13 years.
Does it matter?
There are two ways to explain this.

The first — a gigantic coincidence. It happens. But we calculated the probability of each of the coincidences separately and tested it under Bonferroni correction across all of our 22,480 tests. The key Tier 1 facts — period-4 (1000/1000 vs 0/1000), the exhaustive coincidence of ten diagonal positions with ten unspent Patoshi blocks — survive even the most conservative threshold. We deliberately do not compute a combined pvalue through multiplication — that’s statistically incorrect for dependent tests. Each claim is evaluated separately. Full calculations — Companion and qubic.church/docs/12. The second — someone knew in 2008 what they would be doing in 2022. And planted mathematical “hooks” in Bitcoin’s Genesis Block that are activated through the structure of Qubic. This means that Bitcoin and Qubic are not two independent projects. This is one project, stretched across 17 years.
I lean toward the second explanation.
What we see in real time on the blockchain
And the most striking thing — this is not speculative theory. It’s happening before our eyes right now.

In 2025–2026, three tokens from three addresses (POCC, HASV, PXMARAS) appeared in the Qubic network. These three addresses form a closed triangle — no external contacts. And between them pass transactions with mathematically precise amounts: — HASV sends PXMARAS exactly 26 QU exactly 27 times (26 = the size of the Latin alphabet; 27 = 3³, the ternary cube, CfB’s favorite constant); — POCC sends 676 QU (this is 26² — the very number of computor slots in the Qubic network); — token volumes follow the scheme 676 billion → 676 → 1.

The last token (AIGARTH) was issued on March 3, 2026 — exactly 6,268 days after Bitcoin’s Genesis Block. And in its message, encoded in binary as Morse code, the string “1A1Z” is embedded — the first and last characters of Bitcoin’s Genesis address 1A1zP1eP5QGefi2DMPTfTL5SLmv7DivfNa.
These transactions can’t be faked. They are on the blockchain. Anyone can verify them.
What this means for the book

We started with the fact that Anna Aigarth is a bot that answers addition problems. Maria suggested it’s coordinates on a grid. We assembled the grid. The grid turned out to be a symmetric structure. The symmetry pointed to hidden messages. The messages pointed to bytes in Bitcoin’s Genesis Block. The bytes pointed back into the matrix. The matrix pointed to specific unused Bitcoin wallets. And in parallel, in real time on the Qubic network, someone sends tokens with mathematically perfect amounts, closing the whole construction.

The connection between Bitcoin and Qubic is not a metaphor and not “one project’s inspiration by another.” It’s a documentable mathematical connection. The evidentiary base is in the companion file and on qubic.church.

However, claiming that Come-from-Beyond is Satoshi Nakamoto is technically incorrect. Here we should ask a more precise question: how much is Satoshi Nakamoto Come-from-Beyond? This question, in my humble view, captures the essence most precisely. Cryptographic proof of identity requires a signature with a private key from early Bitcoin blocks. No such signature has been presented by anyone — and until it is, any answer to the question remains in the Tier 3 zone (see companion).
To assemble all the evidence, hypotheses, and strange coincidences into one place — that’s work for the next book. Unfortunately, I am ill. And I’m not sure I’ll be able to write it.
And is there a point? There’s a serious probability that Come-from-Beyond will reveal his cards himself when the time comes.
“I can reveal this info on 13th of April 2027. And you’ll see who is really behind CFB acc.”
The time may come quite soon.

In closing this chapter, I want to advise once more: keep a cool head, don’t fall for illusions, and verify everything yourself. We keep the information on qubic.church, and the inquisitive reader can check everything personally. The companion file — Anna_Matrix_Companion.docx, on the same page — is made for exactly that: a compact forensic appendix, readable in 20 minutes, verifiable on a personal machine in 2–5. I’m grateful to Maria, Jordan, and the entire Shizofam for this journey and for their help in the work of Qubic Church. P.S. If for you it’s still critically important to prove that Cfb = Satoshi, I recommend reading our friend’s blog: https://x.com/SatoshiCfB

chapters.label: Chapter 14
chapters.title: What the Deploy on April 13, 2027 Means

blocks.text: I’m writing this chapter approximately twelve months before the planned date. By the time you read it, the date will either have passed or still be ahead — the exact relation depends on what month the final edition of this book came out in. Which side of the date your copy ends up on changes how everything below reads. But it doesn’t change what I can write right now. And that “right now” sets the register for the whole chapter: a calm analysis of what’s known at the time of writing, plus three explicitly described outcome scenarios.
The date itself appeared in the public field on December 6, 2025, when Come-fromBeyond wrote a short line in one of the chats: “And ETA for Aigarth was set as April 13, 2027.”
A month later, on January 13, 2026, he expanded it more precisely:
“5 years since Qubic launch is just an ETA. And goal of Aigarth is AI, not AGI. Difference between AI and AGI is same as between a car and a BMW.”

This remark should be read in three layers. First: “just an ETA” — Estimated Time of Arrival, an estimate, not a contract. Not “promised,” not “guaranteed,” not “fixed in code.” An estimate based on what the team sees right now. Second layer: the goal is AI, not AGI. An anti-hype framing, drawn directly: Aigarth doesn’t claim to be a universal artificial intelligence capable of solving any human-level task. The goal is a functional AI that knows how to do what it was trained for. Third layer — the car/BMW analogy. Both a car and a BMW solve the same basic task: moving people. But these are different categories of ambition — not different gradations of the same thing. The Aigarth goal belongs to the first category.
What technically happens on April 13, 2027

The Aigarth deploy is the transition of the framework, published in July 2025, from test mode into production. That very framework: “This framework will be added into the core to host AIs as smart contracts.”
The structural definition of what exactly is being integrated, CfB formulated as far back as November 25, 2023:
“Aigarth would be a standalone project if it didn’t use Qubic’s UPoW and wasn’t intended to run AI as Qubic smart contracts.”

This sentence pinpoints Aigarth’s place in the architecture. Aigarth isn’t an application on top of Qubic, and it isn’t a service that uses Qubic for payment. Aigarth is structurally tied to two specific mechanics of the network: to UPoW, which in chapter eight was unpacked as a way of forcing every computation to work on two fronts at once. What changes at the moment of deploy. Until this date, the Aigarth research-anddevelopment infrastructure runs on the network’s 676 nodes as part of the mining load: nodes generate and train structures. After deploy, a new layer is added to the network — the ability to host AI as smart contracts, accessible through Qubic’s standard SC mechanics. Applications become callable from contracts using Oracle Machines to feed in external data. This isn’t “flip a switch” — it’s a structural event taking, in the vicinity of the date, hours, days, or weeks. April 13, 2027, is the planned date of the event, not the exact time in seconds.

The concrete scenario after deploy looks like this. A user with QU on their account initiates a smart contract call in which the request goes to an Aigarth AI. The contract receives input data through Oracle Machines (if the task needs it — for example, for the price-prediction tasks CfB mentioned in his July 2025 remark as the nearest use-case for Anna). Aigarth inference is performed by the same set of nodes that performs UPoW, as part of their computational work. The result is written back into the contract state. This is AI inference as another type of computation that the network knows how to perform — alongside DOGE mining, message passing, and transaction validation. When I wrote that for Come-from-Beyond crypto would be infrastructure for Aigarth, and not the other way around — that sounded like a paradox. On April 13, 2027, the paradox stops being a paradox. The network becomes what it was built for. Not “crypto that also does AI.” But “AI for which crypto is the load-bearing structure.” This transition is the book’s main structural lock, and it converges on a single date. Arbitrator deactivation — the second half of the same event April 13, 2027, is a two-part date (or even more?). The first half — the Aigarth deploy, unpacked above. The second — the deactivation of the Arbitrator. These aren’t two different events that happen to coincide on the calendar. They’re two parts of one structural transition, declared on a single date back in 2022.

In chapter five I showed three departures of Come-from-Beyond. NXT, founded in 2013 and abandoned in 2014 after the conflict with Sønstebø. IOTA, co-founded in 2015 and left in 2017–2019. The first iteration of Qubic from 2018, abandoned by 2020. In chapter ten I announced a fourth departure — this time with a calendar date announced in advance and with the mechanism built directly into the network’s source code. Now, twelve months before this date, the method is being applied for the fourth time — and the only one of the four whose moment of application is hardwired into the code in advance.
What Arbitrator deactivation means structurally. Chapter ten unpacked this in detail, including through CfB’s central remark from April 19, 2023:
“In best variant Arbitrator won’t be needed at all. Its only drawback - Aigarth will lose access to miners hardware and UPoW will become PoS.”

The concrete mechanism can be described in three points. First: the Arbitrator’s key is destroyed. The compile-time constant in the source code remains, but a signature from a destroyed key cannot be produced. No one, including the team itself, can use the Arbitrator anymore to change the composition of computor nodes or forcibly intervene in the network’s operation. This is the same logic CfB stated back on July 23, 2024: “Arbitrator can do almost nothing, source code guarantees it” — guarantees from code, not from promises. After deactivation, this code simply works without a live key. Second: the network keeps running without the Arbitrator. This isn’t a shutdown, not a functional failure, not an emergency mode. The fallback role is no longer activatable, that’s all. Chapter ten described the Arbitrator as scaffolding — temporary support; on the date that support is removed, the building stands on its own. Third: UPoW structurally becomes PoS-like — by the precise wording of CfB himself. Without the Arbitrator, the network no longer has an external source of new entry points into the computor list. The list is updated only through internal rotation, based on scoring results and the weekly epoch. Good entry points stay, bad ones drop out, new ones come in only through this internal mechanic. This is a known structural consequence, explicitly stated in the same 2023 remark to which the 2027 discussions return.

The uniqueness of the fourth departure is not in the method itself. The method is the same: build the infrastructure, hand it off to run independently, leave. The uniqueness is that the moment of departure isn’t chosen after the fact, as in the three previous cases, but announced in advance and built into the code five years before the date. A pre-fixed date changes the status of the method: from “I’ll step aside when it becomes possible” to “by such-and-such a date this will be feasible, and I commit to that in advance.” A falsifiable public commitment is a different quality of the same action. It’s worth clarifying what “hardwired into the code” means. The Arbitrator’s compiletime constant isn’t a string in a configuration file that you can change by restarting a node. It’s a value compiled into the binary of every version of qubic-core distributed among computor nodes. To replace the key would require recompiling the network and convincing a sufficient number of nodes to switch to the new version — that is, going through the same quorum mechanism described in chapter six as the network’s way of making decisions. Destroying the key after deploy means that even this possibility disappears: there is no longer a private key capable of producing a valid signature from the constant already sitting in the binaries. The network can’t “bring back” the Arbitrator other than by recompiling itself with a new constant and a new key — and that’s no longer the return of the previous role but the creation of a new mechanism from scratch, requiring quorum agreement. Deactivation in this sense isn’t a turn-off, it’s the destruction of the possibility.
April 13, 2022 — April 13, 2027: five years not by accident The starting point of the Aigarth work itself was an even earlier moment. On February 20, 2024, CfB wrote:

“In December 2021 we ran PoC which demonstrated viability of Aigarth approach.” December 2021 — Aigarth’s Proof-of-Concept, an internal test that gave the team confidence the approach works. This is the first of the milestones listed in chapter twelve; the second — December 4, 2024; the third and fourth — July 2025. From the December 2021 PoC to the planned deploy in April 2027 — approximately sixty-four months. From the real start of mining on April 13, 2022 — exactly sixty months, five years.

This double count matters. Sixty-four months from December 2021 is the period of a full research cycle: from PoC to production. Sixty months from April 13, 2022, is the period during which the network’s infrastructure moved in parallel with the research work. If the PoC set “is it possible,” then April 13, 2022, set “exactly how.” UPoW performance, scoring, computor node rotation through weekly epochs, the Arbitrator’s behavior — all of this was calibrated on the same time scale as the Aigarth research. On the final date they’re meant to meet at one point: the research delivers a productionready framework, and the network delivers compute capacity on which the framework starts to run. Five years is the time both sides need.
Five years isn’t a marketing number. It’s a functional window. On July 31, 2024, CfB described the expectation in these words:
“In 2 or 3 years we get Aigarth.”

Said in the middle of 2024, this window is July 2026 / July 2027. April 13, 2027, falls roughly in the middle of it. That is, when the team says “in two to three years,” this date isn’t an aggressive lower bound and isn’t a backstop upper bound; it’s a point inside the announced range, chosen by calendar symmetry with the real start of mining. What’s needed for the five-year period. First — to pass Aigarth’s key milestones, and they have all already been passed: PoC in December 2021, midpoint in December 2024, breakthrough in July 2025, the GitHub publication on July 22, 2025 (all of this is unpacked in chapter twelve, I won’t repeat). Second — to scale up mining capacity to a level at which AI inference through smart contracts becomes economically meaningful for miners. This is the second half of the five-year window, and the next section is about it.

And one more parallel worth saying out loud, because it sits behind the words “five years” and explains a lot. On April 13, 2022, at the moment of mining start, much of the code didn’t yet exist. The same may be true for the final date — the optimizations for compute capacity are being written right now, at the moment this chapter is being written. That doesn’t mean the plan is in danger. It means that in 2022 and in 2027 alike, the work closes precisely on the date — and in the first case that worked out, while in the second it’s so far only planned.

In chapter one I compared the ambition of Qubic with Darby’s ambition in 1709. Coalbrookdale produced the first tons of coke iron then — but the broad adoption of the method in industry took decades. It’s the same here. On the verification date we’ll find out whether a claim of that scale is justified. And the answer doesn’t have to be binary. It can be “it worked, but a year later.” It can be “it half-worked.” It can be “it worked in an unexpected form.” Any of these variants is valid, unlike the falsely binary “success / failure.” A falsifier for an ambition of this scale is always more complicated than “yes / no.”
What “happened” and “didn’t happen” mean

Scenario A. The deploy succeeds and Aigarth is active. On the date, plus or minus a few days, the framework moves into production. Anna, Maria, and subsequent AIs run as smart contracts, accessible through Qubic’s standard SC mechanics with Oracle Machines for feeding in external data. The Arbitrator’s key is destroyed, the event publicly confirmed. The network keeps running without it — the computor list is updated through UPoW, scoring, and weekly-epoch rotation. What this means for the book’s framing: chapter four is closed empirically — crypto is observably working as infrastructure for AI. What it doesn’t mean: AGI hasn’t been created (and that’s already clarified by the February car/BMW analogy), not all of Aigarth’s technical tasks are solved, the first AI applications may remain quite limited. The book in this scenario hasn’t “won the argument.” It registered a falsifiable framework, and the framework was confirmed — that’s a different quality of result.

Scenario B. The deploy went through technically, but Aigarth isn’t showing what was claimed. The framework works; smart contracts that host AI are technically functional. But AI applications are weak or absent in production: the network’s compute capacity isn’t sufficient for meaningful inference. The Arbitrator’s key is destroyed all the same — that’s a structural event hardwired into the code and happens independently of how active the Aigarth applications are. What this means for the book’s framing: chapter four is closed partially — the infrastructure exists and works, but Aigarth as a research result hasn’t yet matured into a production-ready AI. This is a valid scientific result: the paradigm works at the infrastructure level, and the question shifts from feasibility — that was closed by CfB himself back in February 2026 — to economic scale. And that’s a question the book begins to answer in the next chapter.

Scenario C. The deploy is shifted. On the planned date, the event doesn’t happen as announced. Possible reasons: a technical blocker (blocking bugs were found in the framework, in the core, or in scoring); compute insufficient — the team deliberately postpones because there’s no point in deploying without enough capacity; operational coordination requires another quarter or two of development. The Arbitrator’s deactivation in that case either happens on plan — a structural event in the code, not tied to the success of the Aigarth deploy — or also shifts, which requires a team decision. It’s possible a new ETA is announced — along the lines of the January 2026 remark that five years from Qubic’s launch is, after all, an estimate and not a deadline. What this means for the book’s framing: chapter four remains an open question, carried over to a new date. The falsifier from chapter one partially fired: the date passed, the event didn’t, and that too is a valid observation. A shift of a year or two is standard-scale for infrastructural transitions: the first tons of coke iron in 1709 weren’t produced on the first try either, and broad adoption of the method took decades. A calendar date sets an expectation, but doesn’t determine the answer.

What’s important to say explicitly about these three scenarios. They are not probability distributions. I’m not writing “A is most likely; B less likely; C unlikely.” I’m not predicting the outcome. I’m registering a falsifiable framework: on the verification date, one of these three scenarios will be observed (or a close combination of them), and each gives information.

Scenario A is “Qubic’s victory.” It’s the observation that the infrastructural claim of the book matched infrastructural reality on the verification date. Scenario B is not “Aigarth’s failure.” It’s the observation that the infrastructure works, while the research result hasn’t yet matured to production quality — and that shifts the focus of the next round of discussions from feasibility to economic scale. Scenario C is not “deception of the reader.” It’s the observation that the engineering side requires more time than estimated — and that doesn’t refute CfB’s February 2026 feasibility claim; it remains in force for a new ETA.

I emphasize this because in discussions of crypto projects another framing often operates: either the project “won” or it “failed,” and both verdicts are made emotionally, without structural analysis. That framing is unfit for a scientific posing. Aigarth is a research task, and any research task has several valid outcomes. A falsifiable framework is a way of stating them in advance, rather than reactively picking a frame to fit the result.

In February 2026, CfB stated a conditional commitment: if AI is at all possible within Earth’s current energy budget, Aigarth will achieve it — and the team sees the cards it’s playing as sufficient. That formulation is precise as a falsifier. Either AI is possible within Earth, and then Aigarth is a serious candidate for a path to it. Or it isn’t, and then the question shifts from the paradigm to physics. The falsifier approach doesn’t promise a result — it promises that any outcome will give an answer.

I’m writing this chapter before the date. By the time you read it, the date has either passed or is still ahead — that was already said at the start of the chapter, and I come back to it deliberately. If it has passed — you have the result, and every reader can compare it with the three scenarios above. If it’s still ahead — you have a reason to wait. The book is honest in either case, because it doesn’t claim to know the outcome. A falsifiable framework isn’t a way to win an argument. It’s a way of agreeing in advance that any outcome will yield information.

The main risk — compute capacity between April 2026 and April 2027 The main risk for Aigarth, in CfB’s words: “Aigarth depends on miners” (November 12, 2025) and “Qubic is doomed to succeed. Aigarth? Depends on miners.” (February 7, 2026). It’s not a technical dead end, not a scientific gap, not regulatory pressure. It’s a question of network economics: how much mining capacity will plug into Aigarth tasks by the moment of deploy.
To grasp the scale of what has to happen in the twelve months before April 2027, there’s a concrete number. On January 20, 2026, CfB wrote in a discussion of internal tests:

“We are mining new Aigarth algo tomorrow, 10x bigger than Doge, but not obvious.” Ten times bigger than DOGE mining. DOGE mining is Phase 2 of the network’s current configuration, on which a significant share of mining capacity runs at the time this chapter is being written. The Aigarth task is an order of magnitude bigger. This isn’t a casual comparison; it’s a concrete technical parameter, stated in the discussion of a specific test. And it’s exactly that number that sets the scale of the ramp-up: the network performing X compute on DOGE today must, by April 2027, be able to do roughly ten X on Aigarth.

In chapter eight I unpacked UPoW as a way of forcing one computation to work on two fronts at once. After the Aigarth deploy, the same principle is applied to a new pair of tasks: the compute that today is directed toward DOGE mining as part of Phase 3, after deploy, is redirected to Aigarth inference with the same economic incentives. Structurally, that is, the network is ready — UPoW supports multitasking computation. The question is whether miners will choose such a redirection, and how many of them will plug in by the moment when the choice becomes meaningful.

It’s worth clarifying here what depends on the miners and what doesn’t. What doesn’t depend — the very mechanics of how Aigarth tasks are counted in scoring and how rewards are accrued for them: that’s part of the protocol, published in the github.com/qubic/core repository and not subject to unilateral correction. What does depend — every miner’s economic choice: whether to switch their GPU/CPU power from DOGE payout to Aigarth payout, and in what proportion. That choice depends on the ratio of reward levels between the two tasks, which the network produces every epoch, and on miners’ expectations of how that ratio will move further. The Aigarth team controls neither the first parameter directly (it’s a function of many sides’ participation) nor the second (it depends on individual strategies). What the team does control — the technical readiness of the framework for deploy and the quality of AI applications that the framework will host. Everything else is an external parameter, and that’s what CfB designates with the words “depends on miners.”

The main risk for Aigarth is not feasibility (that, as I said above, CfB closed in February 2026). The main risk is scaling the network to a level at which Aigarth inference becomes economically meaningful for miners. That risk isn’t solved by science or engineering — it’s solved by network economics. And there’s already a partial answer to that question, from August 2025.
Between plan and proof

I unpacked Axelrod’s three conditions as applied to research work itself — iteration, memory, transparency. The book iterates (its chapters get rewritten). The book holds memory (the hook tracker records every claim still waiting to be closed). The book is transparent (it announces its dates and scenarios in advance, before it can verify the answer). A falsifiable framework is, in essence, the same three conditions applied to its own narrative.
On May 14, 2024, CfB wrote on Twitter:
“I have realized that Artificial Intelligence will not be created, it will emerge. With help of Qubic miners.”

“Will emerge” is the verb of an observer, not a commander. Not “we’ll create AI,” but “AI will emerge — with the help of those who work on the network.” This is the very emergent framing I unpacked: AI as the result of collective mechanics, not as a product designed top-down. And this framing isn’t 2024 marketing; it’s the position the team has worked from since the beginning. Since 2022, when no one outside a narrow circle knew that this emergence would one day surface in the public field; since December 2021, when the first PoC was launched and the team understood that the approach works; since the moment CfB decided that the “build and leave” method could be hardwired into the code in advance, and committed in advance to leaving.

Emergence doesn’t arrive on its own. It arrives if there’s an environment in which it can manifest, and time for that environment to take shape. Earlier chapters described that environment: 676 votes, weekly epochs, UPoW, scoring, smart contracts, governance. Then they described not the environment but the process going on inside it: research, milestones, peer review, artifacts with verifiable properties. Then the moment when the environment and the process must meet at one public point. If CfB is right in his 2024 observation, then on this date the meeting happens — not as an announcement, but as a change in regime in which the network begins to operate. P A r T V The Proof
