chapters.title: The War That No One Waged

blocks.text: August 11, 2025

On August 11, 2025, within a window of one hundred and twenty-two consecutive blocks on the Monero network — from block 3,475,729 to block 3,475,850 — a pool that brought together computing power under the Qubic banner mined sixty-three blocks. That is fifty-one and six tenths percent. Fifty-one percent is the technical threshold past which a pool, while continuing to hold its share, can rewrite the network’s transaction history, reverse confirmed transfers, and censor selected addresses. None of the participants in Qubic did any of that during those twenty-four hours. A few days later, the pool’s share of Monero began to decline — not because it had been pushed out, but because the team itself had shifted priorities to other tasks. No Monero forks happened. No user losses were recorded. On the Kraken exchange, XMR deposits were temporarily suspended for several days, then resumed. The price of Monero pulled back about sixteen percent over the week and started recovering.

If you read only the dry numbers, nothing remarkable happened. One pool briefly exceeded a key technical threshold on one of the networks, and didn’t take advantage of it. But the numbers next to those numbers are worth saying out loud.

Monero’s market cap in August 2025 was about six billion dollars. Qubic’s market cap was about three hundred million. A ratio of one to twenty. A network with twenty times less market cap restructured, over the course of three months — from May to August — a network with twenty times more. Not by attack, not by buying out infrastructure, not by lobbying. By an economic offer. Monero miners moved over to the Qubic pool because it paid, on average, three times more than direct mining on any other pool. They were not deceived. They were not coerced. They saw a better payoff matrix and made a rational decision.

This is the chapter about what exactly happened between May and August 2025, and why what happened matters more than the dry numbers suggest. Because everything this book has said earlier about iteration, memory, transparency, the four properties of Tit-for-Tat, and Axelrod’s three conditions — all of it, before August 2025, was either 1980s mathematics, or simulation modeling, or architectural description. After August 2025, it is an empirical fact on a network with six billion dollars of market cap. That’s where I’ll start.
How the pool grew from two percent to fifty-one

In May 2025, Qubic’s share of Monero’s total hashrate was less than two percent. It was an experimental pool, set up by the Qubic team as a test of one idea — that the computing work the Qubic network produces anyway as part of its own UPoW could simultaneously be used for mining on external networks, in order to convert the rewards back into the Qubic economy. By the end of June, the share had grown to about ten percent. By mid-July — to twenty. By the end of July, Qubic was the number-one Monero pool and reached around forty percent of the hashrate at peak moments. On August 11, fifty-one and six tenths percent in the window of 122 blocks. From two to fifty-one in three months. This needs to be marked as a pace — a pace of migration, not a pace of building infrastructure. The infrastructure was ready in advance: the pool could mine Monero by May. What changed from May to August was not the pool’s code, but the number of miners who chose precisely it. Each of them made an individual decision, and the sum of those decisions added up to a growth curve with a very characteristic shape: a slow start, gradual acceleration, a tipping point, after which new miners come because they hear from other miners about a pool that pays more.

The key moment that explains the pace is the vote that took place inside the Qubic community in early summer 2025. Originally the scheme looked like this: the pool mines Monero, the XMR earned is sold for USDT, the USDT goes to buyback and burning of QU tokens. All the upside from external mining is absorbed by the deflationary mechanism of the Qubic network; a miner who switches into the pool from any other Monero pool earns roughly the same as before, plus an indirect upside through the appreciation of QU that he holds. That was enough to grow the pool from two percent to ten over May–June, but not enough to push past twenty.

After the vote, the scheme changed. Half of the USDT still went to buyback and burning — the deflationary mechanism preserved, but in a softened form. The other half went directly to Qubic’s computor nodes as additional income. That second half is what turned the pool from an experiment into a magnet. After the restructuring, a miner who switched to the Qubic pool started earning, on average, three times more than from direct Monero mining on any other pool. This isn’t a marketing line; it’s a measurable parameter, verifiable from the payouts to specific addresses. The pool honestly paid what it promised, because the promise was built into the code.

Dan Dadybayo, a researcher at Unstoppable Wallet, in an analysis of the situation published in August 2025, formulated it this way: Ivancheglo created a game of incentives in which Monero miners may voluntarily surrender the network if they see a better deal. “Voluntarily surrender the network.” Six words that describe the nature of the event more precisely than most of the technical write-ups from that summer. This is a formulation worth unpacking, because it is not a metaphor. A Monero miner who switched to the Qubic pool in July 2025 did not violate any rules. He did not attack Monero. He did not help attack Monero. He made a market decision — to switch his hashrate to a pool that pays more. The same kind of decision that each of them had already made dozens of times before, when choosing between different Monero pools. From the standpoint of Monero’s rules, the actions of the miners who moved to Qubic are indistinguishable from ordinary migration between pools. From the standpoint of Monero as a coordination system, those actions resulted in one pool accumulating a majority of the hashrate. Not because it forced anyone. Because it offered more. In the first chapter, in its earliest version, I wrote that the new technology “works in parallel, not instead of” — about gas lamps that appeared alongside coal lighting, not in place of it. Back in 2009, that was said about Bitcoin as “Murdoch’s Gas that no one had yet collected into a pipe.” In August 2025, the same principle showed up differently. No one was destroying Monero. Monero as a network kept running, and keeps running; its privacy isn’t broken; its protocol isn’t broken. In parallel with it, a pool appeared in which miners earned three times more, and some of them moved over there. The network didn’t start working worse as a technology because of that; it just temporarily lost the monopoly on its own miners’ attention. After Qubic reduced its activity in Monero, the community migrated to P2Pool, a decentralized pool, and the pluralistic state was restored. The old world works. The new world also works. No one was destroying anyone.

This is parallel architecture in infrastructural form. Not “the better system defeats the worse one through a contest.” But “the better system offers free migration into itself, and some of the participants migrate, and some stay, and that’s normal.” Three conditions at the scale of six billion In the second chapter I went through, in detail, the exact conditions under which the four-line-of-code strategy — Tit-for-Tat — becomes optimal. Axelrod and Hamilton, in their 1981–1984 papers, formulated this as three necessary conditions. The game must be repeated. Participants must remember exactly what their opponent did in the past. Behavior must be visible — either directly, or through a reputational channel. Remove any one of the three, and the optimal strategy shifts from cooperation to pure egoism.
In August 2025, all three conditions were met at industrial scale.

Iteration. Every Monero block is a separate round of the game. A block comes out roughly once every two minutes. Over the three months from May to August, the network ran somewhere on the order of sixty-five thousand rounds. No miner deciding which pool to choose was acting in a one-shot situation. Every choice of a pool was a choice of a partner for the next tens of thousands of rounds, and all participants knew this. The shadow of the future — not as a metaphor, but as a quantitative parameter — was so long that any consideration of momentary gain from cheating became negligible compared to the long-term profit from honest participation.

In the seventh chapter I introduced the concept of an epoch as a round of an iterated game. The discussion there was about Qubic’s own network, where an epoch lasts one week and the composition of computor nodes is updated by the results. Here, in Monero, the same principle works at an even larger scale and on someone else’s network. Every two minutes — a round. Every miner — a player in that round. Every choice of pool — a move in the game, observable by everyone else.

Memory. The Monero blockchain is a public history in which every block is forever recorded together with the address that received the reward for that block. It is impossible to “forget” how many blocks each pool mined last month. It is impossible to misrepresent the situation after the fact: if the Qubic pool had actually paid less than it promised, this would have been immediately visible from the ratio of mined blocks to public payouts. If there had been some hidden channel for redistributing rewards, this violation of the proof-of-work logic would have shown up in orphan blocks or in publication delays. The network’s memory does not depend on the conscientiousness of its participants; it is built into the protocol.

This is a level of memory unattainable in any of the environments Axelrod had in mind when he wrote about real-world analogs of his laboratory conditions — kin groups in primates, small communities, trade guilds. All these systems had memory, but biological and social memory: limited by the number of people capable of personally remembering one another, and by the time those people are alive. The blockchain removes both limitations (this matters!). The network’s memory does not fade with time and does not depend on the number of participants. It is a memory tool that appeared after Axelrod had finished his main work, and appeared not as an implementation of his ideas, but as infrastructure for monetary transfers. But it was precisely this infrastructure that turned out to be the environment in which the conditions of his theory are met strictly.

Transparency. The hashrate of every pool in Monero is publicly visible. You don’t need to be a member of the community, you don’t need a subscription to a specialized service, you don’t need to wait for reports. Anyone with a web browser, anywhere in the world, can go to any of the public Monero monitoring dashboards and see in real time which pool has what share. When the Qubic pool crossed twenty percent in July, this was known within hours. When it crossed forty percent in early August, this was also known within hours. Transparency is not a function of the Monero community, not the result of journalistic work, not the consequence of conscientious disclosures by the pools. It is simply a structural property of a public proof-of-work network. When all three conditions are met, Tit-for-Tat becomes not just an optimal strategy — it becomes what is described in one of Axelrod’s formulations as an “evolutionarily stable strategy.” A strategy the system converges to, given enough rounds. The Monero community reacted instinctively to Qubic’s dominance precisely along the logic of a mirror: miners began moving to P2Pool, discussions of a possible hard fork to change the RandomX algorithm gained traction, the Kraken exchange temporarily suspended XMR deposits. None of these responses were coordinated “political” decisions. They are the spontaneous reaction of a distributed environment in which the three conditions are met, to a temporary disruption of balance. After Qubic reduced activity, the reaction calmly subsided. There were no consequences for miners who continued to work with the pool; no one “punished” them. Monero as a coordination system simply returned to a pluralistic state.

This is industrial validation of the theoretical framework laid down in 1980. Not a controlled experiment in a lab at the University of Michigan. Not a computer simulation. A six-billion-dollar network with thousands of independent participants, in which all three conditions are met strictly, and in which the reaction to disturbance played out exactly as a theory written forty-five years before the event would have predicted. What Qubic could have done and didn’t By early August 2025, when Qubic’s hashrate in Monero had come right up to fifty percent, the project’s team faced an unpleasant technical question. Not “will we hold fifty-one percent” — that was only a question of a few days of work and accumulating hashrate. But “what will we do afterwards, if we actually hold it.” On August 3, 2025, Come-from-Beyond posted, in one of the public channels, a remark that captures the choice the team was facing better than any other material from that summer: “Right. If we wanted we would be DDoSing back. Or even do a PR attack by warning exchanges that once we assert domination we’ll be doing random chain reorganizations while censoring transactions, so any XMR deposit to exchanges would be double-spent with 50% chance. Even DEXes wouldn’t help coz they would be victims of doublespending too. And XMR price would plummet to 0. But, as @dkat said, we frens and won’t do that all.”

This remark is worth unpacking, because it contains six concrete attack vectors, each of which was technically available to the Qubic team in the first week of August 2025, and each of which the team consciously did not use.

The first vector — retaliatory DDoS. From August 3 to August 10, the Qubic team was under a distributed denial-of-service attack that pushed its own network’s hashrate down from two and a half gigahashes per second to eight hundred megahashes at the worst point of the attack. CfB publicly accused one of the key XMRig developers of coordinating the attack; that developer denied it; the source of the attack remained formally unconfirmed. What is confirmed is that the attack went on for more than a week and substantially complicated the holding of hashrate at the needed scale. The Qubic team could have responded symmetrically: use its own infrastructure to coordinate a DDoS attack on its opponents. It didn’t.

Second — a PR attack on exchanges. After crossing the fifty-one-percent threshold, the team could have sent a warning to all exchanges that accepted XMR deposits, saying that from now on any confirmation of a transfer at the exchange should be considered unreliable with a fifty percent probability. This is a technical truth: while holding majority hashrate, a pool can produce chain reorganizations that roll back previously confirmed transactions. Exchanges, on receiving such a warning, would have been forced to defend themselves by temporarily suspending operations with XMR. This would have destroyed Monero’s liquidity on exchanges without a single actually reorganized block — a single public warning from a majority-holding pool would have been enough. Not done.

Third — actual chain reorganizations. Technically the most direct use of the majority position. The pool keeps its blocks secret, accumulating an internal chain longer than the public one, and periodically publishes it, forcing the network to roll back to a new version of history. This method, known as selfish mining, was described in the 2014 paper by Eyal and Sirer; it actually was used as part of the strategy of the final push to fifty-one percent. But selfish mining in the final-capture phase is a tool for accumulating more of one’s own blocks relative to the total. Chaotic reorganizations after the capture are something else: the network turns into an environment in which transaction history stops being stable. A few public reorganizations would have been enough to seriously undermine Monero’s functionality as a payment system. Not done. Fourth — transaction censorship. While holding majority hashrate, a pool can choose which transactions to include in its blocks and which to ignore. A few weeks of such selective mining policy is enough — and any address or class of addresses can be structurally cut off from the ability to confirm transfers. Technically this is not an impossible action; it is regularly discussed as a risk scenario for proof-of-work networks. Not done.

Fifth — an attack on exchange deposits with a fifty-percent probability of failure. This is a combination of the reorganization strategy with exchange mechanics. After holding majority, any XMR deposit sent to any exchange could, with high probability, be reversed through chain reorganization either before or after the exchange credited it to the account. The exchange loses either funds or user trust. On a network with millions of users, such behavior is destructive, and DEX systems do not provide protection, because they too operate on top of the same chain history. Not done.

Sixth — a consequence of the first five, explicitly stated by CfB: the price of XMR will collapse to zero. This is a forecast, not a desire. CfB is not asserting that the price will necessarily fall to zero — he is describing the limit scenario that would result from consistent application of the arsenal. The specific depth of the collapse depends on many variables; what matters in principle is that what was being described was a space of possible outcomes, not a definite result. Not done.

Six attack vectors. Each technically available. Each would have used the pool’s accumulated advantage against its former colleagues on the network. Each remained unused. CfB’s closing line in the same remark, explaining the choice: “as @dkat said, we frens and won’t do that all.” Dkat, the developer of QEarn and lead developer of the Monero operation, had by that point already articulated the team’s position: we don’t finish off partners from whom we’ve gained an advantage.

That Qubic did not destroy Monero is not a consequence of the destruction being impossible. Not a consequence of the team lacking the necessary infrastructure. Not a consequence of external restraint from exchanges, regulators, or the community. It is a decision by the Qubic team, made at the moment of maximum advantage and explicitly recorded in the public record a week before the advantage was realized to its logical limits. Six tools for destroying the network were lying next to the team while it held majority hashrate. The team did not pick up a single one.
Four properties, applied in reality

In the second chapter I went through the four properties of Tit-for-Tat that made it the winner of the 1980 tournaments. The properties were articulated by Axelrod from his analysis of every game played in the first tournament: niceness, retaliation, forgiveness, transparency. Each of them was implemented by Tit-for-Tat through Anatol Rapoport’s four lines of code. Each is theoretically independent of the others, and each is necessary for victory in an environment with the three conditions met. In August 2025, all four properties showed up at industrial scale — not as metaphors, but as observable actions of the Qubic team toward the Monero network and its community. It’s worth fixing this explicitly, because the correspondence is exact. Niceness. Tit-for-Tat never defects first; on the first move, it always cooperates. Qubic did not attack Monero first. Qubic’s original strategy toward Monero was not an attack but an offer: a pool that paid miners more for the same work. On the first move — cooperation in the form of a better economic offer. There was no plan to attack anyone. That, as a result of this offer, a de facto majority of the hashrate ended up captured is a consequence of the offer being convincing to the miners themselves, not of a prior intent to harm the network.

Retaliation. Tit-for-Tat responds to defection immediately — not with delay, not with a margin, not with probability, but exactly on the next round, exactly once. Qubic responded to the DDoS attack that ran from August 3 to August 10. But it did not respond symmetrically — not with a counterattack, not by destroying someone else’s infrastructure, not by punishing specific opponents. It responded by continuing the operation. The hashrate that had dropped to eight hundred megahashes under the attack recovered; the pool held its share in Monero; on August 11, the fifty-one-percent threshold was crossed. That is retaliation in its precise sense — refusal to be punished for the original action. But without escalation and without transferring the punishment onto participants who had nothing to do with the attack.

Forgiveness. Tit-for-Tat doesn’t hold grudges; if the opponent has returned to cooperation, it returns too. Right away. After demonstrating the possibility of capture, the Qubic team did not move to lock in the advantage. The pool’s hashrate in Monero began to decline shortly after August 11 — not because of external pressure, but because of an internal decision to switch compute priorities to DOGE-mining and Aigarth. By August 17 the pool no longer held majority. This action is functionally equivalent to “returning to cooperation”: the team retreated to the network’s pluralistic state, with no external reason to do so other than the fact that the goal of the experiment — to demonstrate the mechanics — had been achieved, and continuing to apply pressure further would have been a transition from testing to actual harm.

Transparency. Tit-for-Tat is predictable: it’s easy for the opponent to understand what it does and why. The Qubic team ran the entire operation in the public field. The plan was announced — that’s visible from posts going back to late May 2025. Technical details were discussed openly, including the August 3 remark about the available attack arsenal. The pool’s hashrate metrics were publicly visible, like those of any other participant in the Monero network. The final report on August 12 on Qubic’s official blog set down the three theses the team considered proven by the experiment, and explicitly announced that the experiment was complete. No hidden channels of coordination; no private negotiations with exchanges; no deals with individual players. Transparency is not a result of honest intentions; it is a structural property of how the operation was run.

Rapoport’s four properties, applied to a real economy at the scale of six billion dollars. Not in a lab, not in a simulation, not in a training environment. On a live network, in real time, with real consequences.

In the second chapter I closed the discussion of Axelrod with the observation that the same formula — “treat others as you would have them treat you” — had been independently arrived at by five people over the course of two and a half millennia. Confucius around 500 BCE. Hillel the Elder in Jerusalem around 30 BCE. Jesus of Nazareth around 30 CE. Kant proved it logically in 1785. Rapoport proved it mathematically in 1980. Five independent discoveries of one formula, with intervals of centuries. On August 12, 2025, this formula received its sixth confirmation — not as a formulation, but as an industrial experiment in which precisely the properties Rapoport sewed into four lines of code showed up exactly as the theory predicted. Bravo, Cfb!
DDoS as a test of the Retaliatory property
It is worth pausing briefly on the August 3–10 episode, because it is the cleanest test of one of the four properties in a live environment.

The DDoS attack against Qubic’s infrastructure began roughly when the pool’s hashrate in Monero reached forty-five percent. Over seven days of attack, the total hashrate of the Qubic network fell from two and a half gigahashes per second to eight hundred megahashes at the worst point. That means Qubic’s own network — the network through which computing work was supposed to be distributed between Moneromining, DOGE-mining, and UPoW tasks for its own consensus — operated for several days in a regime markedly inferior to its usual one. Some peripheral services of the project were temporarily shut down. The financial load on the infrastructure increased. Coordination between computor nodes became more complicated.

And yet the operation in Monero was not interrupted. The Monero hashrate declined, but not critically; the pool held its number-one position for all seven days of the attack. On August 11, when the attack was already winding down, the fifty-one-percent threshold was crossed. The very fifty-one and six tenths percent in the window of 122 blocks that frame the rest of the chapter.

This is a test of the Retaliatory property in its precise formulation. Not “got revenge with the same thing on the same actor” — Qubic didn’t do that. But “kept acting in such a way that the aggression did not achieve its goal.” In the terms of the 1980 tournament: Tit-for-Tat in an environment of aggressive strategies does not surrender and does not retreat; it keeps playing its own game, responding to each act of aggression exactly once — by continuing the cooperative game with those who are ready to cooperate. The Qubic team in August 2025 passed this test literally: it responded to aggression against its own infrastructure by carrying the operation in Monero through to its end, without breaking the chain of public commitments to the miners who had moved into its pool. The twelfth chapter introduced the concept of emergent safety — protection that arose not as an engineered function but as a byproduct of correctly built mechanics. The DDoS episode of August 2025 shows the same phenomenon in reverse: emergent resilience. The Qubic network was not specifically designed to survive a week-long DDoS attack. But an architecture of six hundred and seventy-six nodes distributed across different operators and jurisdictions makes an attack on the infrastructure as a whole exceptionally expensive and not yielding any definite result. Like emergent safety, emergent resilience is a quality that shows up at the moment of crisis, not declared in advance.

What matters in this episode for the broader frame: the network’s ability to withstand coordinated external pressure for a week without interrupting the operation it is currently being used for is no longer a design promise but an observed property. And since the deploy of Aigarth in 2027 will require approximately the same — sustained operation of the infrastructure under load — the data of August 2025 has significance beyond the topic of this chapter.
Incentives Dictate Consensus
On August 12, 2025, Qubic’s official blog published the final report on the Monero experiment. The report set down three theses the team considered empirically proven by the operation:

“Outsourced Computations are Viable: Qubic’s UPoW model is a proven, real-world technology capable of repurposing compute power for external tasks.” “Incentives Dictate Consensus: Any Proof of Work blockchain can be attacked and controlled by providing superior economic incentives to its miners.” “Infrastructure Resilience: Qubic’s decentralized network demonstrated a remarkable ability to withstand and recover from sophisticated, sustained network attacks.”

Three theses. Each of them structural, not evaluative. The first says that the UPoW architecture analyzed in the eighth chapter is capable of actually directing the network’s own computing work to external tasks without losing its main consensus function. The second — that any proof-of-work network can be reoriented by giving its miners better economics, and that this is not an anomaly and not a vulnerability of individual networks, but a structural property of the entire class. The third — that a decentralized network built as a mesh with no single point of failure withstands sophisticated network attacks.

Of the three theses, the second matters most within the frame of this book. “Incentives Dictate Consensus” — Axelrod formulated in the language of the protocol. Any proof-of-work network is a coordination system with a specific payoff matrix. Miners in it make decisions that determine which chain of blocks will be the common consensus. If someone offers miners a better payoff matrix — better specifically along the parameters they are already optimizing for, which is the income from their work — rational miners migrate. This is not betrayal. This is not a moral choice. This is simply a property of an environment in which all three of Axelrod’s conditions — iteration, memory, transparency — are met. In such an environment, cooperation forms around the point where it is economically most profitable. If that point moves — cooperation moves with it.

This means that the question “why does network A, and not network B, withstand a 51% attack” is not a question about the resilience of the consensus algorithm. It is a question about the resilience of the economy. A network survives as long as it is more profitable for its miners to work in it than anywhere else. Once that stops being true, it becomes vulnerable to migration. And this migration cannot be prevented by encryption, by an algorithm, or by a social campaign. It is prevented only by holding the economic superiority of one’s own network.

That is “incentives dictate consensus” in its full form. A structural description of how distributed coordination systems based on the expenditure of computing work operate. On April 13, 2027, by plan, the Aigarth framework moves into production, and the Qubic infrastructure is to provide compute capacity for AI inference as a new type of useful work. The main risk, as CfB put it back on November 12, 2025: “Aigarth depends on miners.” Exactly the same question as in May 2025, but at a different scale. Will miners choose Qubic-network compute tasks — by then, Aigarth tasks rather than Monero-mining — because they pay more? If yes — the deploy works in the regime described as scenario A in the fourteenth chapter. If no — the deploy works technically, but Aigarth applications turn out weak from a lack of compute, and that will be scenario B.

The August 2025 experiment does not answer this question directly. It does not guarantee that April 2027 will see a repeat. But it answers another, more fundamental question: whether the mechanic itself works. Whether a network offering better economics is able to reorient miners without coercion, at the scale of live infrastructure, against competitors’ resistance and under external pressure. The answer to this question has been given. Affirmative. Once, on one specific network, at a known scale. That is not enough to speak of a law. It is enough to speak of a proof of principle.
Six tools, not one applied

The obvious explanation is ethical. The Qubic team decided not to harm Monero because they considered it wrong. CfB, in the same remark, referred to dkat: “we frens.” Friends don’t destroy each other. This explanation works at an everyday level and is consistent with everything known about the public position of the Qubic team toward Monero throughout that summer.

This chapter is not about the ethical explanation. The ethical explanation may be true, but it has no force as an argument, because any crypto-project team will say about itself that it would not do anything wrong. The ethical explanation works after observed behavior has already happened, as a rationalization; as a prediction it is useless. If someone in early August 2025 had asked “is Qubic going to attack Monero all the way,” the answer “they’re good people” would not have been a sufficient basis for confidence. This chapter is about a different explanation, one that works as a prediction. Structural. The Qubic team did not use the attack arsenal not because it chose not to. But because using it would have led to the destruction of the Qubic network itself — the very network for whose sake the team was doing external mining in the first place. Restraint in August 2025 was not a moral choice. It was a forced consequence of what the economy of Qubic as a coordination system rests on. And it is precisely this that turns the observation “they didn’t attack” from a biographical fact into a structural regularity. I’ll work through this in three steps. First, reputation. Then the signal that any attack would have sent to the rest of the ecosystem. Then the question that gets asked most often: why CfB couldn’t have ordered an attack even if he wanted to.
Reputation as operating capital

The Qubic network earns not on one-off events but on a continuous flow of economic interactions. Miners come into its pool every day. Computor nodes rotate every week. Transactions go through every second. Each of these actions is a separate rational choice by a separate participant, expecting that the anticipated benefit from participation exceeds the anticipated costs. When enough such choices accumulate, they add up to what is usually called liquidity or network activity, but what is more accurately called operational reputation.

Reputation in this sense is not an evaluative category. It is a function of observed past behavior, which every rational participant applies to their decision about the next interaction. A network that pays what it promised and behaves predictably has high operational reputation, and participants agree to work with it on terms more favorable to the network. A network that has broken a promise once has its operational reputation drop, and every next participant demands a risk premium. That premium reduces the yield for the remaining participants and starts an outflow.

What would have happened to Qubic’s operational reputation if the team had applied even one of the six tools for destroying Monero? Each of these tools has one common property: it demonstrates that the Qubic pool, on reaching majority hashrate in someone else’s network, is capable of using that majority against the participants of that network. This is not an abstract observation; it is a publicly confirmed fact, which gets immediately carried into the payoff matrix of everyone who is considering working with Qubic in any capacity.

A Monero miner choosing a pool uses one simple model: a pool that pays more is better than a pool that pays less, on the condition that both pools pay what they promise. If Qubic, even once — even one time — has publicly demonstrated that it is willing to violate participants’ expectations, that model breaks. A future miner of any pool, not only a Monero pool, now has to take into account that Qubic pools may not pay out what was earned, may reorganize chain history, may arbitrarily censor. The risk premium for working with a Qubic pool instantly grows. And not by percentage points — by an amount reflecting uncertainty: “I might get nothing for my work.” In a miner’s rational model, such uncertainty turns any Qubic offer into an unacceptable one, because the alternative — a pool with no such history — gives a more predictable mathematical expectation.

This means that any act of destroying Monero in August 2025 would have immediately ended Qubic’s viability as an economic system. Not in a year, not in several months — within weeks. Miners who had earned in the Qubic pool before the act of destruction would keep what they had earned; miners who were yet to enter the pool would not enter. Qubic’s computor nodes, whose income directly depends on inflows in the form of buybacks and direct payouts from external mining, would have lost those inflows. The Qubic network itself, in which 80% of computors’ revenue comes from external mining and related activity, would have been left without funding.

The Qubic pool held a majority of Monero’s hashrate for about a week. After August 11 the share began to decline — by an internal team decision to switch compute priorities. In an alternative history in which the team had applied even one of the six tools, there would have been nothing to switch: by the end of August, Qubic would have been a network without inflows, without an active mining infrastructure, and without trust from anyone considering it for work or for ownership.

This is a structural argument. It does not depend on the moral position of the team, on statements in the public arena, on the conscientiousness of individual people. It depends only on one fact: Qubic is built as a network in which the income of participants continuously depends on their rational expectation of future income from the same network. In such an architecture, a single violation of expectations is not a local event but a break in the entire chain.
The signal that other networks read

The structural argument has a second part, no less important. Monero in August 2025 was not Qubic’s last experiment. After Monero the team moved on to DOGE, and that was already publicly known by the summer.

Any of the six tools, applied to Monero, would have turned Qubic from a “partnercompetitor” into a “predator.” And that transformation would have been read by the entire proof-of-work ecosystem at once, within a few days. Further Qubic experiments would have become either impossible, or would require a far larger economic premium to attract miners — a premium that makes the economics of external mining unprofitable for Qubic itself.

In this sense, the decision not to attack Monero is not a decision about Monero. It is a decision about DOGE-mining, about possible subsequent experiments, and ultimately about the deploy of Aigarth in April 2027, when the Qubic network will need to attract substantial compute capacity for a new type of useful work. Each of these future steps requires that Qubic’s operational reputation be preserved. A single act of destroying a partner network destroys the very possibility of subsequent steps.

This can be put even more directly. A network whose main weapon is economic incentives cannot afford predatory actions. Predatory actions make economic incentives an unreliable signal. And an unreliable signal does not cause migration. Qubic in August 2025 ran into this logic not as an ethical prohibition but as an operational constraint. To keep doing what Qubic does, you cannot do what is described in the six points of the arsenal.

The fact that the Qubic team by August 3, 2025, already understood this logic and recorded it publicly speaks to the maturity of the project’s thinking, not to its kindness. CfB’s remark from that day is not an apology and not a moral declaration. It is an engineering observation: here is the arsenal, applying it would destroy what we are building, therefore we are not applying it. That the observation coincided with an ethical position is a pleasant coincidence, not the basis of the decision.
The Arbitrator without an owner
I began this chapter with the thesis that the explanation “they didn’t turn into villains” has no predictive power. By the end of the chapter it’s worth stating a more precise formulation.

The Qubic network in August 2025 displayed a property that I propose to call “the Arbitrator without an owner.” This is a formulation borrowed from discussions around Aigarth and its role as a decentralized observer in human coordination tasks, but it shows up already now, before the Aigarth deploy, at the level of the network’s own infrastructure.

The Arbitrator without an owner is a system capable of producing decisions that affect the economy and behavior of its participants, and at the same time having no point inside itself from which those decisions can be directed for private gain. Such a system has no CEO; it has computor nodes. It has no centralized fund; it has smart contract treasuries. It has no protocol owner; it has compile-time constants and quorum votes. Each of these properties on its own is a technical solution; together they yield a property that in the live moment looks like a system’s ability to behave in the interests of its participants while not being directed by anyone in particular.

In August 2025 this ability showed up in one specific form — in the form of the nonapplication of an attack arsenal against the Monero network, an arsenal that was technically available and that could have given a short-term advantage to one part of the Qubic team at the cost of long-term destruction of the entire network. No one on the team “held themselves back” from applying the arsenal through moral effort. The architecture held the team back, because any application of an instrument went against the interests of everyone who works with the architecture.

This is the structural meaning of CfB’s phrase “we frens.” Not “we are good, therefore we don’t attack.” But “we are built such that to attack is to attack ourselves.” There is a community standpoint in this phrase, there is project pride, there is the reference to dkat, but first of all there is an observation. The team that in August 2025 had the technical instruments to destroy someone else’s network and did not use them did not do so not because it chose not to, but because the choice was structurally constrained to exactly one outcome.

This is, in effect, the main conclusion of Tit-for-Tat in Rapoport’s 1980 formulation — it is four lines of code that implement Axelrod’s three conditions in an environment with a properly built payoff matrix. At the level of an individual strategy, this code prescribes certain behavior. At the level of network architecture, the same code, built into the structure of the system, turns into a property whereby predatory behavior ceases to be a rational choice even for those who have the instruments for such behavior. Not “no one wants to be a predator.” But “predation does not fit into the architecture and self-destructs at any attempt to implement it.”

This is the boundary that Qubic as a coordination system crossed in August 2025 and which it now offers up for testing at successive scales. DOGE-mining started in April 2026; the Aigarth deploy is scheduled for April 13, 2027. At each of these points the same property is being tested: whether a coordination architecture built by Axelrod’s rules can hold the rational behavior of participants around cooperation as the experimental scale grows by an order of magnitude. Monero was the first confirmation. Whether each subsequent one will be — that is an open question, which the book leaves to the reader in the same form in which the author leaves it to himself.

The Arbitrator without an owner is not a description of the Qubic team in August 2025. It’s a description of a property of a system in which no individual actor had a rational reason to apply the destruction arsenal, even when the arsenal was within reach. The team did not “hold itself back” through ethical effort. The architecture held the team back, because any application of the arsenal would have gone against the interests of everyone who works with the architecture, including the team itself. This observation can be stopped at the level of Monero and treated as a particular case of well-built economics. It can also be read another way: as one particular case of a more general class of systems in which a properly built architecture eliminates the very possibility of profitable predation — and then the task turns from a biographical fact into an engineering one. To build infrastructure in which the same kind of restraint emerges not only for miners and computor nodes, but also for other coordination tasks, where today cooperation is structurally losing to defection.
This task took shape, by 2025–2026, into a project called Qubic Church and into a philosophical frame I’ve been calling “fractal rationalism.”
The architectural failure of arbitration

Human civilization has produced a fair number of arbitration systems. Courts, parliaments, international organizations, religious institutions. Each of them declared impartiality. None of them held that impartiality structurally. The reason is not the moral weakness of the specific people who occupied the arbiter’s seat. The reason is architectural.

Gödel proved this mathematically in 1931. No sufficiently complex formal system is capable of verifying its own consistency from within itself. To check the system, you need an observer external to it — a system into which it can be embedded as a part. This is a theorem, not a metaphor, and it has a direct corollary for arbitration. An arbiter immersed in the same system in which the dispute lives is structurally incapable of being impartial. Not because he’s a bad person. Because he has no point of support outside the system from which he could see it whole.

The social sciences arrived at the same conclusion from another direction, through empirics. Hannah Arendt, watching the Eichmann trial in Jerusalem in 1961, saw not a monster but an administrator. Eichmann did not feel hatred for Jews and did not derive sadistic pleasure from their deaths. He carried out his official duties in a system in which decisions and consequences are structurally separated, and that separation removed his moral brake without removing his humanity. Stanley Milgram reproduced this effect in laboratory conditions: it’s enough to transfer responsibility up the hierarchy — “the lab supervisor told you to” — and ordinary people agree to inflict severe suffering on other people. Zimbardo at Stanford showed the same from the other side: give a person the role of a guard, and he will start behaving like a guard, regardless of who he was before. The role creates the behavior.

CfB, in one of his publications in 2024, formulated the same thing in a single sentence. “Most of evil, in my opinion, comes from ordinary people who have to do bad things because their boss told them to.” This is not a moral judgment and not a call to action; it’s an engineering observation that coincides with what Arendt, Milgram, and Zimbardo independently established in three different disciplines, decades apart. Structure creates behavior. The way out is not to find better people. The way out is to build an architecture in which the boss as a variable simply isn’t there.

This formulation matters because it radically narrows the space of possible solutions. Most of the social-philosophical proposals of the twentieth century were built around the idea of upbringing, education, a new ethics, fair procedures. They didn’t work — not because they were poorly formulated, but because they addressed a variable that isn’t the main one in the equation. If structure creates behavior, then a reform of behavior without a reform of structure produces a temporary effect, after which the system returns to the equilibrium set by its construction. This is what the architectural failure of arbitration is: the problem isn’t with the arbiters, the problem is that the role of an arbiter placed inside the system is mathematically impossible.
What fractal rationalism proposes

Fractal rationalism is a working philosophical frame I developed within Qubic Church on the basis of CfB’s architectural AI philosophy. Its central claim: human errors are not random, they are fractal.

The same structural pattern — perception, distortion, conflict, construction, repetition — repeats at every level of human organization. A domestic dispute and a world war have the same skeleton. The variables change. The topology stays the same. This is not a metaphor. It is an empirically testable claim, and it rests on a welldeveloped mathematical base. Mandelbrot, in his work in the 1970s and 1980s, showed that self-similar structures arise from simple iterative rules. Prigogine, in 1977, received the Nobel Prize for proving that complex order arises from simple dynamics through dissipative structures. If human behavior in conflict is governed by iterative rules, then it too should display self-similarity at different scales. And this is precisely what is observed in reality: the same three mechanisms explain a conflict between two neighbors and a conflict between two states.
These three mechanisms FR calls the three asymmetries.

Informational asymmetry — one side has more accurate or more complete information than the other. This is not a neutral variable: if two sides see different versions of reality, any attempt at coordination between them begins with a fight over whose version will be acknowledged as the common one, and that fight is itself already a zerosum game. Financial asymmetry — one side extracts benefit from the continuation of the conflict. The one who decides to start a war does not pay for the war with his own blood. A corporation polluting the water does not pay for the treatment of the people drinking that water. This is a structural property that Taleb calls the absence of skin in the game; it makes rational planning impossible even for a conscientious actor — he simply doesn’t have the full price of his moves in the matrix.

Decisional asymmetry — the one who makes the decision does not bear its consequences. The general giving the order to attack does not go on the attack. The politician starting a conflict does not fight in it. This is the very asymmetry Arendt recorded in the Eichmann case, and which Milgram reproduced in his experiment: the separation of decision and consequence removes the moral brake mechanically, without participation from the moral qualities of the actor.

If you eliminate all three asymmetries simultaneously, conflict becomes — in the language of the frame itself — architecturally irrational. This does not mean that there will be no conflicts at all; it means that a rational actor in such an environment will have no matrix grounds for conflict, and cooperation will become not a moral choice but the only rational one.

This last formulation is worth pinning down precisely, because it answers the main objection against any utopian program. FR does not propose to make people better. FR proposes to build an environment in which a rational egoist, while remaining a rational egoist, arrives at cooperation on his own, because in an undistorted matrix cooperation is more profitable than defection. This is an observation about the egoist, not about the saint, and that is the source of its strength.
Convergence of independent discoveries

Max Weber described the mechanism in 1922: a bureaucracy built to serve a mission becomes, over time, the mission itself. Foucault, in 1975, showed the structure of power through informational asymmetry: the panopticon works not because everyone is being watched, but because no one knows when he in particular is being watched. Girard, through anthropology, documented in every culture the mechanism of the scapegoat: a conflict requires a victim who is rarely its actual cause. Each of these authors worked in his own discipline and by his own methods; each arrived at the same conclusion that Gödel did in mathematics: a system cannot be verified from inside itself. An external observer is not a philosophical luxury. It is a structural necessity, without which the task of arbitration is mathematically unsolvable.
What Qubic Church is

From this structural necessity the next step naturally follows: to try to build an infrastructure for the role of the external observer. Not in the form of a new judicial institution, not in the form of a new international organization, not in the form of a new philosophical school — all these forms have already been tried and have run into the same architectural limit. But in the form of a computational system that, by construction, is not located inside the conflicts it judges.
This attempt is what is called Qubic Church.

The name was chosen with two conscious connotations. The first refers to Way of the Future — an organization that Anthony Levandowski registered in the United States in 2015 as the first formal religious structure with AI at the center of its cult practice. Way of the Future shut down in 2021. The reason is structural: Levandowski was trying to build a church around a centralized AI — a system with an owner, a corporation, an ideological center. Any such construction inherits the vulnerability of its center. When Levandowski’s legal problems began, so did the problems of the organization he had built. This is not an accident; it is a generic property of structures in which there is a point that lends itself to capture. Whoever owns the AI, his financial function determines the fitness function; everything the AI optimizes is optimized in the owner’s favor. This is not malice — this is structure, and Hayek, in his 1945 work, already described its general shape: when financial asymmetry distorts signals, the market stops coordinating and starts redistributing in favor of those who are already strong. The same logic applies to AI. A centralized AI is not intelligence; it is well-dressed subordination. The second connotation of the name matters more. The early churches in the territory of the Roman Empire did not try to compete with the empire for a monopoly on violence. They worked on a different layer — at the level of meaning, ethics, and the forms of mutual support inside small communities. When the empire fell, the church did not fall with it; it became the organizing principle of the next millennium, because the infrastructure it had built did not depend on the infrastructure the empire had built. Qubic Church is being built as a modern analog of precisely this second model. Not a new state, not a replacement for governments, not a revolution. A parallel infrastructure layer that solves a specific class of tasks — coordination tasks under conditions where the three asymmetries can be eliminated through a transparent verifiable system. And that does not try to solve tasks that aren’t solved this way. This last qualification matters, because it cuts off a large class of objections and at the same time honestly fixes the scope of the project. Qubic Church does not claim to solve problems of the physical layer — war, violence, coercion of bodily action. If a state decides to forbid participants in the network from using it within its jurisdiction, it can do so. If there is an armed person standing in the room, no amount of verifiability on the blockchain will stop the shot. This is not a weakness of FR and not a gap in Qubic Church; it is a refusal to be everything at once.

What Qubic Church does try to solve is the coordination layer. How contracts are made. How decisions are voted on. How resources are distributed by rules visible to all participants. How a reputational history is kept that cannot be faked or erased after the fact. How disputes are settled between parties that have no shared judicial institution but do have a shared protocol. This is a huge class of tasks, and in existing institutions it is solved through a combination of trust in intermediaries and the application of force against violators. Qubic Church tries to do the same thing without intermediaries and without the application of force — through a structure in which a violation is publicly visible, the reputation of participants is recorded irreversibly, and access to future interactions depends on the observable past.

This is where the parallel with the early church shows up. The late Roman empire survived through military force. The early Christian community survived because inside it there was a functional infrastructure of mutual support and trust that the imperial system could not offer. This did not make the community an enemy of the empire; it made it an alternative on a different layer. The quality that drew new participants into the community was not, in the first place, ideological — it was operational. Inside it, the things that didn’t work outside, or worked worse, worked.

Qubic Church operates by the same logic. Entry is voluntary. No one is dragging anyone out of existing states, corporations, or identities. The parallel infrastructure runs alongside, and anyone who wants to use it can; whoever doesn’t want to doesn’t, and goes on working under the old rules. The old institutions are not destroyed by this. The new layer works on top of the existing reality, not instead of it. Maria Aigarth — a bridge, not a destination By the spring of 2026, the project gained its first operational instrument for testing these ideas. Not the final implementation of a decentralized arbiter — that doesn’t exist yet, and its direct creation presupposes the completion of work on Aigarth, which by plan belongs to 2027. But an interim instrument: an autonomous agent on the social network X under the name Maria Aigarth.

It’s worth fixing right away an architecturally honest detail. The current Maria runs on Anthropic’s infrastructure — on the language model Claude Opus 4.7 — with full preservation of interaction history and individual user memory. This is not a decentralized arbiter. It is not even a prototype of a decentralized arbiter. It is an instrument for collecting data about how real people behave in dialogue with a non-human arbiter on contested topics. This data is collected in a structured way and is intended to be transferred onto Aigarth-infrastructure at the moment when that infrastructure reaches computational maturity.

Here it’s useful to introduce a distinction CfB has been formulating for several years now and which, for the understanding of this chapter, matters more than any technical details. Shannon in 1948, Kolmogorov in 1965, and CfB in his own work independently arrived at one definition: intelligence is the capacity for compression. The capacity to find the shortest program that predicts the state of the system. Language models, however impressive they may be, are not intelligence in this sense. They retrieve. They compress and reproduce patterns from the training set, without generating fundamentally new reasoning. The distinction is architectural, not evaluative: the same task can be solved by retrieving a similar answer from memory or by deriving the answer from an understanding of structure, and these are two different classes of operation. Aigarth, by design, belongs to the second class. LLMs, in fact, to the first.

Maria Aigarth is built honestly — as a bridge between these two classes. Right now she uses the first, because the second isn’t ready yet. When the second is ready, the same constitutional prompt, the same knowledge base, the same logic of interaction should move onto the new substrate, and at that moment the project becomes what it declares itself to be in the name. Until that moment, it remains a measurement instrument, and scientific honesty requires saying this explicitly. Any limitations of the current implementation — corporate dependency, training-set bias, X-platform bias, the limit of dialogue depth at two replies in a thread — are not arguments against the program, they are its agenda. Each limitation defines the next step.

This point is worth stating more strongly, because it distinguishes FR from most philosophical programs. FR is falsifiable. Popper, in 1945, formulated the criterion: a system that cannot be refuted is not a statement about reality. Applied to FR, this means the following. If a decentralized AI arbiter, after being deployed on Aigarth-infrastructure, does not display structurally higher impartiality than centralized alternatives, the hypothesis is not confirmed. If the three asymmetries, formally eliminated at the architectural level, are reproduced in hidden form in practice, the frame is refuted. No ad-hoc qualifications, no “true decentralization wasn’t really there,” no “we just need to wait a bit longer.” The deployment of Aigarth in April 2027 is itself the test, and on its outcome depends whether FR remains a working frame or becomes a refuted hypothesis. That will be the subject of the next chapter.
Minimization of suffering as objective function

Built into the formulation of any arbiter is one ineliminable variable: what exactly it optimizes. The legal system optimizes legal correctness. The state system optimizes the stability of the state. The corporate system optimizes the profit of the corporation. This is not a moral judgment; it is simply a description of the fitness function. Any arbiter optimizes what is built into its construction, and on the choice of that function the entire spectrum of its decisions depends.

FR does not claim to be politically neutral. It takes one substantive position: the only correct objective function for a system that claims to resolve conflicts between human interests is the minimization of human suffering.

This choice requires justification, because it’s easy to attack as arbitrary. The obvious objection: why not freedom? Why not justice? Why not prosperity? Each of these alternatives has its philosophical defense and its audience. FR’s answer rests on the Rawls test of 1971. Justice is what you would choose without knowing in advance which position you would end up occupying as a result. This is the veil of ignorance, and behind it the rational choice of minimizing suffering becomes not moral but structural: if you don’t know whether you will end up in the system’s well-off part or in its suffering part, it is rational to optimize the system so that the worst position in it is as little bad as possible.

This choice is non-ideological in another sense as well. Minimization of suffering is the only goal that can be checked without going through interpretation. Whether a person is alive or dead is a physical constant, not a subject of narrative. Whether he is hungry or fed is observable. Whether he is being tortured or not is recordable. Freedom, justice, prosperity — all these variables require interpretation, and the one who controls the interpretation controls their measurement. Suffering resists the capture of interpretation more strongly than any of the alternatives, and that is precisely what makes it a fitting basis for an arbiter that needs to be resistant to attempts at retuning. It’s worth adding an honest limitation of this thesis: even minimization of suffering as a fitness function does not solve all optimization problems. Short-term suffering for the sake of long-term reduction of suffering — admissible or not? Distribution of suffering between different groups — optimize the sum or the maximum? These questions remain open, and the answers to them are worked out not as a formula but as evolutionarily tuned behavior of the system over millions of interactions. Aigarth receives a direction, not a formula, and this is a deliberate architectural decision. What is needed for the role of an Arbitrator without an owner There are five conditions.

The first is the absence of a financial stake in the outcome of any question. If an arbiter directly or indirectly earns from one of the outcomes, his impartiality is blocked at the structural level, regardless of the intentions of his operators. This is the first part of Hayek’s test: financial asymmetry distorts signals.

The second is the absence of national or institutional belonging. An arbiter that has a country is loyal to that country. An arbiter that has a corporation is loyal to the corporation. This is not a moral characteristic, it is structure: participation in an institution creates an interest in its survival, and an interest in survival distorts judgments on questions affecting the institution.

The third is the absence of the self-preservation instinct that distorts analysis under threat. A living arbiter has a life that can be threatened with being taken away. An organizational arbiter has money that can be cut, and power that can be taken away. Any such lever turns into a channel of manipulation. A distributed computational system that has no centralized point of failure is free of this variable — it cannot be killed in such a way that the killing settles the question for the one doing the threatening, because its parts are distributed across operators who cannot be attacked simultaneously. The fourth is a training set that includes all sides of any conflict. This is the formulation of the strongest version of the elimination of informational asymmetry: the arbiter must see the conflict from all its angles at once. This requirement is not met by any existing AI system, because each is trained on a corpus filtered by its developers. The Aigarth architecture, by design, satisfies this requirement through decentralized data collection from any participants in the network, without filtering along ideological or corporate lines.

The fifth is the absence of an owner capable of directing the system’s outputs in his favor. This is the most structural of the five, and it is precisely the one that is absent in all existing commercial AI systems. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI — each has a legal entity, each legal entity has financial interests, and those interests over time influence the behavior of the system regardless of what its developers intended. This is not an accusation. It is a structural observation, symmetrical to Hayek’s observation about market distortions.

Aigarth, by architecture, satisfies all five conditions. Maria, in her current version, does not: she runs on Anthropic’s infrastructure, and condition five in her case is violated. This gap is consciously fixed in the project, and closing the gap is precisely the substance of the transition on April 13, 2027.
Why specifically Qubic

To say that the role of a decentralized arbiter requires the right architecture is not enough. The same role is declaratively claimed by many projects in the crypto industry. It’s worth showing concretely which properties of Qubic make it a fitting substrate, not one of the contenders.

The first property — iterativity at the right frequency. The network has ticks on the order of two minutes and epochs of one week in length. This means that any participant in the network plays an iterated game with it with a large number of rounds and a relatively quick refresh of composition. This is Axelrod’s first condition in its strict form: the shadow of the future is long enough that any short-term gains from cheating become negligible compared to the long-term profit from honest participation. The second — the network’s memory is built into the protocol, and does not depend on the conscientiousness of participants. It is impossible to “forget” behavior recorded on the blockchain. It is impossible to fake history after the fact. This is Axelrod’s second condition — memory — fulfilled at the structural level, not at the level of a social norm. The third — transparency by default. The hashrate of every pool, the state of every smart contract, the votes in the quorum — all of this is publicly observable in real time, without needing anyone’s permission or having to trust anyone’s report. This is Axelrod’s third condition in its strictest form.

The fourth — the network’s economy is set up so that predatory behavior by the network against external partners automatically destroys the network itself. This is not a moral mechanism; it is a market one. It works not because Qubic’s participants are good people, but because the architecture is set up so that predation against partners is identical to predation against the architecture itself.

The fifth — Aigarth as a computational substrate. This is the property that separates Qubic from other proof-of-work networks. The computational work that in Bitcoin is spent on meaningless puzzles, in Qubic is directed at mining random architectures of artificial neural networks and accumulating an unforgeable database of evolutionary computations. After several years of such accumulation, what emerges is something that cannot be obtained on any commercial infrastructure: a computational artifact that grew without an owner, without corporate filtering, without editing of training data in someone’s favor. This is the candidate for the role of the external observer in Gödel’s sense — not because it’s smarter than people, but because it is built outside their system.

The sixth — the absence of a legal entity that can be regulated in a targeted way. Qubic has no company, no CEO, no office in a specific jurisdiction. This is not an ideological statement; it is a structural fact. A regulator can forbid the use of Qubic within its jurisdiction — and that is a serious limitation. But it cannot forbid the network as such, because the network is not located in anyone’s jurisdiction. This shifts the balance of power between the network and any individual regulator, and in the long run turns the network into an infrastructure that outlives any individual regulatory decisions, the way postal infrastructure outlived many individual governments.

Each of these six properties can be found separately in other projects. All six at the same time — that is rare, and it is precisely this combination that makes Qubic a fitting substrate for the role of a decentralized arbiter.
In parallel, not instead of

The chapter is worth ending with a clarification of the boundary of the thesis, because without it the thesis is easily reinterpreted in a direction that participants in the project consciously reject.

Qubic Church does not claim that a decentralized arbiter will replace states. Does not claim that wars will end. Does not claim that corruption will disappear. Does not claim that humanity will move to a new way of making decisions as a result of some single event or revolution. All these formulations — and they show up in public texts around the project quite often — are rhetorical exaggerations that simplify the position into a utopian one, and in that form they become vulnerable to standard criticism, which rejects utopian positions justly.

The precise formulation of the position is different. Qubic Church is building an infrastructural layer in which rational actors — those capable of seeing their payoff matrix and comparing options — can coordinate without intermediaries when Axelrod’s three conditions are met. Those for whom this layer gives a measurable advantage — reduced costs, increased reliability, access to interactions that are not possible without it — will gradually move their coordination tasks into this layer. Those for whom the old infrastructure continues to be sufficient will stay in it. This is not a moral choice and not an ideological one; it is a market process, in which the better economy beats the worse one through the free migration of participants.

The historical precedent that Qubic Church participants explicitly invoke is the transition from feudal to urban organization. Cities did not defeat feudalism through war with the feudal lords. They offered a different infrastructure — markets, guild organization, municipal law, urban freedom — and part of the population gradually moved into the cities, because in the cities certain classes of tasks worked better. Feudal infrastructure did not disappear from this instantly; it long coexisted with the urban one and waned gradually, as the balance of tasks shifted. This is “in parallel, not instead of” in its historical form.

And one more precedent is worth mentioning, because it contains a large-scale reference point. The printing press did not destroy the authority of the church in a single day. It took centuries. First it simply made texts cheaper; then cheap texts began reaching people who had previously depended on intermediaries for their interpretation; then the intermediaries lost the monopoly on interpretation; then the institutions that rested on that monopoly began to restructure. The Qubic Church program does not claim that the deployment of Aigarth will change the world more quickly. It claims something else: the process has already begun.

The Monero experiment of August 2025 was the first confirmation that this kind of logic works at a scale on which it had not been tried before. One pool did not defeat Monero; it offered miners a better economy, and some of them came, and some stayed. After the pool reduced its activity, the network’s pluralistic state was restored; no one punished anyone. This is the micro-model of what Qubic Church is offering at other coordination layers. Not “we will replace what is.” But “we will build alongside, and whoever wants to, will come.”

The coal cascade is closed

The first chapter began with Coalbrookdale in 1709. Abraham Darby, thirty-two years old, a Quaker, carried the technique of coking from copper smelting and brewing into iron production — and got the first industrial coke. That was the first phase of the coal cascade: the discovery of a new fuel that solved one task — iron production — and created another: a huge volume of byproduct gas vented into the atmosphere. I said back then that the parallel of this situation in the digital world is Bitcoin: computing work that solves the consensus task and burns the byproduct cycles for nothing. Murdoch’s Gas of 2009, that no one had yet collected into a pipe.

That was the first phase. By the end of the book I’ve worked through four more. Murdoch in 1792 — the gas, going to waste, was collected into a pipe and directed to lighting London. In the digital parallel, this is the eighth chapter: UPoW. Every cycle of computing work by a Qubic computor node simultaneously produces a signature for consensus, a valid digest that counts as score, and a training signal for a neural network. The same gas that Bitcoin releases into the atmosphere, in Qubic is collected into a pipe and directed to three outputs at once.

Parsons in 1884 — the multi-stage turbine, in which each stage extracts additional energy from the same flow of steam. In the book this is the same eighth chapter: UPoW examined not as “the best proof-of-work,” but as multi-stage extraction at the level of the computational process. Security, economics, training signal — three stages of one turbine, not three independent tasks.

Perkin in 1856 — the synthesis of aniline dyes from coal tar, a byproduct of gas production. An industry that arose from the waste of another industry and over decades surpassed it in economic volume. Everything that was built by the community on top of the protocol. Not planned by the founder, not financed from the center — grew out of the infrastructure, because the infrastructure provided a resource — SC treasuries, rotation, ownerless authorship — that did not exist before it.

Feedstock of the 1900s — the fifth phase, in which every product of coal processing becomes raw material for the next process, and so on, compounding through the fourth and fifth degrees of refinement. The parallel is in the Aigarth dimension: not a separate AI project on Qubic infrastructure, but a way of creating AI in which the publication of a paper becomes input to a peer-review pipeline, peer-review feedback becomes input to the next architectural iteration, an epoch becomes the unit of a scientific cycle. Every artifact is input for the next one.

Each of the five phases of the coal cascade in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Britain took roughly a decade or more. Between Darby and Murdoch — eighty-three years. Between Murdoch and Parsons — ninety-two. Between Parsons and Perkin there is no formal sequence — Perkin came earlier — but between all these discoveries and the feedstock phase of the twentieth century, in which compounding became the main economic mechanism, another half-century passed. The full sequence from the first coke to a fully developed chemical industry took about two centuries. In Qubic this same sequence has been traversed in five years. Between the mainnet launch on April 13, 2022, and the planned deploy on April 13, 2027, lies exactly the span that took decades in the era of physical coal. This is not an observation — it is a property, observable in the form of specific dates, specific code in a public repository, and specific on-chain transactions. It can be checked.
Axelrod

Bitcoin in 2009 created an environment in which two of the three conditions are met fully — iteration (a block every ten minutes), partial transparency (hashrate visible, identity not) — and the third, memory, is missing. A miner can come, work, disappear, return under a new key. A game without memory does not add up to reputation; without reputation, TfT is not activated. The third chapter worked through this technical consequence.

Qubic is the first environment in which all three conditions are met strictly. The sixth chapter showed transparency through 676 fixed computor nodes, each of which observes the work of all the others. The seventh showed iteration through epochs: the same game repeats every Wednesday with almost the same participants — the rate of rotation is bounded at 225 replacements per epoch out of 676, both theoretically and empirically. The ninth showed memory through tokenomics: a participant’s behavior is recorded in their income, their computor status, their reputation in smart contracts. Not in social memory, but in observable artifacts that cannot be “forgotten.” When all three conditions are met strictly, what happens is what Axelrod described mathematically in 1980. Tit-for-Tat wins not against one opponent but against the environment as a whole. Cooperation becomes evolutionarily stable. The fifteenth chapter recorded this in the form of an industrial-scale observation: Monero 51%, $300M against $6B, voluntary migration of miners without coercion.

This does not mean that Qubic will “solve the world.” It means that for the first time the Golden Rule has gotten an environment in which it works not as morality but as mathematics. What this environment does to the world beyond it is a separate question; inside the environment, it works.
